questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the reason for the solubility of polar solute in polar solvent from the following.
options: solute - solute interactions, solute solvent interactions and solvent - solvent interactions are of similar magnitude.
solute - solute interactions \gt  solute solvent interactions \gt  solvent - solvent . interactions .
solvent- solvent interactions \gt  solute solvent interactions \gt  solute - solute interactions.
solute - solvent interactions \gt  solute solute interactions \gt  solvent - solvent interactions.
questions.solution:
The solubility of a polar solute in a polar solvent is mainly due to the favorable interactions between the solute and solvent molecules. These interactions are crucial for the dissolution process.
The most appropriate explanation for this is when the solute-solvent interactions are comparable in magnitude to the solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions. This balance allows the solute to dissolve efficiently, as the solvent can break apart the solute molecules while maintaining similar intermolecular forces within the solvent.
Correct answer: (1) Solute-solute interactions, solute-solvent interactions, and solvent-solvent interactions are of similar magnitude. This describes a scenario where the polar solute can easily dissolve in the polar solvent due to similar intermolecular forces being at play in both the solute and the solvent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the relation between the vapour pressure of solution, vapour pressure of solvent and its mole fraction in the solution?
questions.solution:
The relation between the vapour pressure of the solution $\left(P_1\right)$, the vapour pressure of the pure solvent $\left(P_1^*\right)$, and the mole fraction of the solvent $\left(x_1\right)$ in the solution is given by Raoult's Law for an ideal solution.
Raoult's Law states: $P_1=P_1^* \cdot x_1$
Where: - $P_1$ is the vapour pressure of the solvent in the solution, - $P_1^*$ is the vapour pressure of the pure solvent, - $x_1$ is the mole fraction of the solvent in the solution. The correct relation is (1): $P_1=P_1^* \cdot x_1$

Calculate vapour pressure of a solution containing mixture of 2 moles of volatile liquid A and 3 moles of volatile liquid B at room temperature.
$\left(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}^{\circ}=420, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}^{\circ}=610 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}\right)$
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{x}_1=\frac{\mathrm{n}_1}{\mathrm{n}_1+\mathrm{n}_2}=\frac{2}{2+3}=0.4 \\
& \mathrm{x}_2=\frac{\mathrm{n}_1}{\mathrm{n}_1+\mathrm{n}_2}=\frac{3}{2+3}=0.6 \\
& \mathrm{P}_{\text {solution }}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}^0 \mathrm{x}_1+\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}^0 \mathrm{x}_2 \\
& =420 \times 0.4+610 \times 0.6 \\
& =168+366 \\
& =534 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Calculate the molality of solution of non volatile solute having depression in freezing point 0.93 K and cryoscopic constant of solvent $1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A solution of non volatile solute is obtained by dissolving 2 g in 50 g benzene. Calculate the vapour pressure of solution if vapour pressure of pure benzene is 640 mmHg at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
[mol. mass of benzene $=78 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, mol. mass of solute $\left.=64 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \quad \frac{\Delta \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{P}^0}= & \frac{\mathrm{P}^0-\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{P}^0}=\mathrm{x}_2=\frac{\mathrm{W}_2 \mathrm{M}_1}{\mathrm{~W}_1 \mathrm{M}_2} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{640-\mathrm{P}}{640} & =\frac{2 \times 78}{50 \times 64} \\ 640-\mathrm{P} & =640 \times 0.048 \\ \mathrm{P} & =640-31.2 \\ \mathrm{P} & =608.8 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A solution of nonvolatile solute is obtained by dissolving $15 \mathrm{~g}$ in $200 \mathrm{~mL}$ water has depression in freezing point $0.75 \mathrm{~K}$. Calculate the molar mass of solute if cryoscopic constant of water is $1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the depression in freezing point of solution when $4 \mathrm{~g}$ nonvolatile solute of molar mass $126 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ dissolved in $80 \mathrm{~mL}$ water. $\left[\right.$ Cryoscopic constant of water $\left.=1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If $0.01 \mathrm{~m}$ aqueous solution of an electrolyte freezes at $-0.056{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Calculate van't Hoff factor for an electrolyte. (Cryoscopic constant of water $=1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )

$\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathrm{i} \times \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}} \times \mathrm{m}0.056=\mathrm{i} \times 1.86 \times 0.01\therefore \quad \mathrm{i}=\frac{0.056}{1.86 \times 0.01}=3.01$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A solution of $5.6 \mathrm{~g}$ nonvolatile solute in $50 \mathrm{~g}$ solvent has elevation in boiling point $1.75 \mathrm{~K}$. What is the molar mass of solute $\left(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}=3 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$ ?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the molal elevation constant if one gram mole of a nonvolatile solute is dissolved in $1 \mathrm{~kg}$ of ethyl acetate? $\left(\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}}=x \mathrm{~K}\right)$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{M}_2=\frac{1000 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{W}_2}{\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{W}_1} \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\mathrm{M}_2 \Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{W}_1}{1000 \mathrm{~W}_2} \\ & \mathrm{Now}, \mathrm{W}_2=\text { one gram mole }=\mathrm{M}_2 \mathrm{~g} \\ & \mathrm{~W}_1=1 \mathrm{~kg}=1000 \mathrm{~g} \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\mathrm{M}_2 \times x \times 1000}{1000 \times \mathrm{M}_2}=x \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If $0.15 \mathrm{~m}$ aqueous solution of $\mathrm{KCI}$ freezes at $-0.51^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, calculate van't Hoff factor of $\mathrm{KCI}$ (cryoscopic constant of water is $1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution: $\begin{array}{ll} & \Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}^0-\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=0-\left(-0.51^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=0.51{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=0.51 \mathrm{~K} \\ \therefore & \Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathrm{iK}_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore & \mathrm{i}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{m}}=\frac{0.51 \mathrm{~K}}{1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \times 0.15 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1}}=1.82\end{array}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A solution of nonvolatile solute is obtained by dissolving $1.5 \mathrm{~g}$ in $30 \mathrm{~g}$ solvent has boiling point elevation $0.65 \mathrm{~K}$. Calculate the molal elevation constant if molar mass of solute is $150 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following aqueous solutions will exhibit the highest boiling point?
questions.solution:
Elevation in boiling point is a colligative property which depends upon the number of solute particles.
Greater the number of solute particles in a solution, higher the extent of elevation in boiling point.
Na 2 SO 4 ⟶ 2 Na + + SO 4 2 -  . On complete dissociation, i=3  

Δ T b KNO 3 = i  K b · m i = 2

Δ T b urea = i K b · m i  = 1

Δ T b glucose = i K b · m i  = 1

Δ T b Na 2 SO 4 = i  K b · m i = 3

The Van't Hoff factor is the highest for Na2SO4 and will exhibit the highest boiling point.

A true solution is a homogeneous mixture with consistent properties. Filtration cannot separate the solute from the solution in a true solution. The solute's particle size is around the same as the solvent's, and the solvent and solute move through the filter paper together.

questions.q: Maximum depression in freezing point is caused by

Depression in freezing point is a colligative property, so depends upon the number of particles. Among, potassium chloride (KCl), sodium $\quad$ sulphate $\quad\left(\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}\right), \quad$ magnesium sulphate $\left(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\right)$ and magnesium carbonate $\left(\mathrm{MgCO}_{3}\right), \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ produces maximum number

Thus, it causes maximum depression in freezing point.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the number of molecules in 2.125 g of ammonia?
questions.solution:
Molar mass of ammonia ($NH_3$) = $14 + 3 = 17 \text{ g/mol}$

Number of moles of ammonia = $\dfrac{2.125}{17} = 0.125 \text{ mol}$

Number of molecules = $0.125 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 7.527 \times 10^{22}$

Answer: $7.527 \times 10^{22}$

questions.q: What is the SI unit of luminous intensity ?
questions.solution:
Luminous intensity is one of the seven fundamental base quantities in the International System of Units (SI).

The SI unit of luminous intensity is the candela (cd).

Ampere is the SI unit of electric current, Coulomb is the SI unit of electric charge, and Ohm is the SI unit of electrical resistance.

Answer: Candela

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is average atomic mass of chlorine if its two isotopes $\text{Cl}^{35}$ and $\text{Cl}^{37}$ exists in relative abundance of $75\%$ and $25\%$ respectively ?
questions.solution:
Average atomic mass is calculated using the formula:

Average atomic mass = $\dfrac{m_1 \times p_1 + m_2 \times p_2}{100}$

where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the atomic masses of the isotopes, and $p_1$ and $p_2$ are their respective percentage abundances.

Substituting the given values:

Average atomic mass = $\dfrac{35 \times 75 + 37 \times 25}{100}$

Average atomic mass = $\dfrac{2625 + 925}{100}$

Average atomic mass = $\dfrac{3550}{100} = 35.5$

Answer: $35.5$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Chlorine has two isotopes $\text{Cl}^{37}$ and $\text{Cl}^{35}$ with percentage abundance of $25\%$ and $75\%$ respectively. Find average atomic mass of chlorine ?
questions.solution:
Average atomic mass is calculated using the formula:

$\text{Average atomic mass} = \dfrac{\sum (\text{Isotopic mass} \times \text{Percentage abundance})}{100}$

Substituting the given values:

$\text{Average atomic mass} = \dfrac{37 \times 25 + 35 \times 75}{100}$

$\text{Average atomic mass} = \dfrac{925 + 2625}{100}$

$\text{Average atomic mass} = \dfrac{3550}{100} = 35.5$

Answer: $35.5$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What quantity of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in gram is present in $0.25$ mol of it?
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O} = 2 \times 1 + 16 = 18 \text{ g/mol}$

Mass of $\text{H}_2\text{O} = \text{moles} \times \text{molar mass}$

Mass $= 0.25 \times 18 = 4.5 \text{ g}$

Answer: $4.5$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the percentage atom economy when formula weight of product is $65$ u and the sum of formula weight of reactant is $130$ u?
questions.solution:
The percentage atom economy is calculated using the formula:

$\text{Percentage atom economy} = \dfrac{\text{Formula weight of desired product}}{\text{Sum of formula weights of all reactants}} \times 100$

Substituting the given values:

$\text{Percentage atom economy} = \dfrac{65}{130} \times 100 = 50\%$

Answer: $50\%$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the number of molecules present in 70 g dinitrogen.
questions.solution:
Molar mass of dinitrogen ($N_2$) is $28 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $N_2$ = $\dfrac{70}{28} = 2.5 \text{ mol}$

Number of molecules = $n \times N_A$

Number of molecules = $2.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.5055 \times 10^{24}$

Answer: $1.5055 \times 10^{24}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: How many moles of potassium chlorate are heated to produce $22.4\ \text{lit}$ of oxygen at STP ?
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the thermal decomposition of potassium chlorate is:

$2KClO_3 \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_2$

At STP, $22.4\ \text{lit}$ of oxygen gas corresponds to $1\ \text{mole}$ of $O_2$.

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $3\ \text{moles}$ of $O_2$ are produced by heating $2\ \text{moles}$ of $KClO_3$.

Therefore, the number of moles of $KClO_3$ required to produce $1\ \text{mole}$ of $O_2$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}\ \text{mole}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}\ \text{mole}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: How many moles of potassium chlorate are heated to produce $11 \cdot 2$ L oxygen at STP ?
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the decomposition of potassium chlorate is:

$2KClO_{3} \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_{2}$

At STP, the volume of $1$ mole of an ideal gas is $22 \cdot 4$ L.

Number of moles of $O_{2}$ produced is:

$n(O_{2}) = \dfrac{11 \cdot 2}{22 \cdot 4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ mole

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, $3$ moles of $O_{2}$ are produced from $2$ moles of $KClO_{3}$.

Therefore, the number of moles of $KClO_{3}$ required to produce $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mole of $O_{2}$ is:

$n(KClO_{3}) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times n(O_{2}) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ mole

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$ mole

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the number of molecules present in 2.24 $\text{dm}^3$ of carbon dioxide at STP ?
questions.solution:
Volume of $\text{CO}_2$ at STP = $2.24 \text{ dm}^3 = 2.24 \text{ L}$

Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP = $22.4 \text{ L}$

Number of moles of $\text{CO}_2 = \dfrac{2.24}{22.4} = 0.1 \text{ mol}$

Number of molecules = Number of moles $\times N_A$

Number of molecules = $0.1 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{22}$

Answer: $6.022 \times 10^{22}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The ratio of mass of 'x' atoms of an element to mass of carbon atoms is 9:1. Find the mass of 1 mol of x if molar mass of carbon is 12 g/mol.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of one atom of element 'x' be $m_x$ and the mass of one carbon atom be $m_C$.

Given that the ratio of the mass of an atom of element 'x' to the mass of a carbon atom is $9:1$, we have:

$\dfrac{m_x}{m_C} = \dfrac{9}{1}$

The ratio of their molar masses is equal to the ratio of their atomic masses:

$\dfrac{M_x}{M_C} = 9$

Given the molar mass of carbon, $M_C = 12\ \text{g/mol}$, the molar mass of element 'x' is:

$M_x = 9 \times 12 = 108\ \text{g/mol}$

Therefore, the mass of $1\ \text{mol}$ of element 'x' is $108\ \text{g}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the amount of aluminium present in $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ if the compound contains 4 g of sulfur.
[Molar mass of sulfur = 32 g/mol , Molar mass of Al =27 g/mol ]
questions.solution:
In one mole of $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$, there are $2$ moles of Al and $3$ moles of S.

Mass of Al in $1$ mole of compound $= 2 \times 27 = 54$ g

Mass of S in $1$ mole of compound $= 3 \times 32 = 96$ g

The ratio of the mass of Al to the mass of S in the compound is $\dfrac{54}{96} = \dfrac{9}{16}$.

Given the mass of S is $4$ g, the mass of Al is calculated as:

Mass of Al $= 4 \times \dfrac{9}{16} = \dfrac{9}{4} = 2.25$ g

Answer: $2.25$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is number of hydrogen molecules needed to synthesize 3.4 g of ammonia by reaction with nitrogen?
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the synthesis of ammonia is:

$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3$

Molar mass of $NH_3 = 14 + 3 \times 1 = 17 \text{ g/mol}$

Moles of $NH_3$ to be synthesized $= \dfrac{3.4}{17} = 0.2 \text{ mol}$

From the balanced equation, $2 \text{ moles}$ of $NH_3$ require $3 \text{ moles}$ of $H_2$.

Moles of $H_2$ required $= \dfrac{3}{2} \times 0.2 = 0.3 \text{ mol}$

Number of $H_2$ molecules $= 0.3 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.8066 \times 10^{23}$

Answer: $1.8066 \times 10^{23}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Find the mass of sodium carbonate in grams to form 100 ml 0.1 M solution in water?
( Molar mass of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ = 106 g/mol)
questions.solution:
Molarity is given by the formula:

$M = \dfrac{n}{V \text{ (in L)}}$

Substituting the given values:

$0.1 = \dfrac{n}{0.1}$

$n = 0.01$ moles

Mass of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ is calculated as:

$w = n \times \text{Molar mass}$

$w = 0.01 \times 106 = 1.06$ g

Answer: $1.06$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the approximate mass of the precipitate formed when $50$ mL of $16.9\%$ solution of $\text{AgNO}_3$ is mixed with $50$ mL of $7.45\%$ KCl solution? (Molar mass of $\text{AgNO}_3 = 169$ g/mol, KCl $= 74.5$ g/mol, AgCl $= 143.3$ g/mol)
questions.solution:
Mass of $\text{AgNO}_3$ in $50$ mL of $16.9\%$ (w/v) solution $= \dfrac{16.9}{100} \times 50 = 8.45$ g

Moles of $\text{AgNO}_3 = \dfrac{8.45}{169} = 0.05$ mol

Mass of KCl in $50$ mL of $7.45\%$ (w/v) solution $= \dfrac{7.45}{100} \times 50 = 3.725$ g

Moles of KCl $= \dfrac{3.725}{74.5} = 0.05$ mol

The balanced chemical equation is:
$\text{AgNO}_3 + \text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{AgCl} \downarrow + \text{KNO}_3$

Since $1$ mole of $\text{AgNO}_3$ reacts with $1$ mole of KCl to give $1$ mole of AgCl, $0.05$ mol of $\text{AgNO}_3$ will react completely with $0.05$ mol of KCl to form $0.05$ mol of AgCl.

Mass of AgCl precipitate $= 0.05 \times 143.3 = 7.165$ g $\approx 7$ g

Answer: $7$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $1$ g of $\text{H}_2$ contains the same number of molecules as in
questions.solution:
Number of moles of $\text{H}_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$ mol.

Number of moles of $\text{N}_2$ in $14$ g $= \dfrac{14}{28} = 0.5$ mol.

Number of moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in $18$ g $= \dfrac{18}{18} = 1$ mol.

Number of moles of $\text{CO}$ in $16$ g $= \dfrac{16}{28} = \dfrac{4}{7}$ mol.

Number of moles of $\text{N}_2$ in $28$ g $= \dfrac{28}{28} = 1$ mol.

Since the number of moles of $1$ g of $\text{H}_2$ and $14$ g of $\text{N}_2$ are equal, they contain the same number of molecules.

Answer: $14$ g of $\text{N}_2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following contains maximum number of molecules?
questions.solution:
The number of molecules is directly proportional to the number of moles.

Number of moles of $\text{H}_2$ in $0.4$ g = $\dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2$ mol

Number of moles of $\text{O}_2$ in $3.2$ g = $\dfrac{3.2}{32} = 0.1$ mol

Number of moles of $\text{H}_2$ in $16.8 \text{ dm}^3$ at STP = $\dfrac{16.8}{22.4} = 0.75$ mol

Number of moles of $\text{O}_2$ in $11.2 \text{ dm}^3$ at STP = $\dfrac{11.2}{22.4} = 0.5$ mol

Since $0.75$ mol is the maximum among the given options, $16.8 \text{ dm}^3$ of $\text{H}_2$ gas at STP contains the maximum number of molecules.

Answer: $16.8 \text{ dm}^3$ of $\text{H}_2$ gas at STP

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the volume of $99$ g of $\text{CO}_2$ at STP ?
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\text{CO}_2 = 12 + 2 \times 16 = 44 \text{ g/mol}$

Number of moles of $\text{CO}_2 = \dfrac{99}{44} = 2.25 \text{ moles}$

Volume of $1 \text{ mole}$ of a gas at STP $= 22.4 \text{ L}$

Volume of $2.25 \text{ moles}$ of $\text{CO}_2 = 2.25 \times 22.4 = 50.4 \text{ L}$

Answer: $50.4$ L

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the mass of $100$ molecules of oxygen in amu and in grams.
questions.solution:
Mass of one oxygen molecule ($O_2$) = $2 \times 16$ u = $32$ u.

Mass of $100$ oxygen molecules = $100 \times 32$ u = $3200$ u.

Since $1$ u = $1.6605 \times 10^{-24}$ g, the mass in grams is given by:

Mass = $3200 \times 1.6605 \times 10^{-24}$ g = $5.314 \times 10^{-21}$ g.

Answer: $3200$ u and $5.314 \times 10^{-21}$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the number of hydrogen atoms present in 5.4 g of urea?
questions.solution:
Number of hydrogen atoms in 5.4 g of urea

Urea has the formula CO(NH_{2}$)_{2}$, with a molar mass of approximately 60 g/mol (simplified from 60.062 g/mol for calculation). In one molecule, there are 4 hydrogen atoms.

The number of moles in 5.4 g is $n = \frac{5.4}{60} = 0.09$ mol.

Using Avogadro's number, $N_{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$, the number of hydrogen atoms is $0.09 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 4 = 2.168 \times 10^{23}$.

This corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate mass of 0.25 mole of iron (molar mass $=56 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
The mass $m$ of a substance is given by $m = n \times M$, where $n$ is the number of moles and $M$ is the molar mass.

For iron, with $n = 0.25\,\text{mol}$ and $M = 56\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}$, the mass is $m = 0.25 \times 56 = 14\,\text{g}$.

Converting to kilograms: $14\,\text{g} = 14 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg} = 0.014\,\text{kg}$.

In scientific notation, the mass is $1.4 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg}$, which corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate number of molecules present in 5.4 g of urea (Molar mass of urea $=60 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
The number of moles $n$ is determined from the given mass and molar mass: $n = \frac{5.4}{60} = 0.09 \text{ mol}$.

Multiplying by Avogadro's number yields the number of molecules: $0.09 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 5.4198 \times 10^{22}$.

Comparing with the options, the value $5.419 \times 10^{22}$ corresponds to choice B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find out the total number of electrons present in 3.2 g methane?
questions.solution:
The total number of electrons is determined by calculating the number of molecules and multiplying by the electrons per molecule.

The molar mass of methane (C$H_4$) is $12 + 4 \cdot 1 = 16$ g/mol.

The number of moles in 3.2 g is $3.2 / 16 = 0.2$ mol.

Using Avogadro's number, the number of molecules is $0.2 \cdot 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.2044 \times 10^{23}$.

Each methane molecule has $6 + 4 = 10$ electrons, so the total number is $1.2044 \times 10^{23} \cdot 10 = 1.2044 \times 10^{24}$.

This value corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the volume of 56 g dinitrogen at STP
questions.solution:
The molar mass of dinitrogen (N2) is 28 g/mol, calculated from the atomic mass of nitrogen (14 g/mol).

The number of moles in 56 g of dinitrogen is $n = \frac{56}{28} = 2$ moles.

At STP, one mole of gas occupies 22.4 liters, so the volume is $2 \times 22.4 = 44.8$ liters.

The volume of 56 g of dinitrogen at STP is 44.8 liters.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The vapour density of a certain gas is 16. What is the volume occupied by 8 g of gas at STP assuming ideal behaviour?
questions.solution:
Vapour density (VD) relates to molar mass via $M = 2 \times VD$.

Given $VD = 16$, the molar mass is $M = 2 \times 16 = 32 \text{ g/mol}$.

For a mass of $8 \text{ g}$, the number of moles is $n = \frac{8}{32} = 0.25 \text{ mol}$.

At STP, one mole occupies $22.4 \text{ dm}^3$, so $0.25 \text{ mol}$ occupies $0.25 \times 22.4 = 5.6 \text{ dm}^3$.

The volume is $5.6 \text{ dm}^3$, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find out total number of electrons present in 1.6 g methane?
questions.solution:
The molar mass of methane, $\mathrm{CH_4}$, is $12\ \mathrm{g/mol} + 4 \times 1\ \mathrm{g/mol} = 16\ \mathrm{g/mol}$.

Given mass is $1.6\ \mathrm{g}$, so the number of moles is $\frac{1.6}{16} = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Using Avogadro's number, $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, the number of molecules is $0.1 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{22}$.

Each $\mathrm{CH_4}$ molecule contains $6 + 4 \times 1 = 10$ electrons.

The total number of electrons is $6.022 \times 10^{22} \times 10 = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\mathrm{A}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the number of millimoles for 0.160 g sodium hydroxide.
questions.solution:
The number of millimoles of sodium hydroxide in a $0.160$ g sample is determined by first calculating its molar mass.

The molar mass of NaOH is $22.99 + 16.00 + 1.01 = 40.00$ g/mol.

Converting mass to moles gives $\frac{0.160}{40.00} = 0.004$ mol.

Since $1$ mole equals $1000$ millimoles, the millimole quantity is $0.004 \times 1000 = 4$ mmol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the number of moles present in $1 \mathrm{~m}^3$ of any gas at STP?
questions.solution:
The molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (0°C and 1 atm) is 22.4 L/mol. Since $1 \mathrm{m}^3 = 1000$ L, the number of moles in $1 \mathrm{m}^3$ is given by $n = \frac{1000}{22.4} \approx 44.6$ mol.


Final answer: 44.6 mol

questions.q: A gaseous mixture of $\mathrm{O}_2$ and $\mathrm{CH}_4$ are in the ratio $1: 4$ by mass. Find the ratio of their molecules.
questions.solution:
Ratio of molecules is proportional to the ratio of moles. Given mass ratio $m_{\mathrm{O}_2} : m_{\mathrm{CH}_4} = 1 : 4$, let $m_{\mathrm{O}_2} = x$ and $m_{\mathrm{CH}_4} = 4x$.

Using molar masses $M_{\mathrm{O}_2} = 32$ g/mol and $M_{\mathrm{CH}_4} = 16$ g/mol, the moles are:

$n_{\mathrm{O}_2} = \frac{x}{32}$,
$n_{\mathrm{CH}_4} = \frac{4x}{16} = \frac{x}{4}$.

The ratio $n_{\mathrm{O}_2} : n_{\mathrm{CH}_4} = \frac{x}{32} : \frac{x}{4} = 1 : 8$.

Thus, the molecular ratio is $\boxed{1:8}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the difference in molar masses of Undecane and Decane?
questions.solution:
Molar mass difference between undecane and decane

Alkanes follow the general formula $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$. Both undecane and decane belong to this homologous series where successive members differ by a $\mathrm{CH_2}$ unit, which has a molar mass of $12 + (2 \times 1) = 14$ g mol$^{-1}$.

The molar mass of $\mathrm{CH_2}$ corresponds precisely to the mass difference between consecutive alkanes:
$\mathrm{C_{11}H_{24} - C_{10}H_{22} = CH_2}$

Therefore, the difference is $14$ g mol$^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the number of water molecules in 1 mL of water vapours at STP?
questions.solution:
Calculating water molecules in 1 mL vapor at STP

Standard Temperature and Pressure conditions define molar gas volume as 22.4 L/mol. For water vapor occupying $1 \text{ mL} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ L}$, the number of moles is $n = \frac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{22.4} = \frac{1}{22400} \text{ mol}$.

Using Avogadro's number $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \text{ molecules/mol}$, the molecular count becomes $n \times N_A = \frac{1}{22400} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}$.

This simplifies to approximately $2.69 \times 10^{19}$ molecules, corresponding to option D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the number of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions in 222 g unhydrous calcium chloride ? (At. mass $\mathrm{Ca}=40, \mathrm{Cl}=35 \cdot 5$ )
questions.solution:
To calculate the number of chloride ions in $222\text{ g}$ of anhydrous calcium chloride, first determine the molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}$ which is $40\times1 + 35.5\times2 = 111\text{ g/mol}$.

The number of moles is $\frac{222}{111} = 2$ moles of $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}$.

Each entity of $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}$ dissociates into two chloride ions, so the moles of $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions are $2\times2=4$ moles.

Multiplying by Avogadro's constant $\mathrm{N_{A}}$ gives the number of ions as $4 \times \mathrm{N_{A}}$.

This corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is vapour density of $\mathrm{O}_2$ gas?
questions.solution:
The vapour density of a gas is defined as $\text{VD} = \frac{M}{2}$, where $M$ represents the molar mass.

For molecular oxygen $\mathrm{O}_2$, the molar mass is $2 \times 16 = 32$ g/mol.

Substituting into the vapour density formula yields $\frac{32}{2} = 16$.

Among the given options, the correct value is B) $16$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The mass of $4.48 \mathrm{dm}^3$ of certain gas is 5.6 g at STP. Assuming ideal behaviour, identify the probable gas from following.
questions.solution:
The molar mass is determined from the gas sample's mass and volume at STP, where 1 mole occupies $22.4\ \mathrm{dm}^3$.

The number of moles is $n = \frac{4.48\ \mathrm{dm}^3}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm}^3\cdot\mathrm{mol}^{-1}} = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Molar mass is calculated as $M = \frac{5.6\ \mathrm{g}}{0.2\ \mathrm{mol}} = 28\ \mathrm{g}\cdot\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$.

Comparing with the options: C $\mathrm{N}_2$ ($2 \times 14 = 28\ \mathrm{g}\cdot\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$) matches the calculated molar mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the number of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ ion in 222 g anhydrous calcium chloride? (At. mass $\mathrm{Ca}=40, \mathrm{Cl}=35 \cdot 5$ )
questions.solution:
Calculating $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ ions in 222 g of $\mathrm{CaCl}_2$

The molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_2$ is calculated from atomic masses: $\mathrm{Ca} = 40$ g/mol, $\mathrm{Cl} = 35.5$ g/mol.
$\mathrm{CaCl}_2 = 40 + 2 \times 35.5 = 111$ g/mol

The number of moles present is: $\frac{222}{111} = 2$ moles

Each mole of $\mathrm{CaCl}_2$ contains 1 mole of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ ions, giving 2 moles of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ ions.
The total number of ions is: $2 \times \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}} = 2\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$

questions.q: What is the mass in grams of 0.25 mol water?

Molar mass of water is calculated from its chemical formula $\mathrm{H_2O}$ using atomic masses: $M(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 2 \times 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015$ g/mol.

Mass for 0.25 mol is given by $m = n \times M = 0.25 \times 18.015 = 4.50375$ g.

Rounded to one decimal place, the mass is 4.5 g, corresponding to option C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the mass of potassium chloride required to liberate $5.6 \mathrm{~dm}^3$ of oxygen gas at STP ? (molar mass of $\mathrm{KClO}_3=122.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ )
questions.solution:
The decomposition of potassium chlorate yields potassium chloride and oxygen gas, described by the balanced chemical equation:

$2\mathrm{KClO}_3(s) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KCl}(s) + 3\mathrm{O}_2(g)$

Given $5.6\ \mathrm{dm}^3$ of oxygen gas liberated at STP, where the molar volume is $22.4\ \mathrm{dm}^3/\mathrm{mol}$, the amount of oxygen is $\frac{5.6}{22.4} = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Using stoichiometry from the reaction, $3\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{O}_2$ require $2\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{KClO}_3$. Thus, $0.25\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{O}_2$ requires $0.25 \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{6}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{KClO}_3$.

The molar mass of $\mathrm{KClO}_3$ is $122.5\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, so the required mass is $\frac{1}{6} \times 122.5 \approx 20.42\ \mathrm{g}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In a chemical reaction, sum of formula weight of all reactants is 274 u and atom economy is $50 \%$, calculate formula weight of desired product?
questions.solution:
Given a reaction's total formula weight is $274 \text{ u}$ and its atom economy is $50\%$, the formula weight of the desired product can be found from the atom economy formula.

Atom economy is defined as $\frac{\text{formula weight of desired product}}{\text{sum of formula weights of all reactants}} \times 100\%$, which becomes $50\% = \frac{X}{274} \times 100\%$.

Dividing both sides by $100\%$ gives $0.50 = \frac{X}{274}$, so $X = 0.50 \times 274$.

$X = 137$

The desired product has a formula weight of $137 \text{ u}$, corresponding to answer choice A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which law is illustrated by compounds $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2$ formed from two different elements, H and O ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is (3) Law of Multiple Proportions. Explanation: The Law of Multiple Proportions states that when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the different masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in simple whole number ratios. - $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ (water) and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2$ (hydrogen peroxide) are two compounds formed by the combination of hydrogen (H) and oxygen ( O ). - In $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$, the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2:1. - In $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2$, the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2:1 again, but the total amount of oxygen is doubled in $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2$ compared to $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.
This fits the Law of Multiple Proportions, as these two compounds involve different ratios of oxygen atoms that combine with a fixed amount of hydrogen.

questions.q: Chlorine exists in two isotopic forms ${ }^{35} \mathrm{Cl},{ }^{37} \mathrm{Cl}$. If average atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5 , what is the percentage abundance of these isotopes respectively?
questions.solution:
Average atomic mass atomic mass of ${ }^{35} \mathrm{Cl} \times$ percentage $=\frac{+ \text { atomic mass of }{ }^{37} \mathrm{Cl} \times \text { percentage }}{100}$
Let the $\%$ abundance of ${ }^{35} \mathrm{Cl}$ isotope $=x$. $\%$ abundance of ${ }^{37} \mathrm{Cl}$ isotope $=100-x$. Average atomic mass $=35.5$ From formula, Average atomic mass $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{35 \times x+37 \times(100-x)}{100}=35.5 \\ & 35 x+3700-37 x=35.5 \times 100 \\ & -2 x=-3700+3550 \\ & 2 x=150 \\ & x=75 \end{aligned}$
Percentage abundance of ${ }^{35} \mathrm{Cl}=75 \% \text { and }{ }^{37} \mathrm{Cl}=(100-75)=25 \%$

Let the $\%$ abundance of ${ }^{35} \mathrm{Cl}$ isotope $=x$. $\%$ abundance of ${ }^{37} \mathrm{Cl}$ isotope $=100-x$. Average atomic mass $=35.5$ From formula, average atomic mass $=\frac{35 \times x+37 \times(100-x)}{100}=35.5\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & 35 x+3700-37 x=35.5 \times 100 \\ \therefore & -2 x=-3700+3550 \\ \therefore & -2 x=-150 \\ \therefore \quad & x=75 \% \text { and }(100-x)=25 \% \end{array} \\ Ratio of relative abundance $=\frac{\% \text { abundance of }{ }^{35} \mathrm{Cl}}{\% \text { abundance of }{ }^{37} \mathrm{Cl}}=\frac{75}{25}=3: 1

questions.solution:
The element O and H combine separately with the third element P to form P2O3 and PH3 respectively and directly combine to form H2O. In PH3, 31 parts by mass of P combine with 3 parts by mass of H and in P2O3, 62  parts by mass of P combine with 48 parts by mass of O. Thus the masses of H and O which combines with fixed mass of H(say 62 parts by mass) are 6 and 48 and they bear the ratio of 1:8

Now in H2O, 2 parts by mass of H combines with 16 parts by mass of O. So, they combine in ratio 2:16 which is equal to 1:8 which is same as the first ratio.

The sum of the percentage of carbon, hydrogen, and chlorine is not $100 \%$

percentage of oxygen $=100-(18.6+1.55+55.04)=24.81 \%$

Therefore molecular formula $=\mathrm{n} \times($ Empiricalformula $)$

Molecular formula $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{Cl}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}$

For this we make a table as:
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline Elemen & \%Compositio & Atomic & Mole & Simple Ratio \\
\hline \mathrm{t} & \mathrm{n} & Mass & Ratio & \\
\hline \mathrm{C} & 40.00 \% & 12 & (40 / 12) & (3 \cdot 33 / 3 \cdot 33)=1 \\
\hline \mathrm{H} & 6.67 \% & 1 & (6.67 / 1) & (6.667 / 3 \cdot 33)=2 \\
\hline \mathrm{O} & 53.33 \% & 16 & (53 \cdot 33 / 16 & (3 \cdot 33 / 3 \cdot 33)=1 \\
\hline
\end{array}
$\therefore$ Formula of compound is $=\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Molecular formula mass $=180$
Empirical formula mass $=12+2+16=30\mathrm{n}=180 / 30=6$

questions.q: A mixture of 0.5 mol $\text{N}_2$ gas, 1.0 mol $\text{O}_2$ gas and 1.5 mol $\text{H}_2$ gas exerts a total pressure of 18 bar. Find the partial pressure of $\text{O}_{2(g)}$.
questions.solution:
Total number of moles in the mixture is:

$n_{total} = n_{N_2} + n_{O_2} + n_{H_2}$

$n_{total} = 0.5 + 1.0 + 1.5 = 3.0$ mol

Mole fraction of $\text{O}_2$ is:

$x_{O_2} = \dfrac{n_{O_2}}{n_{total}} = \dfrac{1.0}{3.0} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, the partial pressure of $\text{O}_2$ is:

$P_{O_2} = x_{O_2} \times P_{total}$

$P_{O_2} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 18 = 6.0$ bar

Answer: $6.0$ bar

$n = \dfrac{441.6}{2208}$

$n = 0.2$ mole

Answer: $0.2$ mole

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A container contains mixture of He and Ne gases at certain temperature. He is 20 % by mass of mixture. What is the ratio of partial pressure of Helium to Neon ?
questions.solution:
Let the total mass of the mixture be $100$ g.

Mass of He $= 20$ g

Mass of Ne $= 80$ g

Molar mass of He $= 4$ g/mol

Molar mass of Ne $= 20$ g/mol

Number of moles of He, $n_{\text{He}} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5$

Number of moles of Ne, $n_{\text{Ne}} = \dfrac{80}{20} = 4$

According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, the ratio of partial pressures is equal to the ratio of number of moles.

$\dfrac{P_{\text{He}}}{P_{\text{Ne}}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{He}}}{n_{\text{Ne}}} = \dfrac{5}{4}$

Answer: $5:4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What ratio by mass of 'Ne' and $\text{CH}_4$ should be mixed so that partial pressure exerted by each gas is same?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of Ne be $w_1$ and the mass of $\text{CH}_4$ be $w_2$.

Molar mass of Ne $= 20 \text{ g/mol}$
Molar mass of $\text{CH}_4 = 16 \text{ g/mol}$

Number of moles of Ne, $n_{\text{Ne}} = \dfrac{w_1}{20}$
Number of moles of $\text{CH}_4$, $n_{\text{CH}_4} = \dfrac{w_2}{16}$

According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, the partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is directly proportional to its number of moles. Since the partial pressures of both gases are equal, their number of moles must be equal.

$n_{\text{Ne}} = n_{\text{CH}_4}$

$\dfrac{w_1}{20} = \dfrac{w_2}{16}$

$\dfrac{w_1}{w_2} = \dfrac{20}{16} = \dfrac{5}{4}$

The required ratio by mass is $5:4$.

Answer: $5:4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A gas at $10\,^\circ\text{C}$ occupies a volume of 283 mL. if it is heated to $20\,^\circ\text{C}$ keeping the pressure constant. What is the new volume of gas ?
questions.solution:
According to Charles's Law, at constant pressure, $\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}$

Given:
$V_1 = 283 \text{ mL}$
$T_1 = 10\,^\circ\text{C} = 10 + 273 = 283 \text{ K}$
$T_2 = 20\,^\circ\text{C} = 20 + 273 = 293 \text{ K}$

Substituting the values:
$\dfrac{283}{283} = \dfrac{V_2}{293}$

$V_2 = 293 \text{ mL}$

Answer: $293 \text{ mL}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $V_0$ and $V_t$ are volumes of an ideal gas at $0\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $t\ ^\circ\text{C}$ respectively, find ratio $\dfrac{V_t}{V_0}$
questions.solution:
According to Charles's law, at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.

$V \propto T$

$\dfrac{V_t}{V_0} = \dfrac{T_t}{T_0}$

The absolute temperatures are $T_0 = 273\text{ K}$ and $T_t = (273 + t)\text{ K}$.

$\dfrac{V_t}{V_0} = \dfrac{273 + t}{273}$

$\dfrac{V_t}{V_0} = 1 + \dfrac{t}{273}$

Answer: $1 + \dfrac{t}{273}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At constant temperature, a gas occupies a volume of 200 mL at a pressure of 500 mm Hg. What will be its volume at 800 mm Hg pressure?
questions.solution:
According to Boyle's law, at constant temperature, $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$.

Given $P_1 = 500\ \text{mm Hg}$, $V_1 = 200\ \text{mL}$, and $P_2 = 800\ \text{mm Hg}$.

Substituting the values:

$500 \times 200 = 800 \times V_2$

$V_2 = \dfrac{500 \times 200}{800} = 125\ \text{mL}$

Answer: $125\ \text{mL}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following statements is true about ideal gas ?
options: It shows deviation from Boyle's law and Charles' law.
Its molecules are not perfectly elastic.
Intermolecular attraction is present in it, hence a collision takes place with loss of kinetic energy.
questions.solution:
An ideal gas is a hypothetical concept and does not exist in reality. Real gases behave as ideal gases only under conditions of low pressure and high temperature.

According to the kinetic theory of gases, an ideal gas strictly obeys Boyle's law, Charles' law, and other gas laws under all conditions of temperature and pressure. The collisions between its molecules are perfectly elastic, and there are no intermolecular forces of attraction between its molecules.

Thus, the statement that it does not exist is true.

Answer: It does not exist.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the new pressure of the gas enclosed in a cylinder when it compressed from 5 L to 2 L at 1 atm and 300 K. The final temperature in this process is 500 K.
questions.solution:
Using the combined gas law equation:

$\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$

Given values are:

$P_1 = 1$ atm, $V_1 = 5$ L, $T_1 = 300$ K

$V_2 = 2$ L, $T_2 = 500$ K

Substituting the values into the equation:

$\dfrac{1 \times 5}{300} = \dfrac{P_2 \times 2}{500}$

$P_2 = \dfrac{1 \times 5 \times 500}{300 \times 2}$

$P_2 = \dfrac{25}{6} \approx 4.16$ atm

Answer: $4.16$ atm

questions.q: Calculate the compressibility factor of $1$ mole of a certain real gas if it occupies $0.4 \text{ dm}^3$ at $300$ K and $40$ atm. [R $= 0.082$ atm $\text{dm}^3 \text{K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$]

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A gas occupies a volume of $0.35$ dm$^3$ at $290$ K and $2$ atm. Pressure. Calculate the volume of gas at STP.
questions.solution:
Using the combined gas equation:

$\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$

Given:
$P_1 = 2$ atm
$V_1 = 0.35$ dm$^3$
$T_1 = 290$ K

At STP:
$P_2 = 1$ atm
$T_2 = 273$ K

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{2 \times 0.35}{290} = \dfrac{1 \times V_2}{273}$

$V_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 0.35 \times 273}{290}$

$V_2 = \dfrac{191.1}{290} \approx 0.66$ dm$^3$

Answer: $0.66$ dm$^3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the temperature of 2 moles of gas occupying a volume of 5.0 liters at 24.6 atmospheres?
($R = 0.0821$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$

Substituting the given values:

Answer: $476^\circ$C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A syringe has a volume of $10.0\ \text{cm}^3$ at a pressure of $1$ atm. If the end is sealed and the plunger is pushed down (constant temperature), what will be the final volume when the pressure becomes $3.5$ atm?
questions.solution:
Using Boyle's Law at constant temperature:

$P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$

Given $P_1 = 1\ \text{atm}$, $V_1 = 10.0\ \text{cm}^3$, and $P_2 = 3.5\ \text{atm}$.

Substituting the values:

$1 \times 10.0 = 3.5 \times V_2$

$V_2 = \dfrac{10.0}{3.5} = 2.857\ \text{cm}^3$

Rounding to appropriate significant figures, $V_2 = 2.86\ \text{cm}^3$.

Answer: $2.86\ \text{cm}^3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: According to the kinetic molecular theory of gases, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules:
options: Is directly proportional to the absolute temperature
Is the same for all gases at the same volume
questions.solution:
According to the kinetic molecular theory of gases, the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule is given by $E = \dfrac{3}{2}kT$, where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature.

For one mole of an ideal gas, the average kinetic energy is $E = \dfrac{3}{2}RT$, where $R$ is the universal gas constant.

This shows that the average kinetic energy of gas molecules depends only on the absolute temperature and is directly proportional to it. It is independent of pressure, volume, and the nature of the gas.

Answer: Is directly proportional to the absolute temperature

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A container consists mixture of four gases as $5 \mathrm{~g~} \mathrm{H}_2, 8 \mathrm{~g~} \mathrm{He}, 50 \mathrm{~g~} \mathrm{CO}_2$ and 20 g Ne at a certain temperature. Which of the following gases exerts minimum partial pressure?
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \mathrm{X}=x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=x) & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.4 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
questions.solution:
Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that the partial pressure of each gas in a mixture is the product of its mole fraction and the total pressure: $P_i = X_i P_{\text{total}}$. Since $P_{\text{total}}$ is constant, the partial pressure is proportional to the mole fraction, which depends on the number of moles: $X_i = \frac{n_i}{n_{\text{total}}}$. Therefore, the gas with the fewest moles exerts the minimum partial pressure.

Moles are determined from mass and molar mass using $n = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}$.
The molar masses are: $2$ g/mol for $\mathrm{H}_2$, $4$ g/mol for $\mathrm{He}$, $44$ g/mol for $\mathrm{CO}_2$, and $20$ g/mol for $\mathrm{Ne}$.

Calculating for each gas:
$n_{\mathrm{H}_2} = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5$ mol
$n_{\mathrm{He}} = \frac{8}{4} = 2.0$ mol
$n_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = \frac{50}{44} \approx 1.136$ mol
$n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \frac{20}{20} = 1.0$ mol

The minimum number of moles is $1.0$ mol for neon, which will exert the minimum partial pressure.

$\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Equal masses of helium and oxygen are mixed in an empty container at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. What is the fraction of the total pressure exerted by helium?
questions.solution:
Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that the partial pressure of each gas in a mixture equals its mole fraction times the total pressure.

Let $m$ be the equal mass of helium and oxygen, measured in grams. The molar mass of helium is $M_\text{He} = 4\ \text{g/mol}$, and that of oxygen is $M_{\text{O}_2} = 32\ \text{g/mol}$. The mole of helium is $n_{\text{He}} = \frac{m}{4}$, while the mole of oxygen is $n_{\text{O}_2} = \frac{m}{32}$. The total number of moles becomes: $n_{\text{total}} = \frac{m}{4} + \frac{m}{32} = \frac{8m}{32} + \frac{m}{32} = \frac{9m}{32}$ The mole fraction of helium is thus: $X_{\text{He}} = \frac{n_{\text{He}}}{n_{\text{total}}} = \frac{\frac{m}{4}}{\frac{9m}{32}} = \frac{m}{4} \cdot \frac{32}{9m} = \frac{8}{9}$ By Dalton's law, the fraction of the total pressure exerted by helium equals its mole fraction, so: $\frac{P_{\text{He}}}{P_{\text{total}}} = X_{\text{He}} = \frac{8}{9}$


Final Answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A container contains $4 \mathrm{~g}\mathrm{H}_2, 4 \mathrm{~g}\mathrm{He}$ and certain amount of ' Ne ' at a certain temperature. What is the mass of 'Ne' required so that the partial pressure exerted by ' Ne ' is equal to the partial pressure of He ?
questions.solution:
Dalton's Law implies that partial pressures are equal when mole fractions are equal, which requires equal numbers of moles for gases in the same container at constant temperature.

Given $4\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{H_2}$ ($M = 2\ \mathrm{g/mol}$) and $4\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{He}$ ($M = 4\ \mathrm{g/mol}$), the moles are $n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 4/2 = 2\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $n_{\mathrm{He}} = 4/4 = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$.

For $P_{\mathrm{Ne}} = P_{\mathrm{He}}$, the mole fractions must match, so $n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = n_{\mathrm{He}} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$.

With $M_{\mathrm{Ne}} = 20\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, the required mass is $1 \times 20 = 20\ \mathrm{g}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{20\ \mathrm{g}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A container contains equal masses of $\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{He}, \mathrm{CO}_2$ and Ne at a certain temperature. Which of the following gases exerts minimum partial pressure?
questions.solution:
According to Dalton’s law, the partial pressure of a gas is proportional to its mole fraction, or equivalently, to its number of moles when volume and temperature are constant. Given equal masses $m$ of $\mathrm{H}_2$, $\mathrm{He}$, $\mathrm{CO}_2$, and $\mathrm{Ne}$, the number of moles for each is calculated as $n = \frac{m}{M}$, where $M$ is the molar mass.

The molar masses are $M_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 2 \, \text{g/mol}$, $M_{\mathrm{He}} = 4 \, \text{g/mol}$, $M_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = 44 \, \text{g/mol}$, and $M_{\mathrm{Ne}} = 20 \, \text{g/mol}$. Thus, the moles are $n_{\mathrm{H}_2} = \frac{m}{2}$, $n_{\mathrm{He}} = \frac{m}{4}$, $n_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = \frac{m}{44}$, and $n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \frac{m}{20}$.

Since $m$ is constant, the number of moles is inversely proportional to molar mass. The largest molar mass belongs to $\mathrm{CO}_2$ ($44 \, \text{g/mol}$), so it has the smallest number of moles and therefore the minimum partial pressure.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A container contains equal masses of $\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{He}, \mathrm{CO}_2$ and Ne at a certain temperature. Which of the following gas exerts maximum partial pressure?
questions.solution:
According to Dalton's law of partial pressures and the ideal gas law $PV = nRT$, for a gas mixture at constant temperature and volume, partial pressure $P_i$ is proportional to the number of moles $n_i$: $P_i \propto n_i$.

With equal masses $m$ of each gas, the number of moles for each gas is:

$n_{\mathrm{H}_2} = \frac{m}{2}$, $n_{\mathrm{He}} = \frac{m}{4}$, $n_{\mathrm{CO}_2} = \frac{m}{44}$, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \frac{m}{20}$

Comparing the denominators $2 \lt 4 \lt 20 \lt 44$, hydrogen has the largest number of moles and therefore the maximum partial pressure.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the SI unit of rate of diffusion for a gas?
questions.solution:
The rate of diffusion is defined as volume diffused per unit time, $\frac{V}{t}$.

The SI unit for volume is $\mathrm{m}^3$ and for time is $\mathrm{s}$, so the unit is $\mathrm{m}^3\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

Evaluating the options:
A) $\mathrm{dm}^{-3}\cdot\mathrm{s}$ is inverse volume times time,
B) $\mathrm{dm}^3\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ is volume per time,
C) $\mathrm{mL}^{-1}\cdot\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ is inverse volume per time,
D) $\mathrm{mL}\cdot\mathrm{s}$ is volume times time.

Only B has dimensions consistent with volume per time.

The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A container consisting mixture of $28 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~N}_2, 8 \mathrm{~g~} \mathrm{He}$ and 40 g Ne at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the total pressure exerted by the gaseous mixture is 20 bar, What is the partial pressure exerted by $\mathrm{N}_2$ ?
questions.solution:
Partial pressure of $\mathrm{N_2}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If compressibility factor of real gas is 1.05 at STP. What is molar volume of real gas?
questions.solution:
The compressibility factor $Z$ for a real gas is defined as $Z = \frac{V_{m,\text{real}}}{V_{m,\text{ideal}}}$.

At STP, the molar volume of an ideal gas is known to be $22.4\ \text{dm}^3$.

Given $Z = 1.05$, the molar volume of the real gas becomes $V_{m,\text{real}} = Z \times V_{m,\text{ideal}} = 1.05 \times 22.4 = 23.52\ \text{dm}^3$.

Among the options provided, both C and D state $23.52\ \text{dm}^3$, representing the correct value.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following is true according to Gay-Lussac's law?
options: $\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{T}}=$ constant at constant pressure and for fixed mass of gas.
$\frac{\mathrm{p}}{\mathrm{d}}=$ constant at constant temperature and fixed mass of gas.
$\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{T}}=$ constant at constant volume and fixed mass of gas.
$\mathrm{P} \times \mathrm{V}=$ constant at constant temperature and for fixed mass of gas.
questions.solution:
Gay-Lussac's Law states that, for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature: $P \propto T$.

This gives the mathematical relation $\frac{P}{T} = \text{constant}$ at constant volume and fixed mass.

Option C states: $\frac{P}{T} = \text{constant}$ at constant volume and fixed mass of gas, which matches the law exactly.

Option A describes Charles's Law, option B is a derived relation from ideal gas behavior, and option D is Boyle's Law.

Thus, the correct statement is option $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Four vessels of same volume consist equal moles of four gases $\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{Cl}_2$, $\mathrm{N}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ separately at same temperature. The pressure exerted by the gas is maximum for -
questions.solution:
The gases demonstrate real behavior where pressure deviates from the ideal gas law due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

The van der Waals equation $P = \frac{nRT}{V - nb} - \frac{an^2}{V^2}$ governs this behavior, with $a$ representing intermolecular attraction and $b$ representing excluded volume.

For fixed $n$, $V$, and $T$, the compressibility factor $Z = \frac{PV}{nRT}$ approximates to $Z \approx 1 + \frac{n}{V} \left(b - \frac{a}{RT}\right)$, making pressure maximization equivalent to maximizing $\left(b - \frac{a}{RT}\right)$.

At $T = 300$ K, using standard van der Waals constants:

$\text{H}_2$: $0.0266 - \frac{0.244}{24.63} \approx +0.0167$
$\text{N}_2$: $0.0391 - \frac{1.39}{24.63} \approx -0.0173$
$\text{O}_2$: $0.0318 - \frac{1.36}{24.63} \approx -0.0234$
$\text{Cl}_2$: $0.0562 - \frac{6.49}{24.63} \approx -0.2073$

Hydrogen yields the only positive value, indicating $Z \gt 1$ and maximum pressure among the gases.

$\boxed{A}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following equations gives combined relationship of Boyle's law and Charle's law?
questions.solution:
Charles' law is the change in volume with respect to temperature at constant pressure, while Boyle's law is the change in volume with respect to pressure at a constant temperature.
Taking a gas of volume \(V_1\), pressure \(P_1\) and temperature \(T_1\), and let its change have a state \(\left(\mathrm{V}_2, \mathrm{P}_2, \mathrm{~T}_2\right)\), then according to Boyle's law,
\(P_1 V_1=P_2 V_2 \ldots \ldots . . . .(1)\)
Then keeping this constant pressure, move to state \(\left(\mathrm{V}_2, \mathrm{P}_2, \mathrm{~T}_2\right)\) using Charles' law,
\(\frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_2} \ldots \ldots . . . .(2)\)
Solving for \(V_2\), in both (1) and (2) and then equating them, we get-
\(\frac{\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_2}\)
After changing the pressure, volume and temperature of the gas, still their product is equal, suggesting that the relation is constant: \(\frac{P V}{T}=k\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If $P_1$ partial pressure of a gas and $x_1$ is its mole fraction in a mixture, then correct relation between $P_1$ and $x_1$ is
questions.solution:
The correct relation between the partial pressure of a gas \(\left(P_1\right)\) and its mole fraction \(\left(x_1\right)\) in a mixture is given by Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures. According to this law, the partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is proportional to its mole fraction and the total pressure of the mixture. The expression can be written as:
\(P_1=x_1 \cdot P_{\text {total }}\)
From this relationship, we can derive the mole fraction as:
\(x_1=\frac{P_1}{P_{\text {total }}}\)
This corresponds to Option B:
\(x_1=\frac{P_1}{P_{\text {total }}}\)

questions.solution:
(1) $Z=\frac{P V T}{R}$ : This is incorrect because the units on both sides don't match.
(2) $Z=\frac{n R T}{P V}$ : This is incorrect because it's the inverse of the correct formula.

questions.q: Which from following gases of same mass exerts highest pressure at constant temperature?
questions.solution:
Let us consider the mass of each gas $=1 \mathrm{~g}$ Order of molecular weight of the given gases: $\mathrm{H}_2 \lt \mathrm{N}_2 \lt \mathrm{O}_2 \lt \mathrm{Cl}_2\therefore \quad$ The order of no. of moles: $\mathrm{H}_2\gt\mathrm{N}_2\gt\mathrm{O}_2\gt\mathrm{Cl}_2$ From ideal gas equation, $\mathrm{n} \propto \mathrm{V}\therefore \quad$ Volume occupied by the gases is as follows: $\mathrm{H}_2\gt\mathrm{N}_2\gt\mathrm{O}_2\gt\mathrm{Cl}_2$
At constant temperature, (Boyle's law) $P \propto \frac{1}{V}$
Since volume occupied by $\mathrm{Cl}_2$ gas is the least, $\therefore \quad \mathrm{Cl}_2$ gas exerts the highest pressure.

questions.q: Volume of a balloon at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 1 bar pressure is $2 \cdot 27 \mathrm{~L}$. If the pressure of the gas in balloon is reduced to $0.227$ bar, what is the rise in volume of a gas?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Argon possesses
questions.solution: Argon is a monatomic gas, thus its molecules can move in any direction in space. Hence, it can have three independent motions (all translational). Therefore, argon possesses only translational motion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify pair of orbitals having similar $(n + l)$ values from the following.
questions.solution:
The $(n + l)$ value for an orbital is calculated by adding the principal quantum number $n$ and the azimuthal quantum number $l$.

For $s$, $p$, $d$, and $f$ subshells, the values of $l$ are $0, 1, 2,$ and $3$ respectively.

Calculating $(n + l)$ for the given pairs:

For $3s$ and $3p$: $(3 + 0) = 3$ and $(3 + 1) = 4$

For $2p$ and $4s$: $(2 + 1) = 3$ and $(4 + 0) = 4$

For $3d$ and $4p$: $(3 + 2) = 5$ and $(4 + 1) = 5$

For $2p$ and $3p$: $(2 + 1) = 3$ and $(3 + 1) = 4$

The pair $3d$ and $4p$ has the same $(n + l)$ value of $5$.

Answer: 3d and 4p

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the shortest wavelength in hydrogen spectrum emission of Lymen series ($R_H = 109677\,\text{cm}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
For the Lyman series, the transition is from $n_2$ to $n_1 = 1$.

The shortest wavelength corresponds to the maximum energy transition, which occurs when $n_2 = \infty$.

Using the Rydberg formula:

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$

Substituting $n_1 = 1$ and $n_2 = \infty$:

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{\infty^2} \right) = R_H$

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{R_H}$

Given $R_H = 109677 \text{ cm}^{-1}$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{109677} \text{ cm} \approx 9.117 \times 10^{-6} \text{ cm}$

Answer: $9.117 \times 10^{-6}$ cm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the wave number of lowest transition associated with Paschen series?
questions.solution:
The wave number $\bar{v}$ for a transition in a hydrogen atom is given by the Rydberg formula:

$\bar{v} = R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$

For the Paschen series, the lower energy level is $n_1 = 3$.

The lowest transition corresponds to the minimum energy difference, which occurs for the transition from the immediately higher energy level, $n_2 = 4$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$\bar{v} = R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{4^2} \right)$

$\bar{v} = R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{16} \right)$

$\bar{v} = R_H \left( \dfrac{16 - 9}{144} \right)$

$\bar{v} = R_H \left( \dfrac{7}{144} \right) \text{cm}^{-1}$

Answer: $R_H\left(\dfrac{7}{144}\right)\ \text{cm}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following colours has highest energy if wave lengths of violet, blue, yellow and red light are 410 nm, 470 nm, 580 nm and 750 nm respectively ?
questions.solution:
The energy of a photon is given by the Planck-Einstein relation:

$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$

where $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\lambda$ is the wavelength.

From the relation, energy is inversely proportional to the wavelength ($E \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$).

The given wavelengths are:
Violet: $410 \text{ nm}$
Blue: $470 \text{ nm}$
Yellow: $580 \text{ nm}$
Red: $750 \text{ nm}$

Since violet light has the shortest wavelength among the given colours, it has the highest energy.

Answer: Violet

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following colours of visible light has lowest energy?
questions.solution:
The energy of a photon is given by the relation $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

This shows that energy is inversely proportional to the wavelength of light.

In the visible spectrum (VIBGYOR), red light has the maximum wavelength.

Therefore, red light has the lowest energy.

Answer: Red

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the energy of third stationary orbit of Bohr's model of hydrogen atom if the energy of ground state is $-E$ J
questions.solution:
The energy of the $n$-th Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by $E_n = \dfrac{E_1}{n^2}$

Given that the energy of the ground state ($n=1$) is $E_1 = -E$

For the third stationary orbit, $n=3$

Substituting the values, we get $E_3 = \dfrac{-E}{3^2} = -\dfrac{E}{9}$ J

Answer: $-\dfrac{E}{9}$ J

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is uncertainty in velocity of an electron if uncertainty in measurement of position is 50 pm ? $(m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{kg},\ h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{Js},\ \pi = 3.142)$
questions.solution:
According to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle:

$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$

$\Delta x \cdot m \Delta v = \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$

$\Delta v = \dfrac{h}{4\pi m \Delta x}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times 3.142 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 50 \times 10^{-12}}$

$\Delta v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5718.44 \times 10^{-43}}$

$\Delta v = 1.1594 \times 10^6 \text{ ms}^{-1} \approx 1.16 \times 10^6 \text{ ms}^{-1}$

Answer: $1.16 \times 10^6\ \text{ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the number of unpaired electrons present in ground state of Silicon and Chromium, respectively ?
questions.solution:
The atomic number of Silicon (Si) is $14$.

The electronic configuration of Si is $1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{2} 3p^{2}$.

In the $3p$ subshell, there are $2$ electrons which occupy separate orbitals according to Hund's rule. Thus, Si has $2$ unpaired electrons.

The atomic number of Chromium (Cr) is $24$.

The electronic configuration of Cr is $[Ar] 3d^{5} 4s^{1}$.

In the $3d$ subshell, there are $5$ unpaired electrons and in the $4s$ subshell, there is $1$ unpaired electron. Thus, Cr has $6$ unpaired electrons.

The number of unpaired electrons in Si and Cr are $2$ and $6$, respectively.

Answer: 2 and 6

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom in a stationary state corresponding to n = 2 ?
questions.solution:
The energy of an electron in the $n$th stationary state of a hydrogen atom is given by the expression:

$E_n = -R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right)$

where $R_H$ is the Rydberg constant for energy, which is equal to $2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J.

For $n = 2$:

$E_2 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2^2} \right)$ J

$E_2 = -\dfrac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{4}$ J

$E_2 = -0.545 \times 10^{-18}$ J

$E_2 = -5.45 \times 10^{-19}$ J

Answer: $-5.45 \times 10^{-19}$ J

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the observed electronic configuration of Cu ?
questions.solution:
The atomic number of copper (Cu) is $29$.

According to the Aufbau principle, the expected electronic configuration is $[\text{Ar}]\ 3d^9\ 4s^2$.

However, a completely filled $d$-subshell ($3d^{10}$) provides extra stability due to symmetrical electron distribution and higher exchange energy.

Therefore, one electron from the $4s$ orbital is transferred to the $3d$ orbital, resulting in the observed electronic configuration of $[\text{Ar}]\ 3d^{10}\ 4s^1$.

Answer: $[\text{Ar}]\ 3d^{10}\ 4s^1$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
If the velocity of the electron in Bohr's first orbit is $2.19 \times 10^6\ \text{Ms}^{-1}$, Calculate the de Broglie wavelength associated with it.
$[h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ & Mass of electrons $= 9.10938 \times 10^{-31}$ kg $]$
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is given by the relation:

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$

Substituting the given values:

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.10938 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.19 \times 10^6}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{19.949 \times 10^{-25}}$

$\lambda = 0.3321 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{m}$

$\lambda = 332.1 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{m}$

$\lambda \approx 332\ \text{pm}$

Answer: $332$ pm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron in the first Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom if the velocity of an electron in the first orbit is $2.2 \times 10^6 \text{ ms}^{-1}$. [mass of electron $= 9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, plank's constant (h) $= 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s]
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is given by the relation:

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$

Substituting the given values:

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.2 \times 10^6}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{20.02 \times 10^{-25}}$

$\lambda = 0.331 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$\lambda = 3.31 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$

Answer: $3.31 \times 10^{-10}$ m

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If the energy of an electron in the first Bohr orbit of the H-atom is $-2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J then the energy of the electron in the second orbit will be
questions.solution:
The energy of an electron in the $n$-th Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by $E_n = \dfrac{E_1}{n^2}$.

Given $E_1 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J and $n = 2$.

Substituting the values, we get:

$E_2 = \dfrac{-2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{2^2}$

$E_2 = \dfrac{-2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{4}$

$E_2 = -0.545 \times 10^{-18}$ J.

Answer: $-0.545 \times 10^{-18}$ J

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following pairs represents isobars?
questions.solution:
Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

In the pair ${}^{40}\text{K}_{19}$ and ${}^{40}\text{Ca}_{20}$, both have the same mass number $40$ but different atomic numbers $19$ and $20$ respectively.

Thus, they represent a pair of isobars.

Answer: ${}^{40}\text{K}_{19}$ and ${}^{40}\text{Ca}_{20}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The electronic configurations of elements are as-
$A = 1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^6 \ 4s^2$
$B = 1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^5$
Which of the following is formula of ionic compound that could be formed between these two elements A and B?
questions.solution:
Element A has the electronic configuration $1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^6 \ 4s^2$. It has $2$ valence electrons in its outermost shell, so it loses $2$ electrons to achieve a stable noble gas configuration, forming the $\text{A}^{2+}$ ion.

Element B has the electronic configuration $1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^5$. It has $7$ valence electrons in its outermost shell, so it gains $1$ electron to achieve a stable noble gas configuration, forming the $\text{B}^{-}$ ion.

To form a neutral ionic compound, one $\text{A}^{2+}$ ion combines with two $\text{B}^{-}$ ions.

The formula of the compound is $\text{AB}_2$.

Answer: $\text{AB}_2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the atomic number of an element having $ns^1$ electronic configuration and belonging to 3d transition series?
questions.solution:
The 3d transition series belongs to the 4th period, so $n=4$.

The general electronic configuration of the 3d transition series is $[Ar] 3d^{1-10} 4s^{1-2}$.

Elements with an $ns^1$ (i.e., $4s^1$) configuration in this series are Chromium (Cr) and Copper (Cu) due to the extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled d-subshells.

The electronic configuration of Cr ($Z=24$) is $[Ar] 3d^5 4s^1$.

The electronic configuration of Cu ($Z=29$) is $[Ar] 3d^{10} 4s^1$.

Thus, the atomic numbers are 24 and 29.

Answer: 24 and 29

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What are the total number of electrons present in s and p orbitals respectively in the argon?
questions.solution:
The atomic number of argon (Ar) is $18$.

The electronic configuration of argon is $1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{2} 3p^{6}$.

The total number of electrons present in s-orbitals is $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$.

The total number of electrons present in p-orbitals is $6 + 6 = 12$.

Therefore, the number of electrons in s and p orbitals are $6$ and $12$ respectively.

Answer: $6$ and $12$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List I with List II
List I
Element		List II
Number of Neutron
(A). ${}^{24}_{12}Mg$(I). $5$
(B). ${}^{27}_{13}Al$(II). $12$
(C). ${}^{9}_{4}Be$(III). $6$
(D). ${}^{12}_{6}C$(IV). $14$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The number of neutrons in an atom is calculated as the difference between its mass number ($A$) and atomic number ($Z$), i.e., $n = A - Z$.

For ${}^{24}_{12}Mg$, $n = 24 - 12 = 12$. This matches (II).

For ${}^{27}_{13}Al$, $n = 27 - 13 = 14$. This matches (IV).

For ${}^{9}_{4}Be$, $n = 9 - 4 = 5$. This matches (I).

For ${}^{12}_{6}C$, $n = 12 - 6 = 6$. This matches (III).

The correct matching is (A) - (II), (B) - (IV), (C) - (I), (D) - (III).

Answer: (A) - (II), (B) - (IV), (C) - (I), (D) - (III)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the frequency in $\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{z}}$ of orange colour light having wave length $600 \mathrm{~nm} .\left[\mathrm{C}=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}\right]$
questions.solution:
The frequency of light is determined from the relationship $c = \lambda \nu$, where $c = 3 \times 10^{8} \text{ m/s}$ and $\lambda = 600 \text{ nm}$.

Convert the wavelength to meters: $\lambda = 600 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m} = 6 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.

Rearranging the equation gives $\nu = \frac{c}{\lambda} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{6 \times 10^{-7}} = \frac{1}{2} \times 10^{15} = 5 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.

This result corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate velocity of an electron having de Broglie's wavelength 58 nm and mass $9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg} ?\left[\mathrm{~h}=6.63 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}\right]$
questions.solution:
Velocity from de Broglie wavelength

The de Broglie wavelength formula relates a particle's wavelength to its momentum: $\lambda = h / (mv)$.

Solving for velocity: $v = h / (m\lambda)$

Given $\lambda = 58 \times 10^{-9}$ m, $m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, and $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s:

$v = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{(9.1 \times 10^{-31})(58 \times 10^{-9})}$

The denominator simplifies to $527.8 \times 10^{-40}$ kg·m, yielding:

$v = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{527.8 \times 10^{-40}} = 0.01256 \times 10^{6} = 1.256 \times 10^{4}$ m/s

Rounded to three significant figures: $v = 1.26 \times 10^{4}$ m/s, which corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: "Pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same subshell does not occur unless each orbital belonging to that subshell has got one electron each." This statement is known as
questions.solution:
The statement "Pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same subshell does not occur unless each orbital belonging to that subshell has got one electron each" constitutes the definition of Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.

This posited rule mandates that, within degenerate orbitals of a given subshell, each orbital is occupied by a single electron possessing parallel spin prior to any electron pairing occurring, thereby maximizing unpaired electrons and minimizing inter-electronic repulsion.

Among the alternatives, Pauli's exclusion principle ($|$n, l, m_l$, m_s$|$ must be unique per electron) concerns the maximum occupancy and quantum state uniqueness of an orbital; Aufbau's rule specifies the order of orbital filling by energy; and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle ($\Delta x \Delta p \geq \frac{\hbar}{2}$) pertains to fundamental measurement limitations. The statement refers exclusively to Hund's rule.

$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: " It is impossible to determine simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum of an electron. " This statement is called
questions.solution:
The statement regarding the indeterminacy of simultaneous position and momentum measurements for an electron describes the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.

Contrasting with other quantum mechanical rules:
Pauli's exclusion principle specifies unique quantum numbers for electrons in an atom;
Hund's rule governs orbital occupancy and electron spin;
the Aufbau rule dictates the order of electron filling in atomic orbitals.

The correct answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following elements contains maximum number of unpaired electrons?
questions.solution:
To identify the element with the maximum unpaired electrons, electron configurations are analyzed using Hund's rule.

Fluorine ($Z=9$) has configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^5$, yielding one unpaired electron: $\boxed{\uparrow\downarrow}\boxed{\uparrow\downarrow}\boxed{\uparrow}$

Sodium ($Z=11$) has $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$, with one unpaired electron: $\boxed{\uparrow}$

Nitrogen ($Z=7$) has $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$, resulting in three unpaired electrons: $\boxed{\uparrow}\boxed{\uparrow}\boxed{\uparrow}$

Oxygen ($Z=8$) has $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$, producing two unpaired electrons: $\boxed{\uparrow\downarrow}\boxed{\uparrow}\boxed{\uparrow}$

Nitrogen exhibits the maximum with three unpaired electrons.

The correct choice is $\boxed{C}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following d-orbitals has different shape as compared with others?
questions.solution:
The five $d$-orbitals are designated as $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{xz}$, $d_{x^2-y^2}$, and $d_{z^2}$.

Orbitals $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, and $d_{xz}$ all exhibit the characteristic cloverleaf shape, with lobes oriented between their respective axes.

Orbital $d_{z^2}$ possesses a distinct geometry, featuring two primary lobes aligned along the $z$-axis and a toroidal region in the $xy$-plane.

Consequently, $d_{z^2}$ is structurally dissimilar to the other three orbitals.

The orbital with a different shape is $\boxed{D}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the number of node in 2 s orbital?
questions.solution:
The total number of nodes in an orbital is determined by $n - 1$, where $n$ is the principal quantum number.

For the 2s orbital, $n = 2$, so the total number of nodes is $2 - 1 = 1$. Since s orbitals have $l = 0$, all nodes are radial. The radial node count is given by $n - l - 1 = 2 - 0 - 1 = 1$.

The correct answer is B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the numerical value of angular momentum for an electron in first orbit of hydrogen atom ? ( $\mathrm{h}=6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$ )
questions.solution:
The angular momentum of an electron in Bohr's stationary orbit is quantized as $L = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$, where $n$ is the principal quantum number and $h$ is Planck's constant ($6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$).

For the first orbit, $n = 1$, yielding $L = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{2\pi} \mathrm{Js}$.

Numerical evaluation gives $L \approx 1.0545 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$, which rounds to $1.05 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$.

This matches option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following is NOT hydrogen like species?
questions.solution:
A hydrogen-like species is defined as having only one electron.

Li+2: Lithium has atomic number 3, so Li+2 has $3 - 2 = 1$ electron, making it hydrogen-like.

Be+3: Beryllium has atomic number 4, so Be+3 has $4 - 3 = 1$ electron, making it hydrogen-like.

Li+: Lithium has atomic number 3, so Li+ has $3 - 1 = 2$ electrons, which is not hydrogen-like.

He+: Helium has atomic number 2, so He+ has $2 - 1 = 1$ electron, making it hydrogen-like.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the energy per mole of photon of electromagnetic radiation having wave length 700 nm
$\left[\mathrm{h}=6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}, \mathrm{C}=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right]$
questions.solution:
Energy per mole of photons is calculated from the energy of a single photon multiplied by Avogadro's number.

The energy of a photon is given by $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, where Planck's constant $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$, the speed of light $c = 3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{m/s}$, and wavelength $\lambda = 700 \,\mathrm{nm} = 7 \times 10^{-7} \,\mathrm{m}$.

Substituting these values:
$E = \frac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}) \cdot (3 \times 10^8)}{7 \times 10^{-7}} = 2.8397 \times 10^{-19} \,\mathrm{J}$.

Multiplying by Avogadro's number $N_{\mathrm{A}} = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \,\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ gives the energy per mole:
$E_{\mathrm{mole}} = (2.8397 \times 10^{-19}) \cdot (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 1.7109 \times 10^5 \,\mathrm{J/mol}$.

Rounded to three significant figures, the value is $1.71 \times 10^5 \,\mathrm{J/mol}$.

Among the options, A) $1.71 \times 10^5 \,\mathrm{J}$ matches this result.

$\boxed{\mathrm{A}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $"$ No two electrons in an atom can have the identical set of four quantum numbers." The statement is known as
questions.solution:
The statement expresses the Pauli exclusion principle, which asserts that no two fermions (such as electrons) can occupy identical quantum states simultaneously.

An atomic orbital may contain at most two electrons, and they must possess opposite spin quantum numbers. This principle is fundamental to electron configuration and atomic structure.

In contrast, Hund's rule governs the filling of degenerate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing occurs; the Aufbau principle describes the sequential filling of orbitals from lowest to highest energy; and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle relates to the intrinsic limits in precisely measuring conjugate variables like position and momentum.

The correct identification is therefore $\boxed{A}$.

questions.q: Calculate the longest wavelength in hydrogen emission spectrum of Lymen series $\left(R_H=109677 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}\right)$
questions.solution:
The longest wavelength in the Lyman series of hydrogen corresponds to the smallest energy transition, from $n_2 = 2$ to $n_1 = 1$.

Using the Rydberg formula,

$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2} \right) = 109677~\mathrm{cm}^{-1} \left(1 - \frac{1}{4} \right) = 109677~\mathrm{cm}^{-1} \cdot \frac{3}{4}$

This simplifies to

$\frac{1}{\lambda} = 82257.75~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$

The wavelength is therefore

$\lambda = \frac{1}{82257.75} \approx 1.2156 \times 10^{-5}~\mathrm{cm}$

Among the options, this value is closest to $1.216 \times 10^{-5}~\mathrm{cm}$.

The correct choice is B.

questions.q: Which parameter is indicated by the number of waves passing through a given point in one second?
questions.solution:
Frequency refers to the number of waves passing through a given point in one second. It is typically measured in Hertz $(\mathrm{Hz})$, where 1 Hz is equal to one wave passing per second.
Here's a brief explanation of the other options:
- (A) Wavelength: The distance between two consecutive points in phase on a wave (e.g., from crest to crest or trough to trough).
- (C) Wave number: The number of wavelengths per unit distance, typically measured in inverse meters ( $1 / \mathrm{m}$ ).
- (D) Amplitude: The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium position, related to the wave's intensity but not its frequency.

questions.q: When an electron in a hydrogen atom jumps from the third excited state to the ground state, the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the electron becomes
questions.solution:
The De Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$, where $h=$ Planck's constant and $p=$ momentum of the electron. Also, momentum $p=m v$ and kinetic energy $E_K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ From the above equation, we can relate momentum $p$ and kinetic energy $E_K$ as, $p=\sqrt{2 m E_K}$
Now the ratio of wavelength of hydrogen atom when the atom jumps from third excited state to ground state viz $(n=4$ to $n=1$ )

\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{\frac{h}{p_1}}{\frac{h}{p_2}}=\frac{p_2}{p_1}=\sqrt{\frac{E_{K 2}}{E_{K 1}}}

Also, we know $E_{K n}=\frac{-13.6 Z^2}{n^2}$
Using equation (1),

\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{\sqrt{1^2}}{\sqrt{4^2}}

So, the ratio of the wavelength of ground state $\{n=1\}$ to $3^{\text {rd }}$ excited state $\{n=4\}$ is $\frac{1}{4}$.
