questions.q: Calculate the work done in joule if 1 mole of an ideal gas compressed from volume $24 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $13 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant external pressure 3 bar.
questions.solution:
The work done by a gas during a constant external pressure process is given by $W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V$, where $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1$.

Given $V_1 = 24~\text{dm}^3$, $V_2 = 13~\text{dm}^3$, and $P_{\text{ext}} = 3~\text{bar}$, the volume change is $\Delta V = 13 - 24 = -11~\text{dm}^3$.

Converting to SI units: $1~\text{dm}^3 = 10^{-3}~\text{m}^3$ and $1~\text{bar} = 10^5~\text{Pa}$, yielding $P_{\text{ext}} = 3 \times 10^5~\text{Pa}$ and $\Delta V = -11 \times 10^{-3}~\text{m}^3$.

Substituting into the work formula: $W = -(3 \times 10^5) \cdot (-11 \times 10^{-3}) = 3300~\text{J}$.

The calculated work of $3300~\text{J}$ corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following is an example of both intensive property and state function?
questions.solution:
Intensive properties are independent of system size, while extensive properties scale with system size. State functions depend only on the current state, not the path taken to reach it.

Internal energy $U$ is extensive (scales with moles) and a state function. Volume $V$ is extensive (scales with amount) and a state function. Entropy $S$ is extensive (scales with system size) and a state function. Only temperature $T$ is intensive (identical in different-sized systems at equilibrium) and a state function (determined solely by the state).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a certain reaction, $\Delta \mathrm{H}=-210 \mathrm{~kJ}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{S}=-150 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ Find the temperature so that $\Delta \mathrm{G}=0$
questions.solution:
The temperature where $\Delta G = 0$ is determined by the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$.

Given $\Delta H = -210\,\mathrm{kJ}$ and $\Delta S = -150\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, first convert the enthalpy to consistent units: $\Delta H = -210000\,\mathrm{J}$.

Setting $\Delta G = 0$ yields $0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, which rearranges to $T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.

Substituting values gives $T = \frac{-210000\,\mathrm{J}}{-150\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}} = 1400\,\mathrm{K}$.

$\boxed{\mathrm{C}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate $\Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ}$ for a reaction if $\Delta \mathrm{S}^{\circ}=120 \mathrm{JK}^{-1}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}=28000 \mathrm{~J}$
questions.solution:
The standard enthalpy change is determined using the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation: $\Delta G^{\circ} = \Delta H^{\circ} - T\Delta S^{\circ}$, with assumed standard temperature $T = 298\;\text{K}$.

Rewriting for $\Delta H^{\circ}$:

$\Delta H^{\circ} = \Delta G^{\circ} + T\Delta S^{\circ}$

Substituting $\Delta G^{\circ} = 28000\;\text{J}$ and $\Delta S^{\circ} = 120\;\text{J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}$:

$\Delta H^{\circ} = 28000 \;\text{J} + (298\;\text{K})(120\;\text{J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}) = 63760\;\text{J}$

Converting to kilojoules: $63760\;\text{J} = 63.76\;\text{kJ}$.

This value corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the work done in joule if 1 mole of ideal gas is compressed from $25 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $13 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant external pressure 4 bar.
questions.solution:
Work done against constant external pressure is given by $W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V$.

Given $P_{\text{ext}} = 4\ \text{bar}$ with volume change $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 13 - 25 = -12\ \text{dm}^3$.

Convert units to SI: $1\ \text{bar} = 10^5\ \text{Pa}$, so $P_{\text{ext}} = 4 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$.
Volume change: $1\ \text{dm}^3 = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$, so $\Delta V = -12 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$.

The work done becomes:
$W = -(4 \times 10^5) \times (-12 \times 10^{-3}) = (4 \times 10^5) \times (12 \times 10^{-3}) = 4800\ \text{J}$.

This positive value indicates work is done on the system during compression.

Final answer: $4800\ \text{J}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following transformations is endothermic in nature?
questions.solution:
Endothermic processes absorb energy, indicated by positive enthalpy change ($\Delta H \gt 0$), while exothermic processes release energy ($\Delta H \lt 0$).

Freezing ($\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(s)}$) releases energy as molecules form ordered structures.

Melting ($\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$) requires energy absorption to overcome intermolecular forces.

Condensation ($\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$) and deposition ($\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{s})}$) both release energy during phase transition to more condensed states.

Only melting exhibits endothermic behavior.

Final answer: $\boxed{B}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the standard enthalpy change for synthesis of ammonia gas from following data
i. $2 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_{4(\mathrm{~g})} ; \quad \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}_1^0=95.4 \mathrm{~kJ}$
ii. $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_{4(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{~g})} ; \quad \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}_2^0=-187 \cdot 6 \mathrm{~kJ}$
questions.solution:
The standard enthalpy change for the target reaction $\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \to 2\mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{~g})}$ is determined using Hess's Law by summing the given reactions and their enthalpy changes.

$2 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} + \mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \to \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_{4(\mathrm{~g})}$ with $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}_1^0 = 95.4 \ \mathrm{kJ}$
$\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_{4(\mathrm{~g})} + \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \to 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{~g})}$ with $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}_2^0 = -187.6 \ \mathrm{kJ}$

Adding the reactions, the intermediate $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{H}_{4(\mathrm{~g})}$ cancels, yielding the target reaction.

The enthalpy change is $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^0_{\text{target}} = 95.4 + (-187.6) = -92.2 \ \mathrm{kJ}$.

Among the options, A matches: $-92.2 \ \mathrm{kJ}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify from following the correct set of thermodynamic conditions for the reaction to be spontaneous below equilibrium temperature.
questions.solution:
The spontaneity of a reaction is determined by the Gibbs free energy: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, with $\Delta G \lt 0$ indicating spontaneity. At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$, so $T_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.

For $\Delta H \lt 0$ and $\Delta S \lt 0$, $\Delta G$ becomes less negative as temperature increases. Spontaneity requires $|\Delta H| \gt T|\Delta S|$, equivalent to $T \lt \frac{|\Delta H|}{|\Delta S|} = T_{\text{eq}}$, confirming the reaction is spontaneous below the equilibrium temperature.

Other combinations yield different behavior: $\Delta H \gt 0$, $\Delta S \gt 0$ gives spontaneity above $T_{\text{eq}}$; $\Delta H \lt 0$, $\Delta S \gt 0$ is always spontaneous; $\Delta H \gt 0$, $\Delta S \lt 0$ is never spontaneous.

The conditions $\Delta H \lt 0$ and $\Delta S \lt 0$ correspond to option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate work done if 1 mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally from $2 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $2.8 \mathrm{dm}^3$ against constant external pressure 1 atm
questions.solution:
The work done by an ideal gas expanding isothermally against constant external pressure is given by $W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V$.

With initial volume $V_1 = 2 \text{ dm}^3$, final volume $V_2 = 2.8 \text{ dm}^3$, and external pressure $P_{\text{ext}} = 1 \text{ atm}$, the volume change is $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 0.8 \text{ dm}^3$.

Substituting these values yields $W = -(1 \text{ atm})(0.8 \text{ dm}^3) = -0.8 \text{ atm} \cdot \text{dm}^3$.

Converting to joules using $1 \text{ dm}^3 = 1 \text{ L}$ and $1 \text{ L} \cdot \text{atm} = 101.325 \text{ J}$ gives $W = -0.8 \times 101.325 \text{ J} = -81.06 \text{ J}$.

This result corresponds most closely with option B ($-81.04 \text{ J}$), with the minor discrepancy attributable to rounding.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following reactions is exothermic?
questions.solution:
The reaction is exothermic when it releases heat, indicated by a negative enthalpy change ($\Delta H \lt 0$).

Neutralization between a strong base and strong acid, such as $\mathrm{KOH}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \mathrm{HNO}_{3(\mathrm{aq})} \rightarrow \mathrm{KNO}_{3(\mathrm{aq})} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$, is highly exothermic.

Melting ice ($\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(l)}$) is endothermic, requiring energy input. Dissolution of $\mathrm{NaCl}$ ($\mathrm{NaCl}_{(\mathrm{s})} + \mathrm{aq} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+} + \mathrm{Cl}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{-}$) is slightly endothermic with a net heat absorption. Formation of $\mathrm{NO}_2$ from elements ($\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 2\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO}_{2(\mathrm{g})}$) is endothermic, as confirmed by its positive standard enthalpy of formation.

Only option A is exothermic.

Answer: $\boxed{A}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate work done in isothermal reversible expansion of 1 mole ideal gas from initial pressure 10 bar to final pressure 1 bar at 300 K $\left(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$
questions.solution:
The work done by an ideal gas during an isothermal reversible expansion is given by $W = -nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$.

Since pressure and volume vary inversely for an ideal gas at constant temperature, $\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{P_1}{P_2}$, yielding $W = -nRT \ln\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)$.

Substituting the given values $n = 1$ mol, $R = 8.314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, $T = 300$ K, $P_1 = 10$ bar, and $P_2 = 1$ bar:
$W = -(1)(8.314)(300) \ln\left(\frac{10}{1}\right)$

Calculating stepwise:
$8.314 \times 300 = 2494.2$
$\ln(10) \approx 2.303$
$W = -2494.2 \times 2.303 = -5744.1426$ J = $-5.744$ kJ

Among the options provided, $-5.74$ kJ corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
The standard enthalpy change for the reaction

$\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}_{(\ell)} + 3\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$

is calculated using the formula
$\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{rxn}} = \sum n\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathrm{products}) - \sum m\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathrm{reactants})$

Using the given enthalpies of formation:
$\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}H^{\circ}(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}) = -280\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$
$\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}H^{\circ}(\mathrm{CO}_2) = -390\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$
$\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}H^{\circ}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}) = -285\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$
and noting that $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}H^{\circ}(\mathrm{O}_2) = 0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for the elemental form.

The sum for products is
$2 \times (-390\,\mathrm{kJ}) + 3 \times (-285\,\mathrm{kJ}) = -780 - 855 = -1635\,\mathrm{kJ}$

The sum for reactants is
$1 \times (-280\,\mathrm{kJ}) + 3 \times (0\,\mathrm{kJ}) = -280\,\mathrm{kJ}$

The enthalpy change is therefore
$\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{rxn}} = -1635 - (-280) = -1355\,\mathrm{kJ}$

This value corresponds to option C among the given choices.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify from following reactions that exhibits negative work done.
questions.solution:
Negative work occurs when the system expands at constant pressure, which requires a positive change in gaseous moles. The work done is given by $W = -\Delta n_g RT$, where $\Delta n_g$ is the change in the number of moles of gaseous species.

For reaction A: $2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{2(\ell)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} + \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})}$
Gaseous products: 1, reactants: 0, so $\Delta n_g = 1 \gt 0$. Hence, $W \lt 0$.

For reaction B: $\mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}_{(\mathrm{s})}$
Gaseous products: 0, reactants: 2, so $\Delta n_g = -2 \lt 0$. Hence, $W \gt 0$.

For reaction C: $\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{g})}$
Gaseous products: 2, reactants: 2, so $\Delta n_g = 0$. Hence, $W = 0$.

For reaction D: $\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{g})}$
Gaseous products: 2, reactants: 4, so $\Delta n_g = -2 \lt 0$. Hence, $W \gt 0$.

Only reaction A exhibits negative work done.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the enthalpy of solution of potassium chloride if its $\Delta_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{H}=700 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta_{\text {hyd }} \mathrm{H}=-680 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
The enthalpy of solution $\Delta_{\text{sol}} H$ for potassium chloride is related to its lattice enthalpy $\Delta_{\text{L}} H$ and enthalpy of hydration $\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H$ by the equation:

$\Delta_{\text{sol}} H = \Delta_{\text{L}} H + \Delta_{\text{hyd}} H$

Substituting the given values $\Delta_{\text{L}} H = 700 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H = -680 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$:

$\Delta_{\text{sol}} H = 700 + (-680) = 20 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Final answer: $20 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the change in internal energy of the system if 20 kJ work is done on the system and it releases 10 kJ heat in a particular reaction.
questions.solution:
The first law of thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system equals the heat added to it plus the work done on it: $\Delta U = q + w$.

Work done on the system is positive, so $w = +20~\text{kJ}$. Heat released by the system is negative, so $q = -10~\text{kJ}$.

Substituting into the equation:

$\Delta U = -10 + 20 = 10~\text{kJ}$

The change in internal energy is 10 kJ.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the work done in joule if 2 moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally from $15.5 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $20 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant pressure 1 atm .
questions.solution:
The work done during an isothermal expansion at constant pressure is given by $W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V$.

Given $V_1 = 15.5\ \mathrm{dm}^3$ and $V_2 = 20\ \mathrm{dm}^3$, the volume change is $\Delta V = 20 - 15.5 = 4.5\ \mathrm{dm}^3$.

At constant external pressure $P_{\text{ext}} = 1\ \mathrm{atm}$, the work is $W = -(1)(4.5) = -4.5\ \mathrm{atm\cdot dm}^3$.

Converting to joules using $1\ \mathrm{atm\cdot dm}^3 = 101.325\ \mathrm{J}$ yields $W = -4.5 \times 101.325 = -455.9625\ \mathrm{J}$.

Rounded to three significant figures, $W \approx -456\ \mathrm{J}$, which corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 1.8 g water is vapourised by supplying 4 kJ heat at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. What is the heat of vapourisation of water at same temperature?
questions.solution:
Heat of vaporization is the heat required to vaporize one mole of a substance at its boiling point. Given 4 kJ vaporizes 1.8 g of water, and the molar mass of water is 18 g/mol, the number of moles is $n = \frac{1.8}{18} = 0.1$ mol.

The heat of vaporization is calculated as $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = \frac{\text{total heat}}{n} = \frac{4}{0.1} = 40$ kJ/mol.

The result corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the standard enthalpy change of following reaction
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{CH}_{4(\mathrm{~g})}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} \\ & \text { If } \quad \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{CH}_4\right)=-75 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{CO}_2\right)=-394 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)=-286 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
questions.solution:
The standard enthalpy change for the reaction $\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)}$ is determined using the relation $\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{r}} = \sum n \Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}} (\text{products}) - \sum m \Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}} (\text{reactants})$, where $\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}}$ values are given as $-75~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $-394~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $-286~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{H_2O}$, and $0~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}$ for elemental oxygen.

The sum for products is $1 \times (-394) + 2 \times (-286) = -966~\mathrm{kJ}$, and for reactants is $1 \times (-75) + 2 \times 0 = -75~\mathrm{kJ}$.

$\Delta H^{\circ}_{\mathrm{r}} = -966 - (-75) = -891~\mathrm{kJ}$.

The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate standard enthalpy change of reaction
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\frac{5}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} \text { if } \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{CO}_2\right)=-393 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)=-286 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_2\right)=227 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
questions.solution:
The standard enthalpy change for the reaction is calculated using the enthalpy of formation formula:

$\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} = \sum n \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}(\text{products}) - \sum m \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}(\text{reactants})$

For the combustion $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \frac{5}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$, substituting the given values yields:

$\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} = [2 \times (-393\ \mathrm{kJ}) + 1 \times (-286\ \mathrm{kJ})] - [1 \times (227\ \mathrm{kJ}) + \frac{5}{2} \times (0\ \mathrm{kJ})]$

Simplifying the expression:

$\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} = [-786 - 286] - [227 + 0] = -1072 - 227 = -1299\ \mathrm{kJ}$

The standard enthalpy change is $-1299\ \mathrm{kJ}$, corresponding to answer choice C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the change in internal energy of the system if 25 kJ of work done by the system and it absorbs 10 kJ of heat.
questions.solution:
The First Law of Thermodynamics provides the relationship between internal energy, heat, and work: $\Delta U = q + w$.

Applying the standard sign convention, work done by the system is negative ($w = -25\,\mathrm{kJ}$), while heat absorbed by the system is positive ($q = 10\,\mathrm{kJ}$).

Substituting these values yields:

$\Delta U = 10 + (-25) = -15\,\mathrm{kJ}$

The change in internal energy is therefore $-15\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

Final Answer: C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify from following an example of intensive property?
questions.solution:
The distinction between intensive and extensive properties is fundamental in thermodynamics. Intensive properties, such as temperature or density, are independent of the system's size, whereas extensive properties, like mass or volume, scale with the amount of matter.

Surface tension is an intensive property, as it depends on molecular forces and temperature but not on quantity. Volume, internal energy, and number of moles are all extensive, as each increases with the amount of substance.

The intensive property is therefore surface tension.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the work done in following reaction at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$4 \mathrm{SO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{SO}_{3(\mathrm{~g})},\left(\mathrm{R}=8 \times 314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$
questions.solution:
Work done in the reaction is calculated using the formula for constant temperature gas-phase reactions: $W = -\Delta n_g RT$.

The balanced equation $4\mathrm{SO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 2\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{SO}_{3(\mathrm{g})}$ shows a net decrease of 2 moles of gas, giving $\Delta n_g = 4 - 6 = -2\ \mathrm{mol}$.

At $T = 300\ \mathrm{K}$ with $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}$, the work is:

$W = -(-2) \times 8.314 \times 300 = 4988.4\ \mathrm{J}$

The positive value indicates work is done on the system. This matches option A.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following set of thermodynamic conditions is true for the reaction to be spontaneous at high temperature?
questions.solution:
The spontaneity of a reaction is determined by the sign of its Gibbs free energy change, $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. A negative $\Delta G \lt 0$ indicates spontaneity.

Option A ($\Delta H \lt 0$, $\Delta S \lt 0$) yields $\Delta G = \text{negative} - T(\text{negative})$. The reaction is spontaneous only at low temperatures when $|\Delta H| \gt |T\Delta S|$.

Option B ($\Delta H \gt 0$, $\Delta S \gt 0$) gives $\Delta G = \text{positive} - T(\text{positive})$. This results in spontaneity at high temperatures where $T\Delta S \gt \Delta H$.

Option C ($\Delta H \lt 0$, $\Delta S \gt 0$) produces $\Delta G = \text{negative} - T(\text{positive})$, which is always negative, making the reaction spontaneous at all temperatures.

Option D ($\Delta H \gt 0$, $\Delta S \lt 0$) yields $\Delta G = \text{positive} - T(\text{negative})$, which is always positive, rendering the reaction non-spontaneous at all temperatures.

Spontaneity at high temperature requires Option B: $\Delta H \gt 0$ and $\Delta S \gt 0$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Find standard enthalpy of formation of ammonia from following reaction.
$\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{~g})} ; \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^0=-92.0 \mathrm{~kJ}$
questions.solution:
The reaction $\mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{g})}$ has an enthalpy change $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^0 = -92.0\ \mathrm{kJ}$ for the formation of 2 moles of ammonia from its elements in standard states.

Standard enthalpy of formation represents the enthalpy change per mole formed, so $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^0 (\mathrm{NH}_3) = \frac{-92.0\ \mathrm{kJ}}{2\ \mathrm{mol}} = -46.0\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate work done if 1 mole of an ideal gas compressed isothermally and reversibly from $12 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $6 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at 300 K .
$\left[\mathrm{R}=8 \cdot 314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas undergoing isothermal reversible compression, the work done is given by $W = -nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$.

Substituting $n = 1 \text{mol}$, $R = 8.314 \text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$, and $T = 300 \text{K}$, with $V_1 = 12 \text{dm}^3$, $V_2 = 6 \text{dm}^3$, the expression becomes $W = -(1)(8.314)(300) \ln\left(\frac{6}{12}\right)$.

Evaluating the numerical coefficient yields $-2494.2 \text{J}$. Since $\ln(0.5) \approx -0.6931$, the work done is $W = -2494.2 \times (-0.6931) \approx 1728.8 \text{J}$.

Converting to kilojoules, $W \approx 1.7288 \text{kJ}$, which rounds to $1.729 \text{kJ}$ to three decimal places.

The work done is positive, consistent with compression, and matches option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify from following physical transformations that exhibits decrease in entropy.
questions.solution:
Entropy change depends on the transition between physical states. Gases have the highest entropy, followed by liquids, then solids with the lowest entropy due to increasing disorder.

Option A shows melting: $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$, where entropy increases ($\Delta S \gt 0$).

Option B shows vaporization: $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})}$, where entropy increases significantly ($\Delta S \gt 0$).

Option C shows sublimation: $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})}$, where entropy increases ($\Delta S \gt 0$).

Option D shows condensation: $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$, where disorder decreases, so $\Delta S \lt 0$.

The transformation exhibiting decreased entropy is condensation.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
The standard enthalpy change, $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} H^{\circ}$, is calculated using the formula:

$\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} H^{\circ} = \sum n \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^{\circ}(\text{products}) - \sum m \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^{\circ}(\text{reactants})$

Given the reaction $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{4(\mathrm{g})} + 3 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$ and the standard enthalpies of formation: $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^{\circ}(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_4) = -52 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol}^{-1}$, $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^{\circ}(\mathrm{CO}_2) = -390 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol}^{-1}$, $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^{\circ}(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}) = -286 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol}^{-1}$, with $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^{\circ}(\mathrm{O}_2) = 0$.

Substituting into the formula:

$\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} H^{\circ} = [2 \times (-390) + 2 \times (-286)] - [1 \times (-52) + 3 \times 0] = [-780 - 572] - [-52 + 0] = -1352 - (-52) = -1300 \ \mathrm{kJ}$

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following process involves zero work done?
questions.solution:
The work done by a gas during expansion or compression is given by $W = -P_{ ext{ext}}\Delta V$, where $P_{ ext{ext}}$ is the external pressure and $\Delta V$ is the volume change.

Isobaric expansion occurs at constant pressure with $\Delta V eq 0$, yielding non-zero work since $P_{ ext{ext}} eq 0$.

Adiabatic compression involves volume decrease with no heat exchange, producing non-zero work as $P_{ ext{ext}} eq 0$.

Isothermal expansion maintains constant temperature with volume increase, resulting in non-zero work $W = -nRT \ln(V_2/V_1)$.

Free expansion occurs against zero external pressure ($P_{ ext{ext}} = 0$), making $W = 0$ regardless of $\Delta V$.

The process involving zero work is free expansion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the constant external pressure required to expand 2 moles of an ideal gas from volume $15 \mathrm{dm}^{-2}$ to $20 \mathrm{dm}^2$ if amount of work done is $-600 \mathrm{~J}$
questions.solution:
Work done during irreversible expansion against a constant external pressure is defined as $W = -P_{ext} \Delta V$.

Given values are $W = -600\ \mathrm{J}$, $V_1 = 15\ \mathrm{dm}^3$, and $V_2 = 20\ \mathrm{dm}^3$. The volume change is $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 5\ \mathrm{dm}^3$.

Since $1\ \mathrm{J} = 1\ \mathrm{Pa} \cdot \mathrm{m}^3$ and $1\ \mathrm{dm}^3 = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}^3$, convert to SI units: $\Delta V = 5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}^3$.

Substitute into the work formula: $-600 = -P_{ext} \times (5 \times 10^{-3})$.

Solving for $P_{ext}$ gives $P_{ext} = \frac{600}{5 \times 10^{-3}} = 120000\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

Convert to bar using $1\ \mathrm{bar} = 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$: $P_{ext} = \frac{120000}{10^5} = 1.2\ \mathrm{bar}$.

The final answer is $\boxed{\mathrm{A}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the enthalpy of vaporisation of ethanol if 11.5 g of ethanol is completely vaporised by supplying 11.8 kJ of heat.
questions.solution:
The enthalpy of vaporization $\Delta H_{vap}$ represents the heat required to vaporize one mole of ethanol. Given that $11.8\text{ kJ}$ vaporizes $11.5\text{ g}$ of ethanol, we first determine the molar mass of ethanol as $C_2H_5OH$.

The molar mass is $2 \times 12.01 + 6 \times 1.008 + 16.00 = 46.068\text{ g/mol}$. The number of moles vaporized is $\frac{11.5}{46.068} \approx 0.2496\text{ mol}$.

The enthalpy of vaporization is thus $\Delta H_{vap} = \frac{11.8}{0.2496} \approx 47.275\text{ kJ/mol}$, which rounds to $47.2\text{ kJ/mol}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the enthalpy change of vaporisation of benzene if 13 gram of benzene vaporised by supplying 5.1 kJ of heat.
questions.solution:
Enthalpy change of vaporisation calculation for benzene

The molar mass of benzene $(C_6H_6)$ is $6 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 = 78$ g/mol. With $13$ g vaporized, the number of moles is $\frac{13}{78} = \frac{1}{6}$ mol.

Given that $5.1$ kJ of heat is supplied, the enthalpy change per mole is calculated as $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = \frac{5.1}{1/6} = 5.1 \times 6 = 30.6$ kJ/mol.

The calculated value of $30.6$ kJ/mol corresponds to option C.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the entropy change of surrounding if 2 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and 1 mole of $\mathrm{O}_2$ gas combine to form 2 moles of liquid water by releasing 525 kJ heat to surrounding at constant pressure and at 300 K .
questions.solution:
Entropy change of the surrounding is calculated from $\Delta S_{\text{surrounding}} = \frac{q_{\text{surrounding}}}{T}$.

The heat released to the surroundings is $q_{\text{surrounding}} = 525~\text{kJ}$. To match the answer units, convert to joules: $q_{\text{surrounding}} = 525 \times 1000 = 525000~\text{J}$.

At temperature $T = 300~\text{K}$, the entropy change becomes $\Delta S_{\text{surrounding}} = \frac{525000}{300} = 1750~\text{J}~\text{K}^{-1}$.

This result corresponds precisely to option B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following reactions exhibits decrease in entropy?
questions.solution:
Decrease in Entropy Analysis

Entropy decreases when the number of gaseous moles reduces or when matter transitions to a more ordered phase.

For reaction D: $2\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{l})}$, reactants total 3 moles of gas, while products yield 2 moles of liquid. The reduction from 3 gaseous moles to 0 coupled with the gas-to-liquid phase transition results in decreased entropy.

Thus, the correct choice is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate $\Delta S$ total for a certain reaction at 298 K if $\Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ}=-208.6 \mathrm{~kJ}$ and $\Delta S^{\circ}=-36 J^{-1}$
questions.solution:
The total entropy change is determined by summing the system and surroundings contributions: $\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}$.

The entropy change of the surroundings is calculated from the enthalpy change: $\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = -\frac{\Delta H_{\text{system}}}{T}$.
Given $\Delta H^{\circ} = -208.6 \times 10^3 \text{ J}$ and $T = 298 \text{ K}$,
$\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = -\frac{-208.6 \times 10^3}{298} = 700 \text{ JK}^{-1}$.

The total entropy change becomes:
$\Delta S_{\text{total}} = -36 + 700 = 664 \text{ JK}^{-1}$.

This value corresponds to option A.

The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the change in internal energy of the system if 20 kJ of work is done on the system and it releases 10 kJ of heat in a particular reaction.
questions.solution:
The First Law of Thermodynamics gives the change in internal energy as $\Delta U = q + w$, where $q$ is heat added to the system and $w$ is work done on the system.

Heat released by the system corresponds to $q = -10\text{ kJ}$, while work done on the system gives $w = +20\text{ kJ}$.

Substituting these values yields $\Delta U = (-10\text{ kJ}) + (20\text{ kJ}) = 10\text{ kJ}$.

The internal energy increases by $10\text{ kJ}$, making B the correct answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following reactions performs zero work?
questions.solution:
For a reaction to perform zero work at constant temperature and pressure, the change in moles of gas, $\Delta n_g$, must be zero. This is since the work done by an ideal gas is $W = -P\Delta V$, and at constant $T$, $\Delta V = \frac{\Delta n_g R T}{P}$, hence $W = -\Delta n_g R T$.

Calculate $\Delta n_g$ for each reaction, counting only gaseous species:

A: $\mathrm{CH}_{4(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{Cl}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{g})}$
$\Delta n_g = (1 + 1) - (1 + 1) = 2 - 2 = 0$. A performs zero work.

B: $3 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{N}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(\mathrm{g})}$
$\Delta n_g = 2 - (3 + 1) = 2 - 4 = -2$.

C: $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \frac{5}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}$
$\Delta n_g = 2 - \left(1 + \frac{5}{2}\right) = 2 - 3.5 = -1.5$.

D: $2 \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{6(\mathrm{g})} + 7 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 6 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}$
$\Delta n_g = 4 - (2 + 7) = 4 - 9 = -5$.

Only reaction A has $\Delta n_g = 0$, so $\boxed{A}$ is the answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate standard internal energy change for
$\mathrm{OF}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{HF}_{(\mathrm{g})}+\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}$ at 300 K, if $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}$ of $\mathrm{OF}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}, \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})}$ and $\mathrm{HF}_{(\mathrm{g})}$ are 20, -250 and $\quad-270 \quad \mathrm{~kJ} \quad \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \quad$ respectively. $\left[\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} & =\sum \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} \text { of product }-\sum \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} \text { of Reactants } \\ & =[(2 \times-270+0)-(20-250)] \mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ & =-310 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ \Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ} & =\Delta \mathrm{U}^{\circ}+\Delta \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{RT} \\ \Delta \mathrm{U}^{\circ} & =\Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ}-\Delta \mathrm{ng}_{\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{RT} \\ & =-310 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}-(3-2) \times \\ & 8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \times 300 \mathrm{~K} \\ \Delta \mathrm{U}^{\circ} & =-307.50 \mathrm{~kJ} \quad\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate internal energy change of a system if work done by the system is 8 J and heat supplied to it is 40 J .
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta U=q+w \\ & \Delta U=40 J+(-8 J)=32 J\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following equation, relates temperature of a reaction with $\Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{S}^{\circ}$ at equilibrium?
questions.solution: $\begin{array}{ll} & \Delta G^{\circ}=\Delta H^{\circ}-T \Delta S^{\circ} \\ & \text { At equilibrium, } \Delta G^{\circ}=0 \\ \therefore \quad & 0=\Delta H^{\circ}-T \Delta S^{\circ} \\ \therefore \quad & \Delta H^{\circ}=T \Delta S^{\circ}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The enthalpy of vaporisation of a liquid is $30 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and entropy of vaporisation is $75 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. Calculate boiling point of liquid at 1 atm .
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{S}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{T}}(\text { At constant pressure of } 5 \mathrm{~atm}) \\ & 75 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}=\frac{30 \times 10^3 \mathrm{Jmol}^{-1}}{\mathrm{~T}} \\ & \mathrm{~T}=\frac{30000 \mathrm{Jmol}^{-1}}{75 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}} \\ & \mathrm{~T}=400 \mathrm{~K}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find work done on 2 mole of an ideal gas at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ if it is compressed reversibly and isothermally from $5.05 \times 10^6 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$ to $1.01 \times 10^5 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$ pressure.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A system performs mechanical work equal to 15 kJ and looses 2 kJ of heat to surrounding. What is the change in internal energy of a system?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{W}=-15 \mathrm{~kJ}, \mathrm{Q}=-2 \mathrm{~kJ}$
According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{Q}+\mathrm{W}=-2+(-15)=-17 \mathrm{~kJ} .$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Find the constant external pressure required to expand a gas from 2.5 L to 4.5 L if amount of work done is 500 J at 298 K ?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{V}_1 & =2.5 \mathrm{~L}, \mathrm{~V}_2=4.5 \mathrm{~L}, \\ \mathrm{~W} & =-500 \mathrm{~J}=-5 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\left(\because 100 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\right) \\ \mathrm{W} & =-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}} \Delta \mathrm{V} \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}} & =-\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\Delta \mathrm{V}}=-\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right)} \\ & =\frac{-\left(-5 \mathrm{dm}^3 \mathrm{bar}\right)}{(4.5-2.5) \mathrm{dm}^3}=2.5 \text { bar }\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In a particular reaction ' $x$ ' kJ of heat is released by the system and ' y ' kJ of work done is done on the system. What is internal energy change?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Q}=-\mathrm{xkJ}, \mathrm{~W}=+\mathrm{ykJ}$
According to the first law of thermodynamics,
$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore \Delta U =Q+W \\
\Delta U =-x+y k J=y-x k J
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the value of $\Delta \mathrm{G}$ for the following reaction. $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_{4(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}$
if $\Delta \mathrm{H}=57.44 \mathrm{~kJ}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{S}=176 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \Delta \mathrm{H} & =57.44 \mathrm{~kJ} \\ \Delta \mathrm{~S} & =176 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K} \\ \mathrm{~T} & =300 \mathrm{~K} \\ \Delta \mathrm{G} & =\Delta \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{S} \\ \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{G} & =57.44 \mathrm{~kJ}-\left(300 \mathrm{~K} \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right. \\ & =57.44 \mathrm{~kJ}-52.8 \mathrm{~kJ}=4.64 \mathrm{~kJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Under similar conditions enthalpy of freezing is exactly opposite to
questions.solution:
For the reaction, $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{s})} [\text { freezing }]{\text { fusion }} \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{l})}$
Under similar conditions of $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm pressure, $\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}} \mathrm{H}$ is $+6.01 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, whereas $\Delta_{\text {free }} \mathrm{H}$ is $-6.01 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. Thus, enthalpy of freezing is exactly opposite to enthalpy of fusion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
100 ml of $\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}$ and 100 ml of $\mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}$ were allowed to react at 1 bar pressure as
$\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{g})}$
What will be the PV type of work done diuring reaction?
questions.solution:
1 mole of $\mathrm{H}_2$ reacts with 1 mole of $\mathrm{Cl}_2$ to produce 2 moles of HCl.
Hence, 100 mL of $\mathrm{H}_2$ would react with 100 mL of $\mathrm{Cl}_2$ to produce 200 mL of HCl.
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{V}_1 & =100+100=200 \mathrm{~mL}=0.2 \mathrm{dm}^3 \\
\mathrm{~V}_2 & =200 \mathrm{~mL}=0.2 \mathrm{dm}^3 \\
\mathrm{~W} & =-\mathrm{P}_{\text {ext }} \Delta \mathrm{V}=-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}\left(\mathrm{~V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right) \\
\mathrm{W} & =-1(0.2-0.2) \\
& =\text { zero } \mathrm{J}
\end{aligned} \quad\left(\because 100 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\right) .$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the process from following such that volume of system remains constant.
questions.solution:
Isochoric Process:
In isochoric process the change in volume of thermodynamic system is zero. A volume change is zero, so the work done is zero.
- Volume of the system = Constant
- Change in volume \(=0\)
- If, change in volume \(=0\), then work done is zero.
- According to the lst law of thermodynamic law
- \(\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{W}+\mathrm{dU}\)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two moles of an ideal gas are compressed isothermally and reversibly from 40 L to 20 L at 300 K . What is the work done? $\left(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right.$ )
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{W}_{\max } & =-2.303 \mathrm{nRT} \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{~V}_2}{\mathrm{~V}_1} \\ & =-2.303 \times 2 \times 8.314 \times 300 \log _{10} \frac{20}{40} \\ & =3457.97 \mathrm{~J} \\ & =3.458 \mathrm{~kJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the enthalpy change when 12 g carbon react with sufficient hydrogen to form methane. If enthalpy of formation of methane is $-75 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The reaction under consideration is the formation of methane $\left(\mathrm{CH}_4\right)$ from carbon $(\mathrm{C})$ and hydrogen $\left(\mathrm{H}_2\right)$, which can be represented as:
$\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{~s})+2 \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_4(\mathrm{~g})$

The given standard enthalpy of formation for methane $\left(\mathrm{CH}_4\right)$ is:
$\Delta H_f^{\circ}=-75 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

This value indicates the enthalpy change for the formation of one mole of methane under standard conditions.
To calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction involving 12 g of carbon, follow these steps:
Calculate the number of moles of carbon (C):
The molar mass of carbon is approximately $12 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$. Therefore, for 12 g of carbon, the number of moles is:
$\text { moles of } \mathrm{C}=\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { molar mass }}=\frac{12 \mathrm{~g}}{12 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}}=1 \mathrm{~mol}$

Use the number of moles of carbon to find the enthalpy change:
Since 1 mole of carbon produces 1 mole of methane and the enthalpy of formation of methane is $-75 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, the total enthalpy change for the reaction is:
$\Delta H=-75 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol} \times 1 \mathrm{~mol}=-75 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Thus, the enthalpy change when 12 g of carbon react with sufficient hydrogen to form methane is -75 kJ .
Correct answer is Option $\mathrm{C}:-75 \mathrm{~kJ}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which among the following pair of properties are intensive?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is (1) surface tension and viscosity.
Intensive properties are properties that do not depend on the amount or size of the substance, and remain the same regardless of the quantity of the material present. On the other hand, extensive properties depend on the amount of substance.
- Surface tension and viscosity are both intensive properties because they are independent of the amount of substance. Surface tension measures the cohesive force at the surface of a liquid, while viscosity measures the resistance of a liquid to flow. Both are properties that remain constant regardless of the amount of liquid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 2 moles of an ideal gas expands isothermally from $5 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $10 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at a constant external pressure of 1.5 bar. Calculate work done.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{l}}=5 \mathrm{dm}^3, \mathrm{~V}_2=10 \mathrm{dm}^3, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}=1.5 \mathrm{bar} \\ & \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right)=-1.5(10-5)=-7.5 \mathrm{dm}^3 \mathrm{bar}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: An ideal gas expands against constant external pressure of 2 bar from 5 lit to 8 lit and absorbs 10 kJ of heat. What is $\Delta \mathrm{U}$ of the system?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For an ideal gas, the heat of reaction at constant pressure and heat of reaction at constant volume are related by equation
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & q_p=\Delta H \\ & q_v=\Delta U \\ \therefore \quad & \Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_g R T\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the reaction $\mathrm{CH}_{4(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{6(\mathrm{~g})}\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{p}}=3.356 \times 10^{17}$, calculate $\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}$ for the reaction at 298 K .
questions.solution: \(\begin{aligned} & \Delta G^0=-2.303 R T \log _{10} K_p \\ & R=8.314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, T=298 \mathrm{~K} \\ & K_P=3.356 \times 10^{17} \\ & \Delta G^0=-2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298 \times \log _{10}\left(3.356 \times 10^{17}\right) \\ & =-2.303 \times 8.314 \mathrm{Jmol}^{-1} \times 298 \times 17.526 \\ & =-100,000 \mathrm{Jmol}^{-1} \\ & =-100 \mathrm{kJmol}^{-1}\end{aligned}\)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A gas expands isothermally against a constant external pressure of 1 bar from $10 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $20 \mathrm{dm}^3$ by absorbing 800 J of heat from surrounding. Calculate value of $\Delta \mathrm{U}$.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}=1 \mathrm{bar} \\ & \mathrm{V}_1=10 \mathrm{dm}^3, \mathrm{~V}_2=20 \mathrm{dm}^3 \\ & \mathrm{Q}=800 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \mathrm{~W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right)=-1 \mathrm{bar}\left(20 \mathrm{dm}^3-10 \mathrm{dm}^3\right) \\ & \quad=-10 \mathrm{dm}^3 \mathrm{bar}=-1000 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{Q}+\mathrm{W}=800 \mathrm{~J}-1000 \mathrm{~J}=-200 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following equations indicates increase in entropy?
questions.solution: Solid $\mathrm{NaNO}_3$ changes to two aqueous products. Aqueous phase has more randomness than solid phase and hence, entropy of the system increases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from following statements is true about internal energy?
options: It increases with increase in temperature.
It decreases with increase in temperature.
It is not a state function.
questions.solution: The internal energy of a substance increases with increase in temperature due to increase in rotational, translational and vibrational energy of the molecule.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
2 moles of an ideal gas are expanded isothermally and reversibly from 20 L to 40 L at 300 K . Calculate work done.
( $\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
Given: - $n=2 \mathrm{~mol}$, - $R=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, - $T=300 \mathrm{~K}$, - $V_1=20 \mathrm{~L}$, - $V_2=40 \mathrm{~L}$.
Formula for Work Done: $W=-2.303 n R T \log _{10}\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$
Substitute the values: $W=-2.303 \cdot 2 \cdot 8.314 \cdot 300 \cdot \log _{10}\left(\frac{40}{20}\right)$
Simplify the logarithmic term: $\log _{10}\left(\frac{40}{20}\right)=\log _{10}(2) \approx 0.3010$
Calculate: $\begin{gathered} W=-2.303 \cdot 2 \cdot 8.314 \cdot 300 \cdot 0.3010 \\ W=-2.303 \cdot 4988.4 \cdot 0.3010 \approx-3457.97 \mathrm{~J} \end{gathered}$
Answer: $W=-3457.97 \mathrm{~J}$, closest to Option 4: -3,457.97 J.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 10 g each of $\mathrm{NH}_3, \mathrm{~N}_2, \mathrm{Cl}_2$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}$ are expanded isothermally and reversibly at same temperature. Identify gas that performs maximum work.
questions.solution:
$W_{\max }=-2.303 n R T \log _{10} \frac{V_2}{V_1}$
Hence, $W_{\text {max }} \propto \mathrm{n}$
(Given: $\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{T}, \mathrm{V}_2, \mathrm{~V}_1=$ Constant)
$\mathrm{W}_{\max } \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{M} \cdot \mathrm{W}}$ (Given: equal mass)
Hence, lower the molecular mass, greater is the work done. Among the given, $\mathrm{NH}_3$ has the lowest molecular mass which performs maximum work.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the factor from following on which heat of reaction does not depend.
options: Physical states of reactants and products.
Total number of steps in which reaction occurs.
Whether the reaction is carried out at constant pressure or constant volume.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is $(B)$ Total number of steps in which reaction occurs.
The heat of reaction (also known as enthalpy change, $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ ) depends on several factors, but the total number of steps in which a reaction occurs (i.e., whether the reaction occurs in one step or multiple steps) does not affect the heat of reaction. According to Hess's Law, the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same, regardless of the number of steps in which the reaction occurs, provided the initial and final states of the system are the same.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For the reaction,
$2 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{g})}, \Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ}=-573.2 \mathrm{~kJ}$
What is heat of decomposition of water per mol?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which from the following defines enthalpy of a system?
questions.solution:
- (1) Ratio of pressure to volume: This is incorrect. The ratio of pressure to volume is not related to enthalpy.
- (2) Product of pressure and volume: This is also incorrect. The product of $P$ and $V$ is part of the enthalpy formula but doesn't define it by itself.
- (3) Internal energy (U) + PV: This is the correct definition of enthalpy. Enthalpy is the sum of internal energy and $P \times V$.
- (4) Internal energy (U) - PV: This is incorrect. Enthalpy involves adding, not subtracting, PV from internal energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following statements is appropriate as per first law of thermodynamics?
options: Energy of the system remains constant.
Energy of the surrounding remains constant.
Entropy of the universe remains constant.
Energy of the universe remains constant.
questions.solution:
The First Law of Thermodynamics is a statement of the conservation of energy. It says:
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred or transformed from one form to another.
In the context of thermodynamics:
- The energy of a system can change due to heat transfer $(Q)$ or work $(W)$ done by/on the system. This is mathematically expressed as:
$\Delta U=Q-W$
where $\Delta U$ is the change in internal energy of the system.
However, if we consider the system and surroundings together (the universe), the total energy remains constant because energy lost by the system is gained by the surroundings, and vice versa.

questions.solution:
For the reaction,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_{3(\mathrm{~g})} \\
& \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}=\sum \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {reactant }}^{\circ}-\sum \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {product }}^{\circ} \\
& =\left[4 \Delta \mathrm{H}_{(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H})}^{\circ}+\Delta \mathrm{H}_{(\mathrm{C=C})}^{\circ}+\Delta \mathrm{H}_{(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H})}^{\circ}\right] \\
& -\left[6 \Delta \mathrm{H}_{(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H})}^{\circ}+\Delta \mathrm{H}_{(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C})}^{\circ}\right] \\
& =[(4 \times 414 \mathrm{~kJ})+615 \mathrm{~kJ}+435 \mathrm{~kJ}]-[(6 \times 414 \mathrm{~kJ}) \\
& +347 \mathrm{~kJ}] \\
& =(1656 \mathrm{~kJ}+615 \mathrm{~kJ}+435 \mathrm{~kJ})-(2484 \mathrm{~kJ}+347 \mathrm{~kJ}) \\
& =2706 \mathrm{~kJ}-2831 \mathrm{~kJ}=-125 \mathrm{~kJ}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which among the following is NOT an intensive property?
questions.solution:
Internal energy is not an intensive property, but rather an extensive property:
An intensive property is independent of the amount of a substance in a system. In contrast, an extensive property depends on the amount of a substance in a system.
Example: Internal energy is an extensive property because its magnitude depends on the amount of substance in a given state.

& \therefore \quad \mathrm{W}=-1 \text { bar }\left(0.15 \mathrm{dm}^3-0.3 \mathrm{dm}^3\right) \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{W}=0.15 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar } \\
& \therefore \quad W=0.15 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar } \times 100 \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }} \\
& \therefore \quad W=15 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}

The PV work in joules is $15 \mathrm{~J}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A gas absorbs $200 \mathrm{~J}$ heat and expands by $500 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ against a constant external pressure $2 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}$. What is the change in internal energy?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta V=500 \mathrm{~cm}^3=0.5 \mathrm{dm}^3 \\ & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}=2 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}=2 \text { bar } \\ & \text { (since, } 1 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}=1 \text { bar) } \\ & \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}} \times \Delta \mathrm{V} \\ & =-2 \times(0.5) \\ & =-1 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar } \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{W}=-100 \mathrm{~J} \quad\left(\text { since, } 1 \mathrm{dm}^3 \mathrm{bar}=100 \mathrm{~J}\right) \\ & \text { According to first law of thermodynamics, } \\ & \Delta U=Q+W=200 \mathrm{~J}-100 \mathrm{~J}=+100 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which among the following pair of properties is intensive?
questions.solution: A property which is independent of the amount of matter in a system is called intensive property. Examples: Specific heat and pressure

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If $8.84 \mathrm{~kJ}$ heat is liberated for formation of $3 \mathrm{~g}$ ethane, calculate its $\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}$.
questions.solution:
Formation of ethane:
$2 \mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{6(\mathrm{~g})} ; \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}=\text { ? }$
Molar mass of $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_6=30 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\therefore \quad 3 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_6=\frac{3}{30}=\frac{1}{10} \cdot \mathrm{mol}\therefore \quad$ For formation of $\frac{1}{10} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_6, 8.84 \mathrm{~kJ}$ heat is liberated.
$\therefore \quad$ Formation of $1 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_6$ will liberate $88.4 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of heat.
$\therefore \quad \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}$ of $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_6=-88.4 \mathrm{~kJ}$

questions.solution: Std.12|Ch-4|Subopic-4.8

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is change in internal energy when system releases $8 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of heat and performs $660 \mathrm{~J}$ of work on the surrounding?
questions.solution: $\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{Q}+\mathrm{W}=-8000 \mathrm{~J}-660 \mathrm{~J}=-8660 \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the final volume when 2 moles of an ideal gas expand from $3 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant external pressure 1.6 bar and the work done in the process is $800 \mathrm{~J}$.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\text {ext }} \Delta \mathrm{V}=-\mathrm{P}_{\text {ext }}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right) \\ & \mathrm{V}_1=3 \mathrm{dm}^3 \\ & \mathrm{~V}_2=? \\ & \mathrm{P}_{\text {ext }}=1.6 \text { bar } \\ & \mathrm{W}=-800 \mathrm{~J}=8 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\left(\because 100 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\right) \\ & -8=-1.6\left(\mathrm{~V}_2-3\right) \\ & \mathrm{V}_2-3=5 \\ & \mathrm{~V}_2=8 \mathrm{dm}^3\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For $\mathrm{NaCl}_{(\mathrm{s})}$ enthalpy of solution is $4 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and lattice enthalpy is $790 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. What is hydration enthalpy of $\mathrm{NaCl}$ ?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \Delta_{\text {soln }} \mathrm{H} & =\Delta_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{H}+\Delta_{\text {hyd }} \mathrm{H} \\ \therefore \quad \Delta_{\text {hyd }} \mathrm{H} & =\Delta_{\text {soln }} \mathrm{H}-\Delta_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{H} \\ & =4 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}-790 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & =-786 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What is the value of $\Delta \mathrm{H}-\Delta \mathrm{U}$ for the following reaction?
$2 \mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_{6(\mathrm{~g})}$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{g}}=\text { (moles of product gases) } \\ & \Delta \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{g}}=1-3=-2 \mathrm{~mol} \\ & \text { Now, using formula, } \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\Delta \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{RT} \\ \therefore \quad & \Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{U}-2 \mathrm{RT} \\ \therefore \quad & \Delta \mathrm{H}-\Delta \mathrm{U}=-2 \mathrm{RT}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: An ideal gas expands by $1.5 \mathrm{~L}$ against a constant external pressure of $2 \mathrm{~atm}$ at $298 \mathrm{~K}$. Calculate the work done?

Chemistry
questions.q: Which among the following reactions exhibits $\Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{U} ?$
questions.solution: When $\Delta \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{g}}=0, \Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{U}$. For reaction (A), $\Delta \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{g}}=0$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An ideal gas expands by performing $200 \mathrm{~J}$ of work, during this internal energy increases by $432 \mathrm{~J}$. What is enthalpy change?
questions.solution:
Assuming constant pressure,
$\Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}} \Delta \mathrm{V}=\Delta \mathrm{U}-\mathrm{W}$
Work done $(\mathrm{W})=-200 \mathrm{~J}$ (for expansion of a gas)
$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \mathrm{U}=+432 \mathrm{~J} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{U}-\mathrm{W}=+432-(-200)=+632 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the value of $\Delta G$ for following reaction at $300 \mathrm{~K}$.
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \\ & \left(\Delta \mathrm{H}=7 \mathrm{~kJ}, \Delta \mathrm{S}=24.8 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right)\end{aligned}$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \Delta \mathrm{H} & =7 \mathrm{~kJ} \\ \Delta \mathrm{S} & =24.8 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}=24.8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \\ \mathrm{~T} & =300 \mathrm{~K} \\ \Delta \mathrm{G} & =\Delta \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{S} \\ \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{G} & =7 \mathrm{~kJ}-\left(300 \mathrm{~K} \times 24.8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right) \\ & =7 \mathrm{~kJ}-7.44 \mathrm{~kJ}=-0.44 \mathrm{~kJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\Delta \mathrm{V}=0$ (Isochoric process)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If a system absorbs $30 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of heat and perform $12 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of work on the surrounding. What is the increase in internal energy of the system?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \triangle E=\delta Q+\delta W \\ & =30+(-12) \\ & =18 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An ideal gas is allowed to expand from $2 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $6 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3$ against a constant external pressure of 1 bar. The work done in $\mathrm{kJ}$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{W} & =-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right) \\ & =-\left(6 \times 10^{-3}-2 \times 10^{-3}\right) \mathrm{bar}-\mathrm{m}^3 \\ & =-4 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^5 \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m}^2}-\mathrm{m}^3 \\ & =-400 \mathrm{~J}=-0.4 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If $Q$ is the heat liberated from the system and W is the work done on the system then first law of thermodynamics can be written as
questions.solution: $\Delta \mathrm{u}=\mathrm{Q}+\mathrm{W}$

questions.q:
What is the heat of formation of $\mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{g})}$ from following equation?
$\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{g})} \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}=-194 \mathrm{~kJ}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Mark out the enthalpy of formation of carbon monoxide (CO).

Given, Cs+O2g→CO2g, ∆H=-393.3kJ/mol and COg+12O2g→CO2g; ΔH=-282.2 kJ/mol.
questions.solution:
To find:Cs+12O2g → COg=0;    ΔHf∘=??        (I)

Given:

Cs+O2g→CO2g;     ΔHf∘1=-393.3 kJ/mol       IICOs+12O2g→CO2g ;   ΔHf∘2=-282.2 kJ/mol      III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the work done when 2 moles of an ideal gas expand from a volume of $5 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $7 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3$ against a constant external pressure of $2.02 \times 10^5 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$.
questions.solution: W.D. $=-P\left(v^2-v^1\right)\begin{aligned} & =2.02 \times 10^5(7-5) \\ & =-404 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~J} \\ & =-404 \mathrm{~kJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The bond enthalpies of $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}$ and $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bonds are $360,600,400$ and $410 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively. What is the heat of hydrogenation of ethylene?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \Delta \mathrm{H} & =\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{in}}-\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\text {out }} \\ & =\left(\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}}+4 \mathrm{~B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}+\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}}\right)-\left(\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}}+6 \mathrm{~B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}\right) \\ & =\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}}+\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}}-\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}}-2 \mathrm{~B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}} \\ & =600+400-360-2 \times 410=-180 \mathrm{~kJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An ideal gas is compressed from $10 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $1 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at a constant pressure 2 bar. Calculate the work done by gas during compression.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{W} & =-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right) \\ & =-2(1-10) \\ & =+18 \mathrm{bar}-\mathrm{dm}^3 \\ & =1.8 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate bond enthalpy of $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond from following reaction.
$\mathrm{H}_2(g)+\mathrm{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{HCl}(g), \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}=-185 \mathrm{~kJ}$
(Given bond enthalpies of $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bonds are $435.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and $244 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\circ}=\left(\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{in}}-(\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E})_{\text {out }}\right. \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\circ}=\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}}+\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Cl}}-2 \times \mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Cl}} \\ & -185=435+244-2 x \\ & 2 x=435+244+185 \\ & x=432 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the combustion of one mole acetic acid, work done at $298 \mathrm{~K}$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}(l)+2 \mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_2(g)+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(l) \\ & \Delta n_g=2-2=0 \\ & W=-\Delta n_g R T \\ & =-0 \times R T=0.0 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the change in enthalpy in a chemical reaction when work done is $-800 \mathrm{~J}$ and increase in internal energy is $600 \mathrm{~J}$.

As process is isothermal

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A gas is allowed to expand against a constant external pressure of 2.5 bar from an initial volume of $2.5 \mathrm{~L}$ to a final volume of $4.5 \mathrm{~L}$. What is amount of work done?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} W & =-P\left(V_2-V_1\right) \\ & =-2.5(4.5-2.5) \\ & =-5.0 \mathrm{bar}-\mathrm{L} \\ & =-500 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is change in internal energy system does $140 \mathrm{KJ}$ of work on surrounding and $40 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of heat is added to system?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the reaction, $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{OH}(l)+30_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}(l) \Delta \mathrm{U}$ is the heat of reaction at constant volume. Then heat of reaction at constant pressure is

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the change in internal energy of the system if $37.6 \mathrm{~J}$ of work is done by the system with heat loss of $14.6 \mathrm{~J}$ ?
questions.solution:
From I $^{\text {st }}$ law of thermodynamic
According to $\mathrm{I}^{\text {st }}$ law of thermodynamics
$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{E}=\delta \mathrm{Q}+\delta \mathrm{W} \\ & =-14.6+(-37.6) \\ & =-52.2 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The enthalpies of combustion of C(graphite) and C(diamond) are -393.8 and $-395.3 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The enthalpy of conversion of $\mathrm{C}$ (graphite) to $\mathrm{C}$ (diamond) is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{eq}^{\mathrm{n}} 1 \ldots . . \mathrm{C}(\text { graphite })+\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \quad \Delta \mathrm{H}_1=-393.8 \frac{\mathrm{KJ}}{\mathrm{mol}} \\ & \mathrm{eq}^{\mathrm{n}} 2 \ldots . . \mathrm{C}(\text { diamond })+\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \quad \Delta \mathrm{H}_2=-395.3 \frac{\mathrm{KJ}}{\mathrm{mol}} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{eq}^{\mathrm{n}} 1-\mathrm{eq}^{\mathrm{n} 2}=\Delta \mathrm{H}_1-\Delta \mathrm{H}_2 \\ & =-393.8-(-395.3) \\ & =1.5 \frac{\mathrm{KJ}}{\mathrm{mol}}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A gas is allowed to expand in an insulated container against a constant external pressure of 2.5 bar from $4.5 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $7 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3$. What is the change in internal energy of the gas?
questions.solution:
Container is insulated
$\therefore \delta Q=0$
We know $\Delta \mathrm{E}=\delta \mathrm{Q}+\delta \mathrm{W}\begin{aligned} & =0+\left[-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right)\right] \\ & =-2.5(7-4.5) \\ & =-2.5(2.5) \times 100 \\ & =-625 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
When $2.0 \mathrm{~g}$ sucrose is oxidised forming $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)}$ the internal energy changes by $24 \mathrm{~kJ}$. Calculate the value of $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ at $298 \mathrm{~K}$ in $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$.
(Molar mass of sucrose $=342 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{C}_{12} \mathrm{H}_{22} \mathrm{O}_{11}(\mathrm{~s})+12 \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow 12 \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})+11 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{c}) \\ & \Delta \mathrm{ng}=12-12=0 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{E}+\Delta \mathrm{ngRT} \\ & =24 \mathrm{~kJ} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H} \text { for } 2 \text { g sucrose }=-\frac{24}{342} \times 2 \\ & =0.1403 \mathrm{~kJ} \\ & =-140.3 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A certain system is exothermic by $260 \mathrm{~kJ}$ and does $10 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of work. What is the change in internal energy?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta E=8 Q+8 W \\ & =-260+(-10) \\ & =-270 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The difference between enthalpy change and internal energy change for the combustion of one mole of ethyl alcohol is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{OH}(\ell)+3 \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\ell) \\ & \Delta \mathrm{H}=\Delta \mathrm{E}+\Delta_{\mathrm{ng}} \mathrm{RT}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What is the work done at $300 \mathrm{~K}$ for the reaction?
$\mathrm{SO}_2(\mathrm{~g})+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{SO}_3(\mathrm{~g}) ?($ Given $\mathrm{R}=8.314) \mathrm{K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which among the following pair is of extensive and intensive properties respectively?
questions.solution: Theory based

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An ideal gas is compressed from a volume of $1 \mathrm{~m}^3$ to $0.5 \mathrm{~m}^3$ at a pressure of 0.2 bar. what is the value of work done by the gas during compression?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right) \\ & =-0.2(0.5-1) \mathrm{bar}-\mathrm{m}^3 \\ & =0.1 \mathrm{bar}-\mathrm{m}^3 \\ & =10 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate $\Delta \mathrm{U}$ if $2 \mathrm{~kJ}$ heat is released and $10 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of work is done on the system.
questions.solution:
From $\mathrm{I}^{\text {st }}$ law of thermodynamics
$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{E}=\partial \mathrm{Q}+\partial \mathrm{W} \\ & =-2+10 \\ & =8 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is change in internal energy if a system gains $\mathrm{xJ}$ of heat and yJ work is done on it?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \Delta \mathrm{E} & =\delta \mathrm{Q}=\delta \mathrm{W} \\ & =+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Under isothermal condition a gas expands from $0.2 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $0.8 \mathrm{dm}^3$ against a constant pressure of 2 bar at $300 \mathrm{~K}$. Find the work done by the gas.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{W} & =-\mathrm{PdV} \\ & =-2(0.8-0.2) \mathrm{bar}-\mathrm{dm}^2 \\ & =-2(0.6) \times 10^2 \mathrm{~J} \\ & =-120 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If $65 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of work is done on the system and it releases and it releases $25 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of heat. What is change in internal energy of the system?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta E=\delta Q+\delta W \\ & =-25+65 \\ & =40 \mathrm{KJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is internal energy change when $62 \mathrm{~J}$ of work is done on the system and $128 \mathrm{~J}$ of heat is transferred to surrounding?
questions.solution:
Work done on the system $=+62 \mathrm{~J}$
Heat released to the surrounding $=-128 \mathrm{~J}$
From first law of thermodynamics,
$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{q}+\mathrm{W} \\
& =-128+62 \\
& =-66 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When certain volume of gas expands against a constant external pressure of $2.40 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~Pa}$ at $300 \mathrm{~K}$ to $2.2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3$. If the work obtained is $-0.048 \mathrm{~kJ}$. What is the initial volume of the gas?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}}\left[\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right] \\ & -0.048 \times 1000 \mathrm{~J}=-2.4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~Pa}\left[2.2 \times 10^{-3}-\mathrm{V}_1\right] \mathrm{m}^3 \\ & \frac{48}{2.8} \times 10^{-5}=2.2 \times 10^{-3}-\mathrm{V}_1 \\ & \mathrm{~V}_1=2.2 \times 10^{-3}-0.2 \times 10^{-3} \\ & \mathrm{~V}_1=2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For isochoric process, the first law of thermodynamics can be expressed as
questions.solution:
For Isochoric process, Volume remains constant.
$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \mathrm{V}=0 \\
& \mathrm{~W}=-\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{V}=0
\end{aligned}$
First Law of thermodynamics,
$\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{q}+\mathrm{W}$
At constant volume condition, $\left(\mathrm{W}=0, \mathrm{q}=\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{v}}\right)\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{v}}$
Or $\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{V}}$

questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In an isothermal and reversible process, $1 \cdot 6 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{O}_{2}$ expands from $10 \mathrm{dm}^{3}$ to $100 \mathrm{dm}^{3}$ at $300 \mathrm{~K}$, work done in the process is $(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J})$
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{V}_{1}=10 \mathrm{dm}^{3} \quad, \mathrm{~V}_{2}=100 \mathrm{dm}^{3}, \quad \mathrm{~T}=300 \mathrm{~K}$,
$\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, \quad \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}=1.6 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~kg}=16 \mathrm{~g}\therefore \quad \mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}}=\frac{16}{32}=0.5 \mathrm{~mol}$
For isothermal and reversible process,
$\begin{aligned}
W_{\max } &=-2.303 \mathrm{nRT} \log _{10} \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} \\
\therefore W_{\max } &=-2.303 \times 0.5 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log _{10} \frac{100}{10}=-2872 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Based on first law of thermodynamics which of the following is correct
questions.solution:
In isobaric process, pressure is constant and volume increase from V1 to V2 due to the absorption of heat. According to the first law of thermodynamics, ΔU=q+W
At constant pressure, qp=ΔU-W
qp=ΔU-pΔV
qp=U2-U1--pV2-V1
qp=U2+pV2-U1+pV1
qp=H2-H1
qp=ΔH                                                ...(i)
As we know, ΔH=ΔU+pΔV
ΔH=ΔU+W
Putting the value of ΔH in (1)
qp=ΔU+W
Other corrected options are as follows:
• For adiabatic process, ΔU=W
• For an isochoric process, ΔU=qv
• For an isothermal process q=-W

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The function $f(x) = x(x + 3)e^{-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)x}$ satisfies all the conditions of Rolle's theorem in $[-3, 0]$, then $c =$
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = (x^2 + 3x)e^{-\dfrac{x}{2}}$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$f'(x) = (2x + 3)e^{-\dfrac{x}{2}} + (x^2 + 3x)e^{-\dfrac{x}{2}} \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

$f'(x) = e^{-\dfrac{x}{2}} \left( 2x + 3 - \dfrac{x^2 + 3x}{2} \right)$

$f'(x) = e^{-\dfrac{x}{2}} \left( \dfrac{-x^2 + x + 6}{2} \right)$

By Rolle's theorem, there exists $c \in (-3, 0)$ such that $f'(c) = 0$.

$\dfrac{-c^2 + c + 6}{2} = 0$

$c^2 - c - 6 = 0$

$(c - 3)(c + 2) = 0$

$c = 3$ or $c = -2$

Since $c \in (-3, 0)$, we get $c = -2$.

Answer: $-2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The line $x + y = 0$ touches the curve $y^2 = ax^3 + b$ at $(1, -1)$ then values of $a$ and $b$ respectively are ...........
questions.solution:
Since the point $(1, -1)$ lies on the curve $y^2 = ax^3 + b$, substituting $x = 1$ and $y = -1$ gives:

$(-1)^2 = a(1)^3 + b$

$a + b = 1$

Differentiating the equation of the curve with respect to $x$ gives:

$2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3ax^2$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3ax^2}{2y}$

The slope of the tangent at $(1, -1)$ is:

$\left. \dfrac{dy}{dx} \right|_{(1, -1)} = \dfrac{3a(1)^2}{2(-1)} = -\dfrac{3a}{2}$

The given tangent line is $x + y = 0$, which has a slope of $-1$. Equating the slopes gives:

$-\dfrac{3a}{2} = -1$

$a = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Substituting the value of $a$ into $a + b = 1$ gives:

$\dfrac{2}{3} + b = 1$

$b = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: An aeroplane at an altitude of 1 km is flying horizontally at 600 km / hr, passes directly over an observer. Then the rate at which it is approaching the observer when it is 1250 meters away from him is........
questions.solution:
Let the horizontal distance of the aeroplane from the observer be $x$ km and the actual distance be $s$ km.

The altitude of the aeroplane is $h = 1$ km.

From the right-angled triangle formed by the observer, the aeroplane, and the point on the ground directly below the aeroplane, we have:

$s^2 = x^2 + 1^2$

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get:

$2s \dfrac{ds}{dt} = 2x \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

$\dfrac{ds}{dt} = \dfrac{x}{s} \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

We are given the horizontal velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 600$ km/hr.

When the distance $s = 1250$ m $= 1.25$ km, the horizontal distance $x$ is:

$x = \sqrt{s^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{1.25^2 - 1} = \sqrt{1.5625 - 1} = \sqrt{0.5625} = 0.75$ km

Substituting the values into the derivative equation:

$\dfrac{ds}{dt} = \dfrac{0.75}{1.25} \times 600$

$\dfrac{ds}{dt} = \dfrac{3}{5} \times 600 = 360$ km/hr

Answer: $360\ km/hr$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: On the interval $[0, 1]$, the function $f(x) = x^{25}(1 - x)^{75}$ attains its maximum value at the point $x = $....
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = x^{25}(1 - x)^{75}$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$f'(x) = 25x^{24}(1 - x)^{75} - 75x^{25}(1 - x)^{74}$

$f'(x) = 25x^{24}(1 - x)^{74} [ (1 - x) - 3x ]$

$f'(x) = 25x^{24}(1 - x)^{74} (1 - 4x)$

For maximum or minimum, $f'(x) = 0$

$25x^{24}(1 - x)^{74} (1 - 4x) = 0$

$x = 0, 1, \dfrac{1}{4}$

At $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, $f(x) = 0$.

For $x \in (0, 1)$, $f(x) \gt 0$.

Thus, $f(x)$ attains its maximum value at $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the line $ax + by + 5 = 0$ is a normal to the curve $xy = 1$ then .....
questions.solution:
The equation of the given curve is $xy = 1$, which can be written as $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$.

Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get the slope of the tangent:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{x^2}$

The slope of the normal to the curve is given by:

$m = -\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{dy}{dx}} = x^2$

Since $x \neq 0$ for any point on the curve $xy = 1$, we have $x^2 \gt 0$. Thus, the slope of the normal is always strictly positive.

The given equation of the normal is $ax + by + 5 = 0$.

The slope of this line is $-\dfrac{a}{b}$.

For this line to represent a normal to the curve, its slope must be positive:

$-\dfrac{a}{b} \gt 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{a}{b} \lt 0$

This condition implies that $a$ and $b$ must have opposite signs. Among the given options, the only one that satisfies this condition is $a \gt 0, b \lt 0$.

Answer: $a \gt 0, b \lt 0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A spherical iron ball $10$ cm in radius is coated with a layer of ice of uniform thickness that melts at a rate of $50\ \text{cm}^3/\text{min}$. When the thickness of ice is $5$ cm, the rate at which the thickness of ice decreases is...
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the iron ball and $x$ be the thickness of the ice.

Given $r = 10$ cm.

The volume of the ice is $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (r+x)^3 - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.

Differentiating with respect to time $t$:

$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi (r+x)^2 \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

Given that the ice melts at a rate of $50\ \text{cm}^3/\text{min}$, we have $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = -50$.

When $x = 5$ cm, $r+x = 10 + 5 = 15$ cm.

Substituting the values:

$-50 = 4\pi (15)^2 \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

$-50 = 900\pi \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{50}{900\pi} = -\dfrac{1}{18\pi}\ \text{cm}/\text{min}$

The rate at which the thickness of ice decreases is $\dfrac{1}{18\pi}\ \text{cm}/\text{min}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the rate of increase of surface area of a spherical balloon is $5\,\text{cm}^2/\text{sec}$ and rate of increase of volume of a spherical balloon is $10\,\text{cm}^3/\text{sec}$, then the radius of the balloon at that time is...
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius, $S$ be the surface area, and $V$ be the volume of the spherical balloon.

$S = 4\pi r^2$

Differentiating with respect to time $t$:
