questions.q: A steel ball of radius 6 mm has a terminal speed of $12 \mathrm{cms}^{-1}$ in a viscous liquid. What will be the terminal speed of a steel ball of radius 3 mm in the same liquid?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The pressure inside a soap bubble A is 1.01 atmosphere and that in a soap bubble B is 1.02 atmosphere. The ratio of volume of bubble A to that of $B$ is [Surrounding pressure $=1$ atmosphere $]$
questions.solution:
Outside pressure $=1 \mathrm{~atm}$
Pressure inside first bubble $=1.01 \mathrm{~atm}$
Pressure inside second bubble $=1.02 \mathrm{~atm}\therefore \quad$ Excess pressures will be $\Delta \mathrm{P}_1=1.01-1=0.01 \mathrm{~atm}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{P}_2=1.02-1=0.02 \mathrm{~atm}\begin{array}{ll} & \text { Now, } \Delta \mathrm{P} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{r} \propto \frac{1}{\Delta \mathrm{P}} \\ \therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{P}_2}{\Delta \mathrm{P}_1}=\frac{0.02}{0.01}=\frac{2}{1} \\ & \text { Now, } \mathrm{V}=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{~V} \propto \mathrm{r}^3 \\ \therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{~V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^3=\left(\frac{2}{1}\right)^3=\frac{8}{1}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A liquid drop of density ' $\rho$ ' is floating half immersed in a liquid of density ' $d$ '. If ' $T$ ' is the surface tension then the diameter of the liquid drop is ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { Surface Tension }=\mathrm{T} \times 2 \pi \mathrm{r} \\ & \frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \rho \mathrm{~g}=2 \pi \mathrm{rT}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \mathrm{dg}\end{aligned}\begin{array}{ll}\therefore \quad & 2 \pi r T=\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho g-\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 d g\right) \times \frac{1}{2} \\ & 2 \pi T=\frac{4}{3} \pi r^2 g\left(\rho-\frac{d}{2}\right) \\ \therefore & r^2=\frac{2 \pi T}{\frac{4}{3} \pi g\left(\rho-\frac{d}{2}\right)} \\ \therefore & r^2=\frac{3 T}{g(2 \rho-d)} \Rightarrow r=\sqrt{\frac{3 T}{g(2 \rho-d)}} \\ & \text { Diameter }=2 r=\sqrt{\frac{12 T}{g(2 \rho-d)}}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gardening pipe having an internal radius ' $R$ ' is connected to a water sprinkler having ' $n$ ' holes each of radius ' $r$ '. The water in the pipe has a speed ' $v$ '. The speed of water leaving the sprinkler is
questions.solution:
Using the equation of continuity, we have
$\mathrm{A}_1 \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{v}^{\prime}$
where $v$ is speed of water in the pipe and $v^{\prime}$ is the speed of water leaving the pipe.
Area of the pipe $=\pi \mathrm{R}^2$
Area of each hole in the sprinkler $=\pi r^2\therefore \quad$ Total area of the holes in the sprinkler $=n \pi r^2\pi R^2 v=n \pi r^2 v^{\prime}$ ...from (i)
$\therefore \quad \mathrm{v}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{R}^2 \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{nr}^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The pressure inside two soap bubbles, (A) is 1.01 and that of (B) is 1.02 atmosphere respectively. The ratio of their respective radii (A to B) is (outside pressure $=1 \mathrm{~atm}$.)
questions.solution:
Outside pressure $=1 \mathrm{~atm}$
Pressure inside first bubble $=1.01 \mathrm{~atm}$
Pressure inside second bubble $=1.02 \mathrm{~atm}\therefore \quad$ Excess pressures will be $\Delta \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}=1.01-1=0.01 \mathrm{~atm}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}=1.02-1=0.02 \mathrm{~atm}$ Now, $\Delta \mathrm{P} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{r} \propto \frac{1}{\Delta \mathrm{P}}\therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\Delta \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}}=\frac{0.02}{0.01}=\frac{2}{1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal ball of radius $9 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}$ and density $10^4 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$ falls freely under gravity through a distance 'h' and erfters a tank of water. Considering that the metal ball has constant velocity, the value of h is [coefficient of viscosity of water $=8.1 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{pa}-\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ density of water $\left.=10^3 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3\right]$
questions.solution:
Velocity of the ball when the ball hits the surface of water $v=\sqrt{2 g h}$
Terminal velocity of the ball, $v=\frac{2}{9} r^2 g \frac{(P-\sigma)}{\eta}$
Equating (i) and (ii), $\sqrt{2 g h}=\frac{2}{9} \frac{r^2 g}{\eta}(P-\sigma)$
Solving for h , $h=\frac{2}{81} r^4\left(\frac{P-\sigma}{\eta}\right)^2 g$
Substituting the given values in the above equation, we have $\mathrm{h}=\frac{2}{81} \times\left(9 \times 10^{-4}\right)^4 \times\left(\frac{10^4-10^3}{8.1 \times 10^{-4}}\right)^2 \mathrm{~g}=20 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Liquid drops are falling slowly one by one from vertical glass tube. The relation between the weight of a drop ' $w$ ', the surface tension ' $T$ ' and the radius ' $r$ ' of the bore of the tube is (Angle of contact is zero)
questions.solution: $\begin{array}{ll} & \text { Weight of liquid drop }=\text { Force due to surface } \\ & \text { tension } \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{W}=\text { Circumference of the tube } \times \mathrm{T} . \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{W}=2 \pi \mathrm{rT}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball rises to surface at a constant velocity in liquid whose density is 4 times greater than that of the material of the ball. The ratio of the force of friction acting on the rising ball and its weight is
questions.solution:
Frictional force $=$ Viscous Force $=V\left(\rho_1-\rho_2\right) g$
Weight $=\mathrm{mg}=\mathrm{V} \rho_1 \mathrm{~g}$
Where $\rho_1$ is the density of ball and $\rho_2$ is density of liquid.
$\begin{array}{ll} 
& \rho_2=4 \rho_1 \\
\therefore \quad & V\left(\rho_1-4 \rho_1\right) g=V\left(-3 \rho_1\right) g . \\
& \text { Frictional force }=3 V\left(\rho_1 g\right) \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{\text { Frictional force }}{\text { Weight }}=\frac{3}{1}=3: 1 \text { ratio }
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A drum of radius ' $R$ ' full of liquid of density ' $d$ ' is rotated at angular velocity ' $\omega$ ' rad/s. The increase in pressure at the centre of the drum will be
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& P_1+\frac{1}{2} \rho v^2+\rho g h=\text { constant } \quad...(i)
& \text { and } v=R \omega \\
& \text {At centre } R=0 \Rightarrow v_1=0 \quad...(ii)
\therefore \quad & \text { From (i), } \\
& P_1+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2+\rho g h=P_2+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2+\rho g h \\
& P_1+0=P_2+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 \\
\therefore \quad & P_1=P_2+\frac{1}{2} \rho(R \omega)^2 \\

& \mathrm{v}_1=0.5 \mathrm{v}_2
..(ii)\end{aligned}$
Substituting (ii) into (i),
$\begin{aligned} 0.75 \mathrm{v}_2^2=4.8 \times 10^{-3} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}_2 & =0.08 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \text { Rate of flow of glycerine } & =A_2 \mathrm{v}_2 \\ & =5 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.08 \\ & =4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^3 / \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}$

The condition for terminal speed $v_{\mathrm{T}}$ is given by,
weight $(W)=$ buoyant force $(f)+$ viscous force $(F)$
We know, $W=\rho V g, f=\sigma V g$ and $F=K v_{\mathrm{T}}^2\therefore \rho V g=\sigma V g+K v_{\mathrm{T}}^2v_{\mathrm{T}}=\sqrt{\frac{(\rho-\sigma) V g}{K}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two glass plates of area $10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$ have $10 \mathrm{~cm}$ thick water film between them. The surface tension of water is $70 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$. The force required to separate two glass plates from each other is
questions.solution:
Consider complete wetting.
The Laplace pressure jump is given by: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta P=\frac{\sigma}{\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)}=\frac{F}{A} \\ & \Rightarrow F=\frac{A \sigma}{\frac{h}{2}}=\frac{10^{-2} \times 70 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-2}} N=28 \mathrm{~N} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When a liquid of density ' $\rho$ ' flows through a tube of diameter ' $d$ ' with critical velocity ' $\mathrm{V}$ ' then the Reynolds number is
$\text { ( } \eta=\text { coefficient of viscosity of liquid) }$
questions.solution:
Dimensionless number that helps to find the dominant force between inertial force and viscous force. It is defined as,
$\text { Reynold's number }=\frac{\text { inertial force }}{\text { viscous force }}=\left(\frac{\rho \mathrm{Vd}}{\eta}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Due to surface tension, the excess pressure inside a smaller drop is 9 units. If 27 smaller drops of same liquid combine then the excess pressure inside the bigger drop is
questions.solution: Excess pressure Or Pressure jump $=2\left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)=9$ units If 27 such drops combine, total volume is: $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}}=27 \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{S}}$ Using volume conservation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^3=27\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^3\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=(3 \mathrm{r}) \\ & \therefore \text { Excess pressure }=\frac{2 \sigma}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{2 \sigma}{3 \mathrm{r}}=3 \text { units } \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a streamlined flow, the velocity of a fluid at a given point
options: changes from low value to high value
changes from high value to low value
questions.solution: By definition, in a streamlined flow the velocity of flow at any chosen point in the liquid is always the same, i.e., it doesn't vary with time.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A certain number of spherical liquid drops of radius $r$ coalesce to form a single drop of radius $R$ and volume $V$. If $T$ is the surface tension of the liquid, which one of the following statements is true for the energy $(E)$ in the process?
questions.solution:
Change in surface energy is given by
$E=T(\Delta A) \quad---(1)$
The initial area is given by,
$\mathrm{A}=\left(4 \pi r^2\right) n$
The final area is given by,
$\mathrm{a}=4 \pi R^2$
Therefore, the change in area is given by,
$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta A=a-A \\
& \Rightarrow \Delta A=4 \pi\left(n r^2-R^2\right)---(2)
\end{aligned}$
Now, using volume conservation: $\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^2\right) n=\frac{4}{3} R^3\therefore n=\frac{R^3}{r^3} \quad---(3)\Delta A=4 \pi\left[\frac{R^3}{r^3} \cdot r^2-R^2\right]=4 \pi\left[\frac{R^3}{r}-\frac{R^3}{R}\right]=\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3\right) 3\left[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{R}\right]=3 V\left[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{R}\right]$
Introducing above value in equation (1)
$E=3 V T\left[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{R}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two rain drops of same radius $r$ falling with terminal velocity $V$ merge and form bigger drop with radius $R$, terminal velocity is
questions.solution:
Expression for terminal velocity can be obtained by balancing weight of the droplet with viscous retardation force and the buoyancy force.
Terminal velocity is given by $v=\frac{2}{9}\left(\frac{r^2(\rho-\sigma)}{\eta}\right)\therefore v \propto r^2$
Now, let $V^{\prime}$ be the terminal velocity of the merged droplet
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \frac{V}{V^{\prime}}=\frac{r^2}{R^2} \\
& \Rightarrow V^{\prime}=\frac{V R^2}{r^2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water rises in a capillary tube of radius ' $r$ ' upto height ' $h$ ' The mass of water in the capillary is ' $m$ ' The mass of water will rise in a capillary of radius will $\frac{r}{4}$ be
questions.solution: The height of water column in a capillary tube is given by $\mathrm{h}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{perg}}$ From eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} & m \propto r^2 \times \frac{1}{r} \\ & m \propto r \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{m^{\prime}}{m}=\frac{\frac{r}{4}}{r} \Rightarrow m^{\prime}=\frac{m}{4}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A lead sphere of mass' $m$ ' falls in a viscous liquid with terminal velocity ' $V$ ' Another lead sphere of mass ' $8 \mathrm{~m}$ ' will fall through the same liquid with terminal velocity
questions.solution:
The terminal velocity is given by,
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{2}{9} \mathrm{r}^2 \frac{(\rho-\sigma)}{\eta} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{T}} \propto \mathrm{r}^2\end{aligned}$
where $r$ radius sphere
$\begin{aligned} & \text { Mass } \propto \text { volume } \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{m}_1}{\mathrm{~m}_2}=\frac{\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}_1^3\right)}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}_2^3\right)} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{m}}{8 \mathrm{~m}}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_1^3}{\mathrm{r}_2^3} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{8}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^3 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}_2=2 \mathrm{r}_1 \\ & \text { So } \frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{T} 2}}{\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{T} 1}}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_2^2}{\mathrm{r}_1^2}=4 \Rightarrow \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{T} 2}=4 \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{T} 1}=4 \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{T}}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The amount of work done in blowing a sops bubble such that its diameter increases from ' $d$ ' to $\mathrm{D}$ ' is ( $\mathrm{T}$ = surface tension of solution )
questions.solution:
Change in surface area
$\begin{aligned} & =2 \times 4 \pi\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)^2-\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}\right)^2\right]=2 \pi\left(\mathrm{D}^2-\mathrm{d}^2\right) \\ & \therefore \text { Work done }=\text { surface tension } \times \text { change in area } \\ & =2 \pi\left(\mathrm{D}^2-\mathrm{d}^2\right) \mathrm{T}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A water drop of radius ' $r$ ' and volume ' $\mathrm{V}$ ' is kept in between the two identical glass plates such that it forms a thin layer of area ' $\mathrm{A}$ ' between the plates. A force ' $\mathrm{F}$ ' is applied such that the two plates separate from each other. The surface tension ' $\mathrm{T}$ ' of the liquid is
questions.solution: Consider complete wetting. The Laplace pressure jump is given by: On plugging into equation (1), $\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2 \mathrm{~A}}\right)}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{A}}$ \therefore \mathrm{T}=\frac{\mathrm{FV}}{2 \mathrm{~A}^2}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square frame of each side ' $L$ ' is dipped in a soap solution and taken out. The force acting on the film formed is $(\mathrm{T}=$ surface tension of soap solution)
questions.solution:
Soap film has two surfaces.
Net force acting on frame $=2$ (force on one surface)
$\begin{aligned} & =2 \times \mathrm{T} \times \text { (perimeter) } \\ & =2 \times \mathrm{T} \times 4 \mathrm{~L}\end{aligned}$
Net force acting on the square frame $=8 \mathrm{TL}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In capillary tube having area of cross-section ' $\mathrm{A}$ ', water rises to a height ' $h$ '. If cross sectional area is reduced to $\frac{A}{9}$, the rise of water in the capillary tube is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{h}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{r \rho g}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{h} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}}\end{aligned}$
And $\mathrm{A}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{r} \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{A}}\Rightarrow \mathrm{h} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{A}}}$
Now, $\frac{h_2}{h_1}=\sqrt{\frac{A_1}{A_2}}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{h_2}{h}=\sqrt{\frac{A}{A / 9}}=3 \\ & \Rightarrow h_2=3 h\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Eight identical small drops of water are falling down vertically through a medium, each with terminal velocity $v$. If they combine to form a single drop, then its terminal velocity will be
questions.solution:
Let $R$, and $r$ be the radii of the big and small drops respectively. The volume of the big drop $=8 \times$ volume of one small drops
$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{4}{2} \pi R^3=8 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \\ & \therefore R^3=(2 r)^3 \therefore R=2 r\end{aligned}$
The terminal velocity of a drop $v \propto(\text { radius })^2\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{V}{v}=\frac{R^2}{r^2}=\frac{(2 r)^2}{r^3}=4 \\ & \therefore V=4 v\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a liquid flows through a tube, the Reynold's number is 900 , the flow of a liquid is
options: changes from turbulent flow to a streamline flow.
changes from a streamline flow to a turbulent flow.
questions.solution:
Reynold number of liquid is 900 . The nature of liquid flow is streamlined.
For fully developed laminar flow $\mathrm{Re}\lt 2300$, transition region exists between $2300\lt \operatorname{Re}\lt 2900$ and for turbulent flow $2900\lt \operatorname{Re}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two narrow tube of diameters $d_1$ and $d_2$ are joined together to form a Utube open at both ends. If U-tube contains water, the difference in water levels in the limbs is
( $T$ is the surface tension of water, angle of contact is zero and density of water is $\rho, g$ is the acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution: Consider the situation below: When angle of contact is zero degree, the radius of meniscus equals the radius of tube. Excess pressure in the first tube $P_1=\frac{4 T}{d_1}$ Excess pressure in the second tube, $P_2=\frac{4 T}{d_2}$ Hence, the pressure difference in the two limbs of the tube is given by, $\Delta P=P_1-P_2=h \rho g\Rightarrow h=\frac{P_1-P_2}{\rho g}=\frac{4 T}{\rho g}\left(\frac{1}{d_1}-\frac{1}{d_2}\right)=\frac{4 T}{\rho g}\left[\frac{d_2-d_1}{d_1 d_2}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $3 \mathrm{~mm}$ is equal to the pressure of a water column of height $0.8 \mathrm{~cm}$, then the surface tension of the soap solution is ( $\rho_{\text {water }}=1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3, g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
The excess pressure inside the bubble is given as, $P=\frac{4 T}{r}$ as the soap bubble has two liquid-gas interfaces.
The pressure to height column of water is given as, $P=\rho h g$
Since the excess pressure inside the bubble is balanced by the height of the column and it can be written as,
$\frac{4 T}{r}=\rho h g\Rightarrow T=\frac{r \rho h g}{4}$
On plugging the given values:
$T=\frac{1}{4}\left(3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \times \frac{10^3 \mathrm{~kg}}{\mathrm{~m}^3} \times 8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \times 9.8 \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^2}\right)=58.8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small ball of mass $M$, radius $R$ and density $\rho$ moves with terminal velocity through a container filled with glycerine of density $\sigma$. The viscous force acting on the ball is ( $g=$ gravitational acceleration)
questions.solution: Considering force balance on the ball falling with terminal velocity: $F_v+\sigma V g=\rho V g$ where $F_v$ is the viscous force, $V$ is the volume of the ball. Taking the ratio of equation (1) and (2): $F_v=M g\left(1-\frac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two soap bubbles of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ in vacuum coalesce under isothermal conditions. The resulting bubble has a radius equal to
questions.solution:
In Iso-thermal process: $p V=\mathrm{C}$. The pressure inside bubble is: $p \propto 1 / r$ and volume is: $V \propto r^3$.
$\therefore p V \propto r^2$
And $n=\frac{p V}{R T}$, therefore number of moles of gas inside the bubble is proportional to the square of its radius
$\therefore n \propto r^2$
On combining bubbles, the total number of moles is conserved: Therefore, $n_1+n_1=N\therefore r_1^2+r_2^2=R^2$
The above result can also be obtained by total surface energy conservation:
$2 \times\left(4 \pi R^2\right) \sigma=2 \times\left(4 \pi r_1^2\right) \sigma+2 \times\left(4 \pi r_2^2\right) \sigma$
or $R=\sqrt{r_1^2+r_2^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A liquid drop of density ' $Q$ ' is floating half immersed in a liquid of density ' $d$ '. Diameter of the liquid drop is
( $\mathrm{Q} \gt \mathrm{d}, \mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity, $\mathrm{T}=$ surface tension)
questions.solution:
The force balance invovles, surface-tension force and boyancy force balance the weight of the droplet, so the equation is:
$(2 \pi r) T+\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3\right) \mathrm{dg}=\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3\right) \mathrm{Qg}$
Where, $\mathrm{r}$ is the radius of the drop, $\mathrm{T}$ the interfacial tension between the liquids, $g$ is acceleration due to gravity.
Therefore,
$\mathrm{T}=\left(\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{r}^2\right)(\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{d}) \mathrm{g}$
Diameter $=2 r=\left[\frac{6 T}{g(Q-d)}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The surface tension of a soap solution is ' $\mathrm{T}$ '. Work done in blowing a soap bubble of diameter $2 \mathrm{~d}$ is
questions.solution:
In this case, work done = increase in surface energy, i.e.
$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{A}$
Key point: In calculation, area of sphere have been multiplied with 2, since there are two surfaces in soap bubble.
$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{T} \times\left[2\left(4 \pi \mathrm{d}^2\right)\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}=8 \pi \mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{~T}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a capillary tube of radius $1 \mathrm{~mm}$ is immersed in water, the mass of water rising in the capillary tube is $\mathrm{m}$. If the radius of the capillary tube is doubled, then the mass of water that rises in the same capillary tube will be
questions.solution:
For capillary rise, $h_1 r_1=h_2 r_2\therefore \frac{h_2}{h_1}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{1}{2}$
And $m=\pi r^2 h_1 \rho$ and $M=p(2 r)^2 \times h_2 \times \rho\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{M^{\prime}}{M}=\left(\frac{2 r}{r}\right)^2 \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=4 \times \frac{1}{2}=2 \\ & \therefore M=2 \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal wire of density ' $e$ ' floats on water surface horizontally. If it is NOT to sink in water, then maximum radius of wire is ( $\mathrm{T}$ = surface tension of water, $\mathrm{g}$ = gravitational acceleration)
questions.solution: The correct option is (C). There are two free surfaces as shown in the figure: Consider the force balance per unit length as shown in the diagram above: $2 \mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{e} \pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~g}$ Therefore, $r=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{~T}}{\pi \mathrm{eg}}}$. We neglect buoyancy force as it is negligible as compared to surface tension force!

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which one of the following statements is 'NOT' True about the angle of contact of a liquid?
options: Any increase in the temperature of the liquid does not decrease its angle of contact.
If an impurity is added in the liquid then it's angle of contact changes.
Angle of contact depends upon the nature of liquid and solid in contact.
At a given temperature, the angle of contact is constant for a solid-liquid surface.
questions.solution:
The correct option is (A).
Concept: Contact angle decreases with the increasing temperature.
Addition of impurity decreases the surface tension of liquid.
Contact angle depends on the nature of liquid and solid in contact.
Therefore, answer (A) is the only "NOT" true statement.
Concept based question.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A liquid drop having surface energy ' $E$ ' is spread into 216 droplets of the same size. The final surface energy of the droplets is
questions.solution:
The correct option is (D).
Concept: Surface Energy is proportional to the surface area $\mathrm{E} \propto 4 \pi R^2$.
Considering volume conservation, the size of small droplets $r$ is:
$V=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3=216 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$
Therefore, $\mathrm{R}=6 \mathrm{r}$
The total surface area of the new 216 droplets is:
$216 \times\left(4 \pi r^2\right)$
or $6 \times\left(4 \pi R^2\right)$
Given $E \propto 4 \pi R^2$
Therefore, the total surface energy of the new droplets would be $6 \mathrm{E}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Pressure inside two soap bubbles is $1.01 \mathrm{~atm}$ and $1.03 \mathrm{~atm}$. The ratio between their volumes is (Pressure outside the soap bubble is $1 \mathrm{~atm}$ )
questions.solution:
Excess pressure inside a soap bubble is given by
$\Delta \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}}-\mathrm{P}_0=\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}}\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{P}_1=1.01 \mathrm{~atm}-1 \mathrm{~atm}=0.01 \mathrm{~atm} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{P}_2=1.03 \mathrm{~atm}-1 \mathrm{~atm}=0.03 \mathrm{~atm}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\Delta \mathrm{P}_1}{\Delta \mathrm{P}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1} \\ & \frac{0.03}{0.01}=3=\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{~V}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right)^3=(3)^3=27\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the work done in blowing a soap bubble of volume ' $\mathrm{V}$ ' is ' $\mathrm{W}$ ', then the work done in blowing a soap bubble of volume ' $2 \mathrm{~V}$ ' will be
questions.solution:
If $\mathrm{V}$ is the volume then we have
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{V}=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \\
& \mathrm{~V} \propto \mathrm{r}^3 \\
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{~V}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right)^3 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{~V}_1}\right)^{1 / 3}=(2)^{1 / 3} \\
& \mathrm{~W}_1=8 \pi \mathrm{r}_1^2 \cdot \mathrm{T} \text { and } \mathrm{W}_2=8 \pi \mathrm{r}_2^2 \mathrm{~T} \\
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{W}_2}{\mathrm{~W}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right)^2=(2)^{2 / 3}=(4)^{1 / 3} \\
& \mathrm{~W}_2=(4)^{1 / 3} \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water rises up to a height of $4 \mathrm{~cm}$ in a capillary tube. The lower end of the capillary tube is at a depth of $8 \mathrm{~cm}$ below the water level. The mouth pressure required to blow an air bubble at the lower end of the capillary will be ' $\mathrm{X}$ ' $\mathrm{cm}$ of water, where $\mathrm{X}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
At the lower ends of the tube, the total pressure is due to height of water column in the container plus the height of water in the capillary.
$\therefore$ Total pressure is due to $8+4=12 \mathrm{~cm}$ of water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A glass rod of radius ' $r$ ' ' is inserted symmetrically into a vertical capillary tube of radius ' $\mathrm{r}_2$ ' $\left(\mathrm{r}_1 \lt  \mathrm{r}_2\right)$ such that their lower ends are at same level. The arrangement is dipped in water. The height to which water will rise into the tube will be ( $\rho=$ density of water, $\mathrm{T}=$ surface tension in water, $\mathrm{g}$ = acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Vertical component of total force of surface tension

\mathrm{F}=\left(\mathrm{r}_2+\mathrm{r}_1\right) 2 \pi \mathrm{T} \cos \theta

Weight of the liquid in the capillary

\mathrm{W}=\pi\left(\mathrm{r}_2^2-\mathrm{r}_1^2\right) \mathrm{h} \rho \mathrm{g}

This is balanced by the vertical component of the face due to the surface tension

\therefore \pi\left(\mathrm{r}_2^2-\mathrm{r}_1^2\right) \mathrm{h} \rho \mathrm{g}=\left(\mathrm{r}_2+\mathrm{r}_1\right) \times 2 \pi \mathrm{T} \cos \theta

Simplifying and solving for $\mathrm{h}$ we get,

\mathrm{h}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta}{\left(\mathrm{r}_2-\mathrm{r}_1\right) \rho g}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~T}}{\left(\mathrm{r}_2-\mathrm{r}_1\right) \rho g}

(For pure water, $\theta=0^{\circ}, \cos \theta=1$ )

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water rises to a height of $2 \mathrm{~cm}$ in a capillary tube. If crosssectional area of the tube is reduced to $\frac{1}{16}^{\text {th }}$ of initial area, then water will rise to a height of
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{h}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{r} \rho \mathrm{g}} \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{h}_2}{\mathrm{~h}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2} \\ & \text { Area } \mathrm{A}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \therefore \mathrm{A} \propto \mathrm{r}^2 \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{A}_1}{\mathrm{~A}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_1^2}{\mathrm{r}_2^2} \text { or } \frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{A}_1}{\mathrm{~A}_2}}=\sqrt{16} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}=4 \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{h}_2}{\mathrm{~h}_1}=4 \text { or } \mathrm{h}_2=4 \mathrm{~h}_1=4 \times 2=8 \mathrm{~cm}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The speed of a ball of radius $2 \mathrm{~cm}$ in a viscous liquid is $20 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$. What will be the speed of a ball of radius $1 \mathrm{~cm}$ in same liquid?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Work done in increasing the size of a soap bubble from radius of $3 \mathrm{~cm}$ to $5 \mathrm{~cm}$ in millijoule is nearly (surface tension of soap solution $=0.03 \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{w}=8 \pi \mathrm{T}\left(\mathrm{r}_2^2-\mathrm{r}_1^2\right) \\ & =8 \pi \times 0.03(25-9) \times 10^{-4} \\ & =0.384 \pi \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~J} \\ & =0.384 \pi \mathrm{mJ} \approx 0.4 \pi \mathrm{mJ}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The work done in blowing a soap bubble of volume ' $\mathrm{V}$ ' is ' $\mathrm{W}$ '. The work required to blow a soap bubble of volume ' $2 \mathrm{~V}$ ' is [ $\mathrm{T}=$ surface tension of soap solution $]$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V}=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \text { or } \quad \mathrm{r}=\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~V}}{4 \pi}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ & \mathrm{~W}=8 \pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~T}=8 \pi\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~V}}{4 \pi}\right)^{2 / 3} \mathrm{~T} \\ & \mathrm{~W} \propto \mathrm{V}^{2 / 3} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{W}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{W}}=\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{~V}}\right)^{2 / 3}=2^{2 / 3}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin metal disc of radius ' $r$ ' floats on water surface and bends the surface downwards along the perimeter making an angle ' $\theta$ ' with the vertical edge of the disc. If the weight of water displaced by the disc is $\mathrm{W}$, the weight of the metal disc is [ $\mathrm{T}=$ surface tension of water $]$
questions.solution:
The weight of the disc is balanced by the force due to the surface tension and the upthrust of water.
The component of surface tension in vertically upward direction is $\mathrm{T} \cos \theta$ and the force acting due to it $2 \pi \mathrm{r} \mathrm{T} \cos \theta$.
The upthrust is equal to the weight of the water displaced (W).
$\therefore$ Weight of the disc $=2 \pi \mathrm{rT} \cos \theta+\mathrm{W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A glass tube of uniform cross-section is connected to a tap with a rubber tube. The tap is opened slowly. Initially the flow of water in the tube is streamline. The speed of flow of water to convert it into a turbulent flow is
[radius of tube $=1 \mathrm{~cm}, \eta=1 \times 10^{-3} \frac{\mathrm{Ns}}{\mathrm{m}^2}, \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{n}}=2500$ and density of water $=10^3 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$ ]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball rises to the surface of a liquid with constant velocity. The density of the liquid is four times the density of the material of the ball. The viscous force of the liquid on the rising ball is greater than the weight of the ball by a factor of
questions.solution:
The ball is moving with constant velocity.
Hence the net force acting on it is zero.
The weight of the ball, $\mathrm{W}=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \rho_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g}$ (in downward direction)
The viscous force $F_v$ is in downward direction
The buoyant force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \rho_{\ell}$ g (in upward direction)

\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}+\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \\
& \therefore \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}-\mathrm{W} \\
& =\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \mathrm{~g}\left(\rho_{\ell}-\rho_{\mathrm{b}}\right)=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \mathrm{~g} \times 3 \rho_{\mathrm{b}} \quad\left(\because \rho_{\ell}=4 \rho_{\mathrm{b}}\right) \\
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}}{\mathrm{W}}=3
\end{aligned}

Pressure inside the first bubble $=\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}_1}$

Using the formula $\mathrm{PV}=\mathrm{nR} \theta \quad(\theta=$ absolute temp $)\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right) \cdot \frac{4 \pi}{3} \mathrm{r}_1^3=\mathrm{n}_1 \mathrm{R} \theta \quad$ ( $\mathrm{R}$ is molar gas constant)

and $\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}\right) \cdot \frac{4 \pi}{3} \mathrm{R}^3=\left(\mathrm{n}_1+\mathrm{n}_2\right) \mathrm{R} \theta\therefore\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}\right) \cdot \frac{4 \pi}{3} \mathrm{R}^3=\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right) \cdot \frac{4 \pi}{3} \mathrm{r}_1^3+\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right) \cdot \frac{4 \pi \mathrm{r}_2^3}{3}\therefore\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}\right) \mathrm{R}^3=\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right) \mathrm{r}_1^3+\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{4 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right) \mathrm{r}_2^3$
on solving: $\mathrm{T}=\frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{R}^3-\mathrm{r}_1^3-\mathrm{r}_2^3\right)}{4\left(\mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{r}_2^2-\mathrm{R}^2\right)}$

questions.q:
A liquid kept in a cylindrical vessel is rotated about vertical axis through the centre
of circular base. The difference in the heights of the liquid at the centre of vessel and
its edge is $(\mathrm{R}=$ radius of vessel, $\omega=$ angular velocity of rotation, $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration
due to gravity)
questions.solution:
When the cylindrical vessel is rotated at angular speed $\omega$ about its axis, the velocity of the liquid at the sides is maximum, given by $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{r} \omega$
Applying Bernoulli's theorem at the sides and at the center of the vessel, we have
$\mathrm{P}+\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{v}^{2}=$ constant $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}+\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}^{2}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{c}}+\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{c}}{ }^{2}$
where
$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}=$ pressure at the sides
$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=$ velocity of the liquid at the sides
$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{c}}=$ pressure at the center
$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{c}}=$ velocity of the liquid at the center
$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{c}}-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{r}^{2} \omega^{2} \ldots(\mathrm{I}) \quad \because \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{c}}=0$
Since $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is greater than $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}$, the liquid rises at the sides of the vessel. Let $\mathrm{h}$ be the difference in the levels of the liquids at the sides and at the center, so we have
$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{c}}-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{s}}=\rho g h \ldots(\mathrm{II})$
from (I) and (II) we have
$\rho g h=\frac{1}{2} \rho r^{2} \omega^{2}\Rightarrow h=\frac{r^{2} \omega^{2}}{2 g}$

questions.solution: When the surface area of a liquid is increased, molecules from the interior of the liquid rise to the surface. questions.solution:
Hooke in 1679 , showed experimentally that if strain is small, then the stress is proportional to strain. The ratio of stress to strain is constant for material of the given body and is called modulus of elasticity $E$. Thus, $E=\frac{\text { stress }}{\text { strain }}=$ constant
Hence, if stress is increased, then the ratio of stress to strain remains constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boat crosses a river from one bank A to another bank B which is opposite. The distance between them is D. The speed of water is $V_W$ and that of boat relative to water is $V_B$. If $V_B = 2V_W$, the time taken by the boat to cross the river directly along AB is $\left(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, $\left(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let the boat be steered at an angle $\theta$ upstream with respect to the line AB to cross the river directly.

For the boat to move exactly along AB, the component of its velocity parallel to the river flow must cancel the river's velocity $V_W$.

$V_B \sin \theta = V_W$

Given $V_B = 2V_W$, substituting this yields:

$2V_W \sin \theta = V_W \Rightarrow \sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30^\circ$

The net velocity of the boat along the line AB is the component of $V_B$ perpendicular to the river flow:

$V = V_B \cos \theta = V_B \cos 30^\circ = V_B \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

The time taken to cross the river of width $D$ is:

$t = \dfrac{D}{V} = \dfrac{D}{V_B \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \dfrac{2D}{V_B \sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2D}{V_B\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is released from height 'h' which makes perfectly elastic collision with ground. The frequency of periodic vibratory motion is (g=acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Time taken by the ball to fall from height $h$ to the ground is given by $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

Since the collision is perfectly elastic, the ball rebounds with the same speed and reaches the same height $h$. The time taken to go up is also $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

The total time period of one complete oscillation is $T = 2t = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

The frequency of the periodic motion is $f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone falls from the top of a tower of height $100$ m and at the same time another stone is projected vertically upwards from the ground with a velocity $25$ m/s. The two stones meet after
questions.solution:
Let the two stones meet after time $t$.

For the stone falling from the top of the tower:
Displacement downwards, $h_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$

For the stone projected upwards from the ground:
Displacement upwards, $h_2 = 25t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$

When the two stones meet, the sum of their displacements is equal to the height of the tower.
$h_1 + h_2 = 100$

$\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 + 25t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 100$

$25t = 100$

$t = 4$ s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Spherical insulating ball and a spherical metallic ball of same size and mass are dropped from the same height. Choose the correct statement out of the following {Assume negligible air friction}
options: Time taken by them to reach the earth's surface will be independent of the properties of their materials.
Insulating ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the metal ball.
Both will reach the earth's surface simultaneously.
Metal ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the insulating ball.
questions.solution:
As the metallic ball falls through the Earth's magnetic field, it cuts the magnetic field lines, which induces an electromotive force (EMF) in it.

Since the ball is a conductor, this induced EMF generates eddy currents within the metallic ball.

According to Lenz's law, these eddy currents oppose the motion that causes them, creating an upward magnetic retarding force.

As a result, the net downward acceleration of the metallic ball becomes less than the acceleration due to gravity $g$.

The insulating ball is a non-conductor, so no eddy currents are induced in it. It falls with the full acceleration $g$.

Because the insulating ball has a greater downward acceleration, it will reach the Earth's surface earlier than the metallic ball.

Answer: Insulating ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the metal ball.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The velocity time graph of a body moving in a straight line is shown in a figure. The ratio of displacement to distance travelled by the body in time $0$ to $10$ s is
questions.solution:
Displacement is the algebraic sum of the areas under the velocity-time graph, and distance is the sum of their absolute values.

Calculating the areas for each time interval:
Area for $0$ to $2$ s: $A_1 = 8 \times 2 = 16$ m
Area for $2$ to $4$ s: $A_2 = -4 \times 2 = -8$ m
Area for $4$ to $8$ s: $A_3 = 4 \times 4 = 16$ m
Area for $8$ to $10$ s: $A_4 = -4 \times 2 = -8$ m

Total displacement $= A_1 + A_2 + A_3 + A_4 = 16 - 8 + 16 - 8 = 16$ m

Total distance $= |A_1| + |A_2| + |A_3| + |A_4| = 16 + 8 + 16 + 8 = 48$ m

Ratio of displacement to distance $= \dfrac{16}{48} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Thus, the required ratio is $1:3$.

Answer: $1:3$

questions.q: A car passes three points A, B and C at $3$ m/s, $6$ m/s and $9$ m/s respectively in a straight line with uniform acceleration. If distance $AB = 60$ m then find the distance BC.
questions.solution:
Using the equation of motion $v^2 - u^2 = 2as$ for the interval AB:

$v_B^2 - v_A^2 = 2a(AB)$

$6^2 - 3^2 = 2a(60)$

$36 - 9 = 120a$

$27 = 120a \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{27}{120} = \dfrac{9}{40}$ m/s$^2$

Applying the same equation for the interval BC:

$v_C^2 - v_B^2 = 2a(BC)$

$9^2 - 6^2 = 2 \times \dfrac{9}{40} \times BC$

$81 - 36 = \dfrac{9}{20} \times BC$

$45 = \dfrac{9}{20} \times BC$

$BC = \dfrac{45 \times 20}{9} = 100$ m

Answer: $100$ m

questions.q: If a ball is thrown vertically upwards with speed ' $u$ ', the distance covered by it during the last ' $t$ ' second of its ascent is ( $g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Distance during last t seconds of ascent

A ball thrown upward with initial speed $u$ reaches its peak when final velocity is zero. The distance covered in the last $t$ seconds of ascent equals the distance it would fall from rest in time $t$.

For free fall from rest: initial velocity $u' = 0$, acceleration $g$, time $t$.

$s = u't + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$

Substituting $u' = 0$:

$s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$

The correct option is D.

questions.q: A car moving at a speed ' $V$ ' is stopped in a certain distance when the breaks produce a deceleration 'a'. If the speed of the car is 'nv', what must be the deceleration of the car to stop it in the same distance and in the same time?
questions.solution:
A car stops from speed \(v\) under deceleration \(a\).
Using
\(v=a t \quad \text { and } \quad s=\frac{1}{2} v t\)
(the distance-time relations during uniform deceleration).
Now the new speed is \(n v\).
Let required deceleration be \(\boldsymbol{A}\).
For same stopping time:
\(n v=A t \quad \Rightarrow \quad A=n a\)
For same stopping distance:
\(s=\frac{1}{2} v t=\frac{1}{2}(n v) t^{\prime}\)
But time is same, so:
\(\frac{1}{2} v t=\frac{1}{2} n v t \cdot \frac{a}{A}\)
Or use direct formula for distance:
\(\frac{v^2}{2 a}=\frac{(n v)^2}{2 A}\)
Thus,
\(\frac{v^2}{a}=\frac{n^2 v^2}{A} \Rightarrow A=n^2 a .\)
\(n^2 a\)

questions.q: A boy throws a ball vertically upwards from a bridge with velocity $5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. It strikes water surface after 2 s . The height of the bridge is $\left(\right.$ Take $\left.g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
The height of the bridge is determined using kinematic equations with upward defined as positive. The ball's initial velocity is $u = +5\,\text{m/s}$, the time until impact is $t = 2\,\text{s}$, and acceleration due to gravity is $a = -10\,\text{m/s}^2$.

The displacement equation $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ applies, where $s = -h$ represents the downward displacement from the bridge to the water surface. Substituting the values:

$-h = (5)(2) + \frac{1}{2}(-10)(2)^2$
$= 10 - 20$
$= -10$

Solving yields $h = 10\,\text{m}$.

The height of the bridge is 10 meters.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The acceleration (a) - time (T) graph for the body starting from rest is given below. The maximum speed of the body is
questions.solution:
The area under the acceleration–time graph represents the change in velocity.

Given initial velocity $u = 0 \, \text{m/s}$, the maximum speed occurs at $t = 10 \, \text{s}$ since acceleration is positive throughout.

The graph forms a right triangle from $t = 0$ to $t = 10$ seconds, with base $10 \, \text{s}$ and height $8 \, \text{m/s}^2$.
The area is $\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 8 = 40 \, \text{m/s}$.

Thus, $v_\text{max} = 40 \, \text{m/s}$.

The correct option is A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At any time ' $t$ ', the co-ordinates of moving particle are $x=a t^2$ and $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{bt}^2$. The speed of the particle is
questions.solution:
The position of the particle at time $t$ is defined by $x = at^2$ and $y = bt^2$. Differentiating both coordinates with respect to time, the velocity components are $v_x = 2at$ and $v_y = 2bt$.

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector:

$v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{(2at)^2 + (2bt)^2} = \sqrt{4a^2t^2 + 4b^2t^2} = \sqrt{4t^2(a^2 + b^2)} = 2t\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

This result corresponds to option A.

$\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration. The ratio of the distance covered by the body in the $\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }}$ second of its motion to the total distance travelled in n second is
questions.solution:
A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration of magnitude $a$. The distance covered in the $\mathrm{n}^{\text{th}}$ second is $S_n^{\text{th}} = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$. With initial velocity $u = 0$, this becomes $S_n^{\text{th}} = \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$.

The total distance traveled in $n$ seconds is $S_n = \frac{1}{2}an^2$.

The ratio is then $\frac{S_n^{\text{th}}}{S_n} = \frac{\frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)}{\frac{1}{2}an^2} = \frac{2n - 1}{n^2}$, which simplifies to $\frac{2}{n} - \frac{1}{n^2}$.

The correct option is C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The velocity time graph of a body moving in a straight line is shown in figure. The ratio of displacement to distance travelled by the body in time 0 to 8 s is
questions.solution:
The displacement is the net area under the velocity-time graph, while distance is the total area taken as positive.

From $t = 0$ to $2$ s: displacement $+6$ m, distance $6$ m.
From $t = 2$ to $3$ s: displacement $-2$ m, distance $2$ m.
The remaining segments follow similarly, yielding displacements of $+4$, $-2$, and $+4$ m, with distances of $4$, $2$, and $4$ m respectively.

The total displacement is $6 - 2 + 4 - 2 + 4 = 10$ m.
The total distance is $6 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 4 = 18$ m.

The ratio simplifies to $10:18 = 5:9$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two bodies A and B move in same straight line starting from same position. Body A moves with constant velocity 'u' and body B moves with constant acceleration ' $a$ '. When their velocities become equal, the distance between them is
questions.solution:
Define $x=0$ as the initial position at $t=0$. Body A moves with constant velocity $v_A = u$, so its position is $x_A = u t$. Body B accelerates from rest with constant acceleration $a$, giving velocity $v_B = a t$ and position $x_B = \frac{1}{2} a t^2$.

Equate their velocities to find when they are equal: $u = a t$, so $t = \frac{u}{a}$.

At this time, $x_A = u \cdot \frac{u}{a} = \frac{u^2}{a}$ and $x_B = \frac{1}{2} a \left( \frac{u}{a} \right)^2 = \frac{u^2}{2a}$. The distance between them is the absolute difference, which simplifies to $D = \left| \frac{u^2}{a} - \frac{u^2}{2a} \right| = \frac{u^2}{2a}$.

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body travelling with uniform acceleration crosses two points A and B with velocities $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ respectively. The speed of the body at mid point of A and B is (nearly)
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the body be ' $a$ ' and the distance between points A and B be ' d '. $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \mathrm{v}^2-\mathrm{u}^2=2 \mathrm{ad} \quad \ldots\left(\text { from } \mathrm{v}^2=\mathrm{u}^2+2 \mathrm{as}\right) \\ & \mathrm{ad}=\frac{\mathrm{v}^2-\mathrm{u}^2}{2}=\frac{(30)^2-(20)^2}{2} \\ &=250 \end{aligned}$
When the body is at the mid-point of $A B$, then speed of the body is $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}_1^2-(20)^2=2 \mathrm{a}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~d}}{2}\right) \\ & \mathrm{v}_1^2-400=\mathrm{ad} \\ & \mathrm{v}_1=\sqrt{650} \\ & \mathrm{v}_1=25.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The co-ordinates of a moving particle at any time ' t ' are given by $x=\alpha \mathrm{t}^3$ and $y=\beta \mathrm{t}^3$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants. The speed of the particle at time ' $t$ ' is given by
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & X=\alpha t^3 \hat{i}+\beta t^3 \hat{j} \\ & \begin{aligned} V=\frac{d X}{d t}=3 \alpha t^2 \hat{i} & +3 \beta t^2 \hat{j} \\ \text { Magnitude of } V & =\sqrt{\left(3 \alpha t^2\right)^2+\left(3 \beta t^2\right)^2} \\ & =\sqrt{9 \alpha^2 t^4+9 \beta^2 t^4} \\ & =\sqrt{9 t^4\left(\alpha^2+\beta^2\right)} \\ & =3 t^2 \sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A ball is released from the top of a tower of height H m. It takes T second to reach the ground. The height of the ball from the ground after $\frac{T}{4}$ second is
questions.solution:
Let the body be at $x$ from the top after $\frac{t}{4} \mathrm{~s}$. $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{ut}+\frac{1}{2} a \mathrm{t}^2=\frac{1}{2} a \mathrm{t}^2\ldots(\because u=0)\therefore \quad x=\frac{1}{2} g\left(\frac{\mathrm{t}}{4}\right)^2=\frac{g t^2}{32} \Rightarrow 32 \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{gt}^2...(i)\mathrm{H}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2 \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}=\mathrm{gt}^2...(ii)$
From (i) and (ii), we get $2 \mathrm{H}=32 \mathrm{x} \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\frac{2 \mathrm{H}}{32}\therefore \quad$ Height of the body from the ground $=\mathrm{H}-\frac{2 \mathrm{H}}{32}=\frac{15 \mathrm{H}}{16}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two cars start from a point at the same time in a straight line and their positions are represented by $\mathrm{x}_1(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{at}+\mathrm{bt}^2$ and $\mathrm{x}_2(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{Ft}-\mathrm{t}^2$. At what time do the cars have the same velocity?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Velocity } v=\frac{d x}{d t} \\
\therefore \quad & v_P=\frac{d x_P}{d t}=a+2 b t \\
& v_Q=\frac{d x_Q}{d t}=F-2 t \\
& a v_P=v_Q ...(given)\\
& a+2 b t=F-2 t \\
\therefore \quad & (2+2 b) t=F-a \Rightarrow t=\frac{F-a}{2(1+b)}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet is fired on a target with velocity V. Its velocity decreases from $v$ to $v / 2$. When it penetrates 30 cm in a target. Through what thickness it will penetrate further in the target before coming to rest?
questions.solution:
When the velocity of the bullet changes from V to $\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2}$ the distance travelled by the bullet is 30 cm . Using $3^{\text {rd }}$ kinematic equation, $\begin{aligned} & v^2=u^2+2 a s \\ & \left(\frac{V}{2}\right)^2=V^2+2 a(30) \\ & \frac{V^2}{4}=V^2+60 a \\ & \frac{-3 V^2}{4}=60 a \\ & a=\frac{-V^2}{80} \end{aligned}$
Further, when a bullet penetrates. it comes to rest. So, the final velocity of the bullet becomes zero. Using the relation, $v^2=u^2+2 \mathrm{as}\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}^2=\mathrm{u}^2+2 \mathrm{as} \\ & 0=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2}\right)^2+2\left(-\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{80}\right) \mathrm{s} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{4}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{40}\right) \mathrm{s} \\ & \mathrm{s}=\frac{40}{4}=10 \mathrm{~cm}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A driver applies the brakes on seeing the red traffic signal 400 m ahead. At the time of applying brakes, the vehicle was moving with $15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and retarding at $0.3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. The distance of the vehicle from the traffic light one minute after application of brakes is
questions.solution:
After applying the brakes, the vehicle stops after time t , $\mathrm{t}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{u}}{\mathrm{a}}\right)=\left(\frac{0-15}{-0.3}\right)=50 \text { seconds }$ i.e. vehicle stops before one minute. \Rightarrow Displacement will only occur for 50 seconds. $\therefore \quad$ Displacement is given by $\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{ut}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{at}^2\therefore \quad \mathrm{s}=15 \times 50+\frac{1}{2} \times(-0.3) \times(50)^2\ldots .(\because \mathrm{a}$ is the retardation in vehicle) $\mathrm{s}=375 \mathrm{~m}$
Distance from traffic light $=400-375=25 \mathrm{~m}$

Given that the maximum heights are equal for both spheres:

$H_1 = H_2$

$\dfrac{u_1^2 \sin^2 \theta_1}{2g} = \dfrac{u_2^2 \sin^2 \theta_2}{2g}$

$u_1 \sin \theta_1 = u_2 \sin \theta_2$

Substituting $\theta_1 = 30^\circ$ and $\theta_2 = 45^\circ$:

$u_1 \sin 30^\circ = u_2 \sin 45^\circ$

$u_1 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = u_2 \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$\dfrac{u_1}{u_2} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1}$

The ratio of their initial velocities is $\sqrt{2} : 1$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2} : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car is travelling at 40 m/s on a circular path of radius 40 m. It is increasing its speed at the rate of $2\ \text{m/s}^2$. Its net acceleration is (in $\text{m/s}^2$) nearly
questions.solution:
Given $v = 40\ \text{m/s}$ and $R = 40\ \text{m}$.

Tangential acceleration, $a_t = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Centripetal acceleration, $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = \dfrac{40^2}{40} = 40\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Net acceleration, $a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2} = \sqrt{40^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{1600 + 4} = \sqrt{1604} \approx 40\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Answer: $40\ \text{m/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle completes 2 revolutions in a circular path of radius 3 cm. The angular displacement of the particle will be (in radian)
questions.solution:
Angular displacement for one complete revolution is $2\pi$ radians.

For $2$ complete revolutions, the angular displacement is given by $\theta = 2 \times 2\pi = 4\pi$ radians.

The radius of the circular path does not affect the angular displacement.

Answer: $4\pi$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The equation of the trajectory of a ball projected at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal, is given as $y = x - \dfrac{gx^2}{2}$
The initial velocity of the ball is
[Given : $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, $\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ]
questions.solution:
The standard equation of trajectory of a projectile is given by

$y = x \tan \theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2 \cos^2 \theta}$

Comparing this with the given equation $y = x - \dfrac{gx^2}{2}$, we get

$\tan \theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ$

and

$\dfrac{g}{2u^2 \cos^2 \theta} = \dfrac{g}{2}$

$u^2 \cos^2 \theta = 1$

Substituting $\theta = 45^\circ$,

$u^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = 1$

$\dfrac{u^2}{2} = 1$

$u^2 = 2$

$u = \sqrt{2} \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $\sqrt{2}\,\text{m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is performing U.C.M. along a circle of radius $R$. In half the period of revolution, its displacement and distance covered are respectively
questions.solution:
In half the period of revolution, the particle moves from its initial position to the diametrically opposite point on the circular path.

The displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions, which is equal to the diameter of the circle.

Displacement = $2R$

The distance covered is the actual path length along the circular trajectory, which is half of the circumference.

Distance = $\dfrac{2\pi R}{2} = \pi R$

Answer: $2R, \pi R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles having mass 'M' and 'm' are moving in a circular path with radius 'R' and 'r' respectively. The time period for both the particles is same. The ratio of angular velocity of the first particle to that of the second particle will be
questions.solution:
Angular velocity is given by $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$

Since the time period $T$ is the same for both particles, their angular velocities are equal.

$\omega_1 = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ and $\omega_2 = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$

$\dfrac{\omega_1}{\omega_2} = \dfrac{1}{1}$

The ratio of their angular velocities is $1:1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two stones of masses $m$ and $3m$ are whirled in horizontal circles, the heavier one in a radius $\dfrac{r}{3}$ and the lighter one in radius $r$. When both the stones experience same centripetal forces, the tangential speed of lighter stone is '$n$' times that of the value of heavier stone. The value of '$n$' is
questions.solution:
Let the mass, radius, and tangential speed of the lighter stone be $m_1 = m$, $r_1 = r$, and $v_1$ respectively.

Let the mass, radius, and tangential speed of the heavier stone be $m_2 = 3m$, $r_2 = \dfrac{r}{3}$, and $v_2$ respectively.

The centripetal force on the lighter stone is $F_1 = \dfrac{m_1 v_1^2}{r_1} = \dfrac{m v_1^2}{r}$.

The centripetal force on the heavier stone is $F_2 = \dfrac{m_2 v_2^2}{r_2} = \dfrac{3m v_2^2}{\dfrac{r}{3}} = \dfrac{9m v_2^2}{r}$.

Given that both stones experience the same centripetal force, $F_1 = F_2$.

$\dfrac{m v_1^2}{r} = \dfrac{9m v_2^2}{r}$

$v_1^2 = 9 v_2^2$

$v_1 = 3 v_2$

Since the tangential speed of the lighter stone is $n$ times that of the heavier stone, $n = 3$.

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a projectile motion, the range R is 'n' times the maximum height H. So the angle of projection is
questions.solution:
The horizontal range $R$ of a projectile is given by

$R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g}$

The maximum height $H$ is given by

$H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

Given that $R = nH$, substituting the expressions for $R$ and $H$

$\dfrac{2u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g} = n \left( \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g} \right)$

Cancelling $\dfrac{u^2 \sin\theta}{g}$ from both sides

$2 \cos\theta = \dfrac{n \sin\theta}{2}$

$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{4}{n}$

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{4}{n}$

$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{n}\right)$

Answer: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{n}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body moves along a circular path of diameter $30\ \text{cm}$. It starts from one end of diameter, moves along the circular path and reaches the other end of diameter in 3 second. The angular speed of the body in radian per second is
questions.solution:
The angular displacement of the body when it moves from one end of the diameter to the other end along the circular path is $\pi$ radians.

Time taken, $t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Angular speed, $\omega = \dfrac{\theta}{t}$

$\omega = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\ \text{rad/s}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A ball P is projected at an angle of $60^\circ$ with the vertical with certain initial speed. Another ball Q of the same mass as that of ball P is projected vertically upwards with the same initial speed as that of P. At the highest point, the ratio of potential energy of ball P to that of ball Q is
$(\sin 30^\circ = 0.5)$
questions.solution:
Let the initial speed of both balls be $u$ and their mass be $m$.

For ball P, the angle of projection with the vertical is $60^\circ$, so the angle with the horizontal is $\theta_P = 90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$.

The maximum height reached by ball P is $H_P = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 30^\circ}{2g} = \dfrac{u^2 (1/2)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{u^2}{8g}$.

The potential energy of ball P at the highest point is $U_P = mgH_P = mg \left(\dfrac{u^2}{8g}\right) = \dfrac{mu^2}{8}$.

For ball Q, it is projected vertically upwards, so the angle of projection with the horizontal is $\theta_Q = 90^\circ$.

The maximum height reached by ball Q is $H_Q = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 90^\circ}{2g} = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$.

The potential energy of ball Q at the highest point is $U_Q = mgH_Q = mg \left(\dfrac{u^2}{2g}\right) = \dfrac{mu^2}{2}$.

The ratio of their potential energies at the highest point is $\dfrac{U_P}{U_Q} = \dfrac{\dfrac{mu^2}{8}}{\dfrac{mu^2}{2}} = \dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Answer: $1 : 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two balls A and B are projected at an angle of $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively, so that the maximum heights reached are same for both. The ratio of initial velocity of projection of ball A to that for ball B is
$(\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2},\ \sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\ \sin 60^\circ = \cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$
questions.solution:
The maximum height reached by a projectile is given by $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$

For ball A, $H_A = \dfrac{u_A^2 \sin^2 45^\circ}{2g}$

For ball B, $H_B = \dfrac{u_B^2 \sin^2 60^\circ}{2g}$

Since $H_A = H_B$, we have:

$\dfrac{u_A^2 \sin^2 45^\circ}{2g} = \dfrac{u_B^2 \sin^2 60^\circ}{2g}$

$u_A \sin 45^\circ = u_B \sin 60^\circ$

$\dfrac{u_A}{u_B} = \dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ}$

Substituting the values $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:

$\dfrac{u_A}{u_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}$

The ratio of initial velocity of projection of ball A to that for ball B is $\sqrt{3} : \sqrt{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two objects are projected with same velocity 'u' at different angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the horizontal. If $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$, the ratio of horizontal range of the first object to the second object will be $[\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\theta]$
questions.solution:
The horizontal range of a projectile is given by $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$.

For the first object projected at angle $\alpha$, the range is $R_1 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\alpha)}{g}$.

For the second object projected at angle $\beta$, the range is $R_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\beta)}{g}$.

Given $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$, we have $\beta = 90^\circ - \alpha$.

Substituting $\beta$ in the expression for $R_2$:

$R_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2(90^\circ - \alpha))}{g} = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(180^\circ - 2\alpha)}{g}$

Using the identity $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, we get:

$R_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\alpha)}{g}$

Thus, $R_1 = R_2$, which means the ratio of their horizontal ranges is $1 : 1$.

Answer: $1 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle describes a horizontal circle of radius 'r' in conical funnel with smooth inner surface with a speed of $0.5$ m/s. The height of the plane of the circle from the vertex of the funnel is (acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let $\theta$ be the semi-vertical angle of the conical funnel.
The radius of the circular path is $r$ and its height from the vertex is $h$.
From the geometry of the cone, we have:
$\tan \theta = \dfrac{r}{h}$

The forces acting on the particle are its weight $mg$ acting vertically downwards and the normal reaction $N$ acting perpendicular to the inner surface of the funnel.
The normal reaction makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. Resolving $N$ into vertical and horizontal components, we get:
$N \sin \theta = mg$
$N \cos \theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$

Dividing the vertical component by the horizontal component, we obtain:
$\tan \theta = \dfrac{rg}{v^2}$

Equating the two expressions for $\tan \theta$:
$\dfrac{r}{h} = \dfrac{rg}{v^2}$

$\Rightarrow h = \dfrac{v^2}{g}$

Given $v = 0.5$ m/s and $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, substituting the values:
$h = \dfrac{(0.5)^2}{10} = \dfrac{0.25}{10} = 0.025$ m

Converting to centimeters:
$h = 0.025 \times 100$ cm $= 2.5$ cm

Answer: $2.5$ cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is moving with constant angular acceleration $4\,\text{rad/s}^2$ in circular path. At what time the magnitudes of its tangential acceleration and centripetal acceleration will be equal ?
questions.solution:
Given angular acceleration $\alpha = 4 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

Tangential acceleration is given by $a_t = r\alpha$.

Centripetal acceleration is given by $a_c = r\omega^2$.

Equating the magnitudes of tangential and centripetal acceleration:

$a_t = a_c$

$r\alpha = r\omega^2$

$\omega^2 = \alpha$

Assuming the particle starts from rest, the angular velocity at time $t$ is $\omega = \alpha t$.

Substituting $\omega$ in the above equation:

$(\alpha t)^2 = \alpha$

$\alpha^2 t^2 = \alpha$

$t^2 = \dfrac{1}{\alpha}$

Substituting $\alpha = 4 \text{ rad/s}^2$:

$t^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$t = 0.5 \text{ s}$

Answer: $0.5$ s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two boys are standing at points A and B on ground where distance AB = a. The boy at point B starts running perpendicular to line AB with velocity '$V_1$'. The boy at point A starts running simultaneously with velocity 'V' and catches the other boy in time 't'. The value of 't' is
questions.solution:
Let the meeting point be C.

In the right-angled triangle ABC, the initial distance AB is $a$.

Since the boy at B runs perpendicular to AB, the angle at B is $90^{\circ}$.

The distance travelled by the boy from B is $BC = V_1 t$.

The distance travelled by the boy from A is $AC = V t$.

Using Pythagoras theorem in $\triangle ABC$:

$(AC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (BC)^2$

$(V t)^2 = a^2 + (V_1 t)^2$

$V^2 t^2 - V_1^2 t^2 = a^2$

$t^2 (V^2 - V_1^2) = a^2$

$t = \left[\dfrac{a^2}{V^2 - V_1^2}\right]^{\dfrac{1}{2}}$

Answer: $\left[\dfrac{a^2}{(V^2 - V_1^2)}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle at rest starts moving with constant angular acceleration '$\alpha$' in a circular path of radius 'r'. At certain instant, the magnitude of centripetal acceleration is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{rd}$ the tangential acceleration. The relation between linear speed (V) and angular acceleration ($\alpha$) is
questions.solution:
The tangential acceleration of the particle is given by $a_t = r\alpha$.

The centripetal acceleration of the particle is given by $a_c = \dfrac{V^2}{r}$.

According to the given condition, the magnitude of centripetal acceleration is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the tangential acceleration:

$a_c = \dfrac{1}{3} a_t$

Substituting the expressions for $a_c$ and $a_t$:

$\dfrac{V^2}{r} = \dfrac{1}{3} (r\alpha)$

$V^2 = \dfrac{r^2 \alpha}{3}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$V = r\sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha}{3}}$

Answer: $V = r\sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha}{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A batsman hits a ball with a velocity 'v', making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the vertical. After some time direction of velocity is making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. The speed of the ball at this instant is
$\left[\cos(60^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \cos(30^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]$
questions.solution:
The initial angle of the velocity with the vertical is $60^\circ$. Therefore, the initial angle with the horizontal is $90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$.

The horizontal component of the initial velocity is $u_x = v \cos(30^\circ)$.

Let the speed of the ball be $v'$ when its direction of motion makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. The horizontal component of velocity at this instant is $v'_x = v' \cos(60^\circ)$.

In projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

Equating the horizontal components of velocity:

$v' \cos(60^\circ) = v \cos(30^\circ)$

Substituting the given trigonometric values:

$v' \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = v \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

$v' = \sqrt{3}v$

Answer: $\sqrt{3}v$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle performing U.C.M. of radius $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ m makes 'x' revolutions in time t. Its tangential velocity is
questions.solution:
The radius of the circular path is $r = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ m.

The particle makes $x$ revolutions in time $t$, so its frequency is $n = \dfrac{x}{t}$.

The angular velocity is given by $\omega = 2\pi n = \dfrac{2\pi x}{t}$.

The tangential velocity is $v = r\omega$.

Substituting the values, we get $v = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{t}\right) = \dfrac{\pi^2 x}{t}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi^2 x}{t}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string of length 'L' fixed at one end carries a mass 'm' at the other end. The string makes $\dfrac{3}{\pi}$ r.p.s. around the vertical axis through fixed end. The tension in the string is
questions.solution:
For a mass rotating in a horizontal circle as a conical pendulum, the horizontal component of the tension provides the necessary centripetal force.

$T \sin \theta = m \omega^2 r$

From the geometry of the pendulum, the radius of the circular path is $r = L \sin \theta$. Substituting this into the equation gives:

$T \sin \theta = m \omega^2 (L \sin \theta)$

$T = m \omega^2 L$

The frequency of revolution is given as $f = \dfrac{3}{\pi}$. The angular velocity $\omega$ is:

$\omega = 2 \pi f = 2 \pi \left( \dfrac{3}{\pi} \right) = 6$

Substituting the value of $\omega$ into the expression for tension:

$T = m (6)^2 L = 36 mL$

Answer: $36 mL$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In non uniform circular motion, the ratio of radial acceleration to tangential acceleration is (V is the velocity, r is the radius and $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration)
questions.solution:
Radial acceleration is given by $a_r = \dfrac{V^2}{r}$

Tangential acceleration is given by $a_t = r\alpha$

The ratio of radial acceleration to tangential acceleration is $\dfrac{a_r}{a_t} = \dfrac{\dfrac{V^2}{r}}{r\alpha} = \dfrac{V^2}{r^2\alpha}$

Answer: $\dfrac{V^2}{r^2\alpha}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The angular speed of the minute hand of a clock in degrees per second is
questions.solution:
The minute hand of a clock completes one full revolution in $1$ hour.

Total angle covered in one revolution is $360^{\circ}$.

Total time taken is $1 \text{ hour} = 3600 \text{ seconds}$.

Angular speed $\omega = \dfrac{360^{\circ}}{3600 \text{ s}} = 0.1^{\circ} \text{/s}$

Answer: $0.1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The position vector of a particle is $\vec{r} = a \cos \omega t \hat{i} + a \sin \omega t \hat{j}$. Calculate the angle between its position vector and the velocity vector.
($\cos 0=1, \cos 90=0, \cos 60=0.5, \sin 30=0.5, \sin 0=0$)
questions.solution:
Given position vector $\vec{r} = a \cos \omega t \hat{i} + a \sin \omega t \hat{j}$

Velocity vector $\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = -a \omega \sin \omega t \hat{i} + a \omega \cos \omega t \hat{j}$

The dot product of $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{v}$ is:

$\vec{r} \cdot \vec{v} = (a \cos \omega t)(-a \omega \sin \omega t) + (a \sin \omega t)(a \omega \cos \omega t)$

$\vec{r} \cdot \vec{v} = -a^2 \omega \sin \omega t \cos \omega t + a^2 \omega \sin \omega t \cos \omega t = 0$

Since $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$, the angle between the position vector and the velocity vector is $90^\circ$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a circular path of constant radius $r$ such that its centripetal acceleration $a_c$ is varying with time $t$ as, $a_c = k^2 r t^2$. The power delivered to the particle by the forces acting on it is ($K$ = constant)
questions.solution:
Given centripetal acceleration $a_c = k^2 r t^2$

Using the formula $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$:

$\dfrac{v^2}{r} = k^2 r t^2$

$v^2 = k^2 r^2 t^2$

$v = k r t$

The kinetic energy of the particle is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} m (k r t)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m k^2 r^2 t^2$

The total power delivered by all forces acting on the particle is equal to the rate of change of its kinetic energy:

$P = \dfrac{dE}{dt}$

$P = \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} m k^2 r^2 t^2 \right)$

$P = \dfrac{1}{2} m k^2 r^2 (2t)$

$P = m k^2 r^2 t$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two girls are standing at the ends 'A' and 'B' of a ground where $A B=b$. The girl at ' $B$ ' starts running in a direction perpendicular to ' AB ' with velocity ' $\mathrm{V}_1$ '. The girl at 'A' starts running simultaneously with velocity ' $\mathrm{V}_2$ ' and in shortest distance meets the other girl in time ' t '. The value of ' $t$ ' is
questions.solution:
Establish a coordinate system where girl A starts at $(0,0)$ and girl B at $(b,0)$. Girl B runs perpendicular to AB with velocity $V_1$, placing her position at time $t$ at $(b, V_1 t)$.

Girl A runs directly toward this meeting point with velocity $V_2$. The distance traveled by A is the straight-line distance between initial positions, given by the Pythagorean theorem:

$(V_2 t)^2 = b^2 + (V_1 t)^2$

Solving for $t$:

$V_2^2 t^2 - V_1^2 t^2 = b^2$
$t^2 (V_2^2 - V_1^2) = b^2$
$t = \frac{b}{\sqrt{V_2^2 - V_1^2}}$

This solution requires $V_2 \gt V_1$ for real $t$. The expression matches option D.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two boys are standing at points $A$ and $B$ on ground, where distance $A B=x$. The boy at $B$ stars running perpendicular to $A B$ with velocity $V_1$. The boy at A starts running simultaneously with velocity v and meets the other boy in time $t$. The value of $t$ is
questions.solution:
Let the initial position of boy A be the origin $(0,0)$ and boy B be at $(x,0)$, with boy B running perpendicular to AB with velocity $V_1$.

At time $t$, boy B's position is given by $(x, V_1 t)$, while boy A's position is $(v_x t, v_y t)$.

For the boys to meet, their positions must be equal: $(v_x t, v_y t) = (x, V_1 t)$, yielding $v_x = x/t$ and $v_y = V_1$.

The magnitude constraint $v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2$ becomes $v^2 = (x/t)^2 + V_1^2$.

Solving for $t$ gives $t^2 = x^2/(v^2 - V_1^2)$, requiring $v \gt V_1$ for real values.

The expression matches option C.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body when projected at an angle ' $\theta$ ' with the horizontal reaches a maximum height ' H '. The time of flight of the body will be ( $g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Time of flight in terms of maximum height

The maximum height $H$ and time of flight $T$ for a projectile with initial velocity $u$ at angle $\theta$ are given by:

$H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

$T = \frac{2u \sin\theta}{g}$

From the height equation, $u^2 \sin^2\theta = 2gH$, so $u \sin\theta = \sqrt{2gH}$.

Substituting into the time equation yields:

$T = \frac{2}{g} \cdot \sqrt{2gH} = 2\sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}$

This corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inextensible string of length ' $\ell$ ' fixed at one end, carries a mass ' m ' at the other end. If the string makes $\frac{1}{\pi}$ revolutions per second around the vertical axis through the fixed end, the tension in the string is [The string makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical]
questions.solution:
Conical pendulum analysis

The mass experiences tension $T$ along the string and gravitational force $mg$ downward.
Resolving tension into components: vertical component $T \cos\theta$ balances gravity, giving $T \cos\theta = mg$.

The horizontal component $T \sin\theta$ provides centripetal force for circular motion with radius $r = l \sin\theta$.

Given frequency $f = \frac{1}{\pi}$, angular frequency becomes $\omega = 2\pi f = 2$ rad/s.
Centripetal force is $F_c = m\omega^2 r = m(2)^2(l \sin\theta) = 4ml \sin\theta$.

Equating horizontal forces: $T \sin\theta = 4ml \sin\theta$.
Since $\sin\theta \neq 0$, dividing yields $T = 4ml$.

$\boxed{4ml}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two stones of masses m and 3 m are whirled in horizontal circles, the heavier one in a radius $\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}}{3}\right)$ and lighter one in a radius r . The tangential speed of lighter stone is ' $n$ ' times the value of heavier stone. When the magnitude of centripetal force becomes equal the value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
The centripetal forces are equal: $F_L = F_H$. For stones with masses $m_L = m$, $m_H = 3m$ and radii $r_L = r$, $r_H = \frac{r}{3}$, with tangential speeds related by $v_L = n v_H$, the force equality becomes:

$\frac{m (n v_H)^2}{r} = \frac{3m v_H^2}{r/3}$

Simplifying both sides yields:

$\frac{m n^2 v_H^2}{r} = \frac{9m v_H^2}{r}$

Canceling common factors ($m$, $v_H^2$, and $r$) from both sides gives $n^2 = 9$, so $n = 3$.

Answer: $\boxed{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vehicle is moving with a constant speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ in a circular horizontal track of radius 20 m . A bob is suspended from the roof of a vehicle by a massless string. The angle made by the string with the vertical will be (acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
A vehicle moving at constant speed in a circular horizontal track establishes a centripetal acceleration, causing the suspended bob to make an angle $\theta$ with the vertical. The bob's mass is $m$ and the tension in the string is $T$.

For vertical equilibrium, the vertical component of tension balances the gravitational force: $T \cos\theta = mg$.

The horizontal component provides the centripetal force for circular motion: $T \sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}$.

Dividing the horizontal equation by the vertical equation eliminates $T$ and $m$: $\frac{T \sin\theta}{T \cos\theta} = \frac{mv^2/r}{mg}$, which simplifies to $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$.

Substituting the given values $v = 10\,\text{m/s}$, $r = 20\,\text{m}$, and $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ yields $\tan\theta = \frac{10^2}{20 \times 10} = 0.5$.

Therefore $\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.5)$, and the correct option is A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a particle moving in a circle with constant angular speed, which of the following statements is 'false'?
options: The velocity vector is tangent to the circle.
The acceleration vector is tangent to the circle.
The velocity and acceleration vectors are perpendicular to each other:
The acceleration vector points to the centre of the circle.
questions.solution:
A: The velocity vector is tangent to the circle in all curvilinear motion, including circular motion. This holds for uniform circular motion.

B: The acceleration vector points radially inward as centripetal acceleration, not tangent to the circle. Only a tangential acceleration component would exist if angular speed were changing, which it is not.

C: Since velocity is tangent and acceleration is radial, they are perpendicular at every point.

D: Uniform circular motion produces purely centripetal acceleration directed toward the circle's center.

Statement B is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle performing uniform circular motion of radius $\frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{~m}$ makes x revolutions in time $t$. Its tangential velocity is
questions.solution:
Tangential velocity is determined by the ratio of total distance to total time. The circumference is $C = 2\pi R$, and with $R = \frac{\pi}{2}$ m, $C = 2\pi \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi^2$ m.

For $x$ revolutions, the total distance is $S = x\pi^2$ m. Tangential velocity is then $v = \frac{S}{t} = \frac{x\pi^2}{t}$, which corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin uniform rod $A B$ of mass ' $\mathrm{m}$ ' and length ' $l$ ' is hinged at one end A to the ground level. Initially the rod stands vertically and is allowed to fall freely to the ground in the vertical plane. We know,
Loss in P.E = Gain in rotational K.E.
When the centre of mass of the rod falls through a distance $\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$,
Loss in P.E $=m g \frac{L}{2}$  ...(i)
and,
Gain in Rotational K.E $=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\mathrm{ML}^2}{3}\right] \omega^2$  ...(ii)
Equating (i) and (ii)

\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{MgL}}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{ML}^2}{3} \omega^2 \\
& \omega^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{~g}}{\mathrm{~L}} \\
& \omega=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{~g}}{\mathrm{~L}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{~g}}{l}} \quad \ldots(\because \text { here } \mathrm{L}=l)
\end{aligned}

$\ldots(\because$ here $\mathrm{L}=l)$
